At Ukraine’s National Prayer Breakfast, Faith Meets the Reality of War
Religious leaders, military chaplains, journalists, diplomats, and international supporters gathered in Kyiv to pray for Ukraine—and to reflect on what faith, justice, and solidarity mean more than four years into Russia’s full-scale war.
On the eve of Ukraine’s 35th Independence Day, religious leaders, military personnel, chaplains, government officials, and international guests gathered in Kyiv for the National Prayer Breakfast of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Held under the patronage of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the annual interfaith gathering is intended as a space for prayer and dialogue around peace, unity, justice, freedom, and responsibility. This year also carries particular symbolism: Ukraine is marking 35 years of independence and the collapse of the Soviet system, which for decades imposed state atheism and persecuted religious communities.
Former US Vice President Mike Pence and retired Lieutenant General Keith Kellogg were among the international guests attending this year’s gathering.
But amid Russia’s continuing war, the conversations extended far beyond religion in the abstract. Speakers and guests reflected on life under missile and drone attacks, religious persecution in Russian-occupied territories, the meaning of a just peace, and the role faith plays for those living through war firsthand.
UNITED24 Media attended the National Prayer Breakfast and spoke with participants about why they came—and what they were praying for.
“This atmosphere is a phenomenon”
For Murat Suleimanov, Mufti of the Spiritual Administration of Muslims of Ukraine “Umma,” the significance of the gathering lay in the diversity of the people in the room.
Ukraine’s ability to bring different faiths together, he said, has itself become a source of strength during the war.
Ukraine has united representatives of different ethnicities and faiths. That is our strength. If we know how to reach agreement and help one another, no enemy will be able to defeat us.
Murat Suleimanov
Mufti of the Spiritual Administration of Muslims of Ukraine “Umma”
Suleimanov said the cooperation he sees among Ukraine’s religious communities continues to surprise colleagues abroad.
This atmosphere is a phenomenon. You have a priest, a mufti, a rabbi, and others together, working for peace and for Ukraine’s victory.
Murat Suleimanov
Mufti of the Spiritual Administration of Muslims of Ukraine “Umma”
Faith, he added, has also shaped his own response to the war—not as a reason to withdraw from events around him, but as an impetus to act.
Now there are so many trials. Faith helps me not to sit and complain, but to do even more good.
Murat Suleimanov
Mufti of the Spiritual Administration of Muslims of Ukraine “Umma”
“I believe in God more there than I do here”
For Yakov Syniakov, head of the chaplaincy service of the 7th Rapid Response Corps of Ukraine’s Air Assault Forces, questions of faith are inseparable from the battlefield.
Syniakov is the first and currently only Jewish military chaplain serving as an officer in the Armed Forces of Ukraine. He described religious differences as secondary to the values that hold a society together.
We have to find the things that unite us, not divide us. Whether someone belongs to a Christian denomination, is Jewish, Hindu, Buddhist—it does not change the fact that they should be a good person.
Yakov Syniakov
Head of the chaplaincy service of the 7th Rapid Response Corps of Ukraine’s Air Assault Forces
His most personal answer came when he was asked whether faith had helped him overcome difficult times in his life.
I’m a military chaplain. I’m a combat veteran. I’m not on the front line now, but I’m close. We run from drones, from everything flying at us. Maybe it sounds like a joke, but I believe in God more there than I do here.
Yakov Syniakov
Head of the chaplaincy service of the 7th Rapid Response Corps of Ukraine’s Air Assault Forces
Syniakov has experienced war at its most intimate.
Explosions have gone off near me. I’ve saved people. People have died in my arms. I cried like a child. There’s nothing wrong with that. If I didn’t have faith, I wouldn’t know how to go on.
Yakov Syniakov
Head of the chaplaincy service of the 7th Rapid Response Corps of Ukraine’s Air Assault Forces
“I thought I would be writing about rebuilding”
The gathering also brought international visitors to Kyiv at a moment when Russia continues its large-scale attacks on Ukrainian cities.
Jill Nelson, Christianity Today’s Ukraine and Israel correspondent, has covered Ukraine since 2014.
For her, returning to Kyiv meant confronting the distance between what she once expected Ukraine’s future to look like and where the country finds itself in 2026.
I did not think that in 2026 I would be continuing to cover a full-scale invasion that’s four and a half years in. I thought that I would be covering stories of rebuilding, stories of rehabilitation, and instead we’re at the place we’re at right now.
Jill Nelson
Christianity Today’s Ukraine and Israel correspondent
Nelson described a Kyiv where ordinary life and the reality of war exist side by side: crowded parks and restaurants, weddings and children alongside nightly air raid alerts and fear of Russian strikes.
There’s both resilience here, but there is a need to protect the people of Ukraine, and I would love for the world to see and understand that.
Jill Nelson
Christianity Today’s Ukraine and Israel correspondent
Asked what she was praying for, Nelson’s answer was also practical.
I am praying that Ukraine receives the Patriot interceptors that it needs to protect its population. I’m praying for a just end to this war—one that takes into consideration the long-term security needs of this country.
Jill Nelson
Christianity Today’s Ukraine and Israel correspondent
Faith under Russian occupation
For Steven Moore, founder of the Ukraine Freedom Project and a former Republican congressional chief of staff, the event also offered an opportunity to challenge the image Russia projects to religious conservatives abroad.
Putin will tell you that he’s a great Christian. Putin will lead you to believe that he is a defender of Christendom and a very holy man, and it’s utter nonsense.
Steven Moore
Founder of the Ukraine Freedom Project
Moore argued that international Christians should see for themselves what Russia’s war has meant for religious communities in Ukraine.
That broader pattern has been documented by the US Commission on International Religious Freedom, which says Russian authorities in occupied Ukrainian territories have banned religious groups, seized places of worship, detained religious leaders and imposed Russia’s restrictive religious laws.
USCIRF’s 2026 annual report said at least 47 Christian religious leaders had been killed and at least 700 houses of worship and other religious sites damaged or destroyed since the full-scale invasion.
For Moore, that makes religious freedom part of what is at stake in the war.
Ukraine is fighting for freedom. Ukraine is fighting for its life.
Steven Moore
Founder of the Ukraine Freedom Project
Praying for a peace that is “secure” and “stable”
John Herbst, senior director of the Atlantic Council’s Eurasia Center and a former US ambassador to Ukraine, described the breakfast itself as an expression of Ukraine’s religious pluralism.
It demonstrates the tolerance of Ukrainian society. It’s all religions.
John Herbst
Senior director of the Atlantic Council’s Eurasia Center
But when asked what he was praying for, Herbst returned to the question hanging over nearly every discussion about Ukraine: what peace would actually mean.
I pray for an independent, strong, secure Ukraine, and I look forward to the day that Moscow ends its aggression in Ukraine and a secure peace, a stable peace, is established.
John Herbst
Senior director of the Atlantic Council’s Eurasia Center
Herbst said that achieving it would require greater material support from Ukraine’s partners, particularly air defense.
There are not enough supplies of anti-ballistic missile batteries and interceptors, and the US needs to produce a lot more.
John Herbst
Senior director of the Atlantic Council’s Eurasia Center
“Prayer is important, action is important”
Ken Isaacs, vice president of programs and government relations at the Christian humanitarian organization Samaritan’s Purse, first came to Ukraine on February 24, 2022, and spent much of the following year in the country.
He said returning for the National Prayer Breakfast was partly about maintaining international attention on a war that has become easier for those outside Ukraine to look away from.
Ukraine needs to have greater visibility in the world. What’s going on here? What is continuing to go on here? Ukraine is on a front line, and in many ways it’s a front line for Europe.
Ken Isaacs
Vice President of Programs and Government Relations at the Christian humanitarian organization Samaritan’s Purse
For Isaacs, the language of peace does not mean denying Ukraine the right to defend itself.
As Christians, we’re called to justice. We’re called to peace. But that doesn’t mean that you don’t push back, you don’t fight back, you don’t protect yourself, you don’t defend yourself.
Ken Isaacs
Vice President of Programs and Government Relations at the Christian humanitarian organization Samaritan’s Purse
And while hundreds gathered in Kyiv to pray, he said faith cannot end there.
I think prayer is important, but I also think action is important.
Ken Isaacs
Vice President of Programs and Government Relations at the Christian humanitarian organization Samaritan’s Purse
For those gathered in Kyiv, prayer was not an escape from the reality of war, but another way of confronting it.
If I didn’t have faith, I wouldn’t know how to go on.
Yakov Syniakov
Head of the chaplaincy service of the 7th Rapid Response Corps of Ukraine’s Air Assault Forces

Ukraine Sets Out Its Vision for Life After Service at the 9th International Veterans Forum
Ukrainian officials outlined plans to overhaul veteran legislation, expand digital services and employment programs, and strengthen rehabilitation and family support as the country prepares for a veteran population expected to exceed 3 million after the war.
Ukrainian officials, military representatives, and international partners gathered in Kyiv for the 9th International Veterans Forum “Honoring Resilience,” held on the eve of Ukraine’s Independence Day.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Participants included President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi, Veterans Affairs Minister Vitalii Kim, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, and retired US General Keith Kellogg.
UNITED24 Media attended the forum. Here are the key takeaways.
Zelenskyy calls for an overhaul of veteran legislation
Opening the forum, Zelenskyy called for Ukraine to rethink how the state supports veterans, arguing that existing legislation too often treats them simply as another category of benefit recipients.
“Our respect for veterans must be reflected in the concrete, systemic work of state institutions and communities,” Zelenskyy said.
He proposed consolidating veteran-related legislation into a single “Veteran Code” and said veterans’ families, as well as the families of fallen service members, prisoners of war, and those missing in action, should be fully included in state veteran policy.
Ukraine currently has more than 1.5 million veterans, with that number expected to exceed 3 million after the war.
President Zelenskyy also highlighted the recently adopted legislation establishing the Ukrainian Pantheon, intended to preserve the memory of prominent historical figures and Ukrainians who defended the country.
During the forum, he presented state honors to veterans and combat medics, including border officer Natalia Izhychyna, doctor Mariia Korinna, and volunteer hospital administrator Yulia Serhiimikhailova.
Government pushes digital services and common standards
Verkhovna Rada Chairman Ruslan Stefanchuk said parliament had recently advanced legislation expanding medical care, prosthetics funding, and professional retraining for veterans and Ukrainians released from Russian captivity.
Stefanchuk said parliament is also considering three additional bills developed in cooperation with the veteran community.
Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said reducing bureaucracy would be a central part of the government’s approach.
“A veteran must never be a courier carrying paper documents between government offices,” Koretskyi said.
He pointed to the VeteranPro platform, which he said brings together nearly 3,000 services and has already supported more than 350,000 users.
By 2027, the government aims to bring more than half of veteran services under unified standards and ensure that at least 80% of Ukrainian communities have clearly structured support systems.
Koretskyi also said the government plans to establish 20 new state-run veteran spaces and has launched educational support programs covering more than 11,000 children of Ukrainian service members.
Support from military service through civilian life
Veterans Affairs Minister Vitalii Kim outlined five priorities for the government’s veteran policy, beginning with support before a service member formally becomes a veteran.
Kim argued that assistance should begin during military service and continue through the transition to civilian life rather than starting only after discharge.
“A person cannot finish their service and immediately lose their support system,” he said.
He also called for the state to be more proactive in serving veterans, rather than forcing them to navigate multiple agencies and hotlines.
“The state should call the veteran first. And its very first words must be: ‘Thank you for your service. How can I help you?’”
Kim said this approach should extend to how Ukraine commemorates those killed in the war, including common standards for military cemeteries and memorial sectors.
The ministry is also expanding digital access to veteran documentation and services through the Diia app and administrative service centers, with support from Ukraine’s Ministry of Digital Transformation.
Families should increasingly be able to prepare and submit documents digitally rather than repeatedly visiting government offices, Kim said.
Another priority is family support. Kim said Ukraine is testing programs in which psychologists work with military couples together as they adjust to life during and after service.
The broader objective, he said, is to ensure veteran status provides access to new opportunities rather than creating what he described as a “permanent status of social dependency.”
Ukraine wants to share veterans’ battlefield expertise with Europe
Kim also argued that veteran policy should not focus exclusively on what Ukraine can learn from its international partners.
After years of full-scale war, Ukrainian veterans now possess battlefield experience that European countries increasingly need, particularly in drone warfare and military technology, he said.
“Our veterans’ unmatched combat management and battlefield drone expertise is the best in the world, and there is a massive European demand for these military technologies,” Kim said.
That theme continued during a panel moderated by Ukrainian MP Lesya Zaburanna.
Zaburanna said the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe is expected to consider a resolution on European veteran policy in October 2026, which she described as the first such initiative introduced in 17 years.
Oleksandr Tarasenko, deputy commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, said years of high-intensity warfare have given Ukrainian troops the ability to quickly assess which technologies work under real battlefield conditions.
“Our soldiers have a unique capability born from years of high-intensity, regular warfare against a massive state aggressor,” Tarasenko said.
That experience, he added, is already being shared with Ukraine’s partners through joint exercises and military networks.
Masi Nayyem, co-founder of the military human rights center Pryntsyp, stressed that veterans should be viewed as a national resource rather than a burden, while warning against overlooking their rehabilitation needs.
Because many demobilized Ukrainians remain in the operational reserve and may return to military service, Nayyem said the distinction between an active-service member and a veteran can be particularly fluid during a prolonged war.
Physical and psychological rehabilitation, therefore, has to remain at the center of long-term veteran policy, he argued.
Government targets 100,000 jobs for veterans
Employment was another major focus of the forum.
Koretskyi said the government is working toward creating 100,000 additional jobs for veterans, involving state-owned companies, private employers, and government institutions.
He cited his previous experience at Naftogaz, where the return of around 5,000 veterans required the company itself to adapt.
“The company and its entire 100,000-strong collective had to adapt to the veterans, not the other way around,” Koretskyi said.
He also invited the veteran community to nominate a representative to serve as his permanent adviser, saying that government policy must be based “on reality, not theory.”
Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal said Ukraine’s energy sector could become a major source of employment for veterans.
According to Shmyhal, the sector is opening around 6,000 positions across state-owned and private energy companies, creating dedicated roles in engineering, technical security, and testing programs intended to streamline veteran recruitment.
Germany announces additional veteran support
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said a Ukrainian flag given to him by commanders of Ukraine’s 1st Separate Assault Regiment hangs opposite his desk in Berlin.
“Before Russia’s war of aggression, these men were not soldiers. One was a student, one a family doctor, one a social worker, one a historian,” Wadephul said. “They did not choose this war ... yet they chose to defend their country.”
Wadephul announced an additional €3 million in German funding for veteran support and community hubs in Ukraine.
He said veterans would play an important role in Ukraine’s democratic resilience and should have opportunities to shape the country’s future after the war.
Retired US General Keith Kellogg also spoke about a recent visit to the Superhumans rehabilitation center in Odesa, where he met Ukrainian service members recovering from amputations.
“I saw amputees learning how to adapt to their injuries,” Kellogg said, adding that many told him they hoped to return to military service.
“This is the reason why your veterans are winning this war. No one can defeat the heart and love of their country like these heroes.”

Russian military reveals man-portable laser gun (VIDEO)
The Russian military has showcased a new man-portable laser system designed to safely disable mines and unexploded ordnance from up to 100 meters away.
The gun featured in a report by the military’s official media outlet, Zvezda TV, on Sunday is derived from a larger system designed for remotely controlled small ground vehicles. The channel demonstrated both variants alongside other modules intended for the tracked Kurier (“courier”) platform, which is being widely adopted by the Russian military.
The smaller gun is powered by a backpack-style battery pack and features a 1-kilowatt laser. Its beam is strong enough to burn through a plastic casing within seconds, provided the operator maintains a steady aim. The video showed that the best results are achieved when the weapon is mounted on a tripod.
The larger variant has twice the power and places the projector on a retractable lifting platform, allowing the laser to be fired from behind cover. Its greater stability and beam strength give it a range of up to 500 meters, according to the developer. Both the rover-mounted module and the man-portable gun have entered serial production.
A laser bomb-disposal system works by igniting the high explosives inside the targeted munition and burning them without causing a detonation. Operating from a distance is necessary in high-risk environments and helps reduce the danger posed by booby traps equipped with advanced sensors that may be triggered when a bomb-disposal specialist or conventional robot approaches.
The Zvezda report also demonstrated other modules developed for the Kurier platform, including some designed by a frontline engineering unit involved in the Ukraine conflict. One of its creations is fitted with a drill and is used to prepare holes for poles before anti-drone nets are installed over roads in the battle zone.
Both Russia and Ukraine are developing new uses for remotely operated vehicles, which are increasingly being deployed for combat, resupply, medical evacuation, and military engineering missions.

South Korea says US cut joint marine drill over Iran war constraints
The cancellation follows US President Donald Trump’s order last week to scale down the separate annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises
South Korea said on Monday that the United States had cancelled a large joint amphibious landing exercise scheduled for next month due to constraints on force availability caused by the war with Iran.
The biennial Ssangyong drills involve marine forces from South Korea and the US and are designed to strengthen combined operations, typically involving warships, aircraft and ground forces rehearsing amphibious landings.
The cancellation follows US President Donald Trump’s order last week to scale down the separate annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises, cutting the joint drills from 11 days to five.
Trump at the time cited their high cost and said they sent an “inappropriate and hostile” signal to North Korea, while highlighting his relationship with its leader, Kim Jong-un.
“The US Marine Corps formally notified our forces in June that its ability to deploy forces during this year’s Ssangyong exercise would be constrained due to the situation in the Middle East,” Han Seung-jeon, a spokesman for the South Korean Marine Corps, told reporters at a news briefing.
Seoul and Washington were continuing consultations on resuming the amphibious exercise, he said, without giving details.

Riga and Vilnius outpace Tallinn in flights due to market size
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Riga and Vilnius outpace Tallinn in flights due to market size
Although Tallinn has fewer direct destinations, Tallinn Airport is still the largest airport in the Baltics in terms of revenue, surpassing both Latvia and Lithuania, says airport chief Riivo Tuvike. Last year Tallinn Airport's revenue was 74 million euros.
This success comes from the fact that Tallinn Airport does not rely solely on aviation fees, which make up only about 30% of its income. The company actively earns revenue from terminal retail, parking, aircraft maintenance hangars and commercial real estate in Airport City.
Tallinn Airport has also experienced a historic surge in passenger numbers this summer, driven by expanding flight options and more affordable ticket prices.
The airport shattered its all-time passenger records during June and July. Tuvike noted that in July, the airport welcomed 384,000 passengers, representing a 19 percent increase compared to the previous year. The appetite for travel has not disappeared since the pandemic, and that higher local wealth combined with lower prices has fueled this growth.
Looking at history, in 1991 Tallinn Airport had 758,000 passengers, but the following year, 1992, only about 205,000, so there was a large drop. "Looking at the current year, we believe we will reach 3.7–3.8 million passengers, which is quite a noticeable increase," Tuvike said.
The long-term goal is serving five million travelers annually by 2030.
Passenger volume dictates the decisions
When asked why the airport does not aggressively lower its fees to attract even more airlines, Tuvike points out that market demand and passenger volume — not just cheap airport fees — ultimately dictate an airline's route decisions.
"We could lower the fees even to zero, but if there are no passengers, the airlines will not open those routes," Tuvike said.
"Perhaps our concern in Tallinn is that the region we are able to serve is only about one million passengers. In the end, the number of potential passengers dictates how many possible direct routes there can be," he noted.
Despite the current positive passenger trends, the regional aviation market faces challenges, particularly concerning the financial health of Latvian carrier airBaltic. AirBaltic remains Estonia's most important airline and operates as a home carrier, but Tuvike believes the Estonian government should not buy a stake in the struggling airline.
The entire Baltic region is a very small area in a global scale, Tuvike said. He added that operating a profitable airline in such a limited market is extremely difficult and suggested there are more reasonable areas for state investment.
The airport chief reassured travelers that even if airBaltic were to exit the market, Estonia's flight connections would not collapse. He explained that Tallinn has actively diversified its airline portfolio, such as by facilitating the expansion of low-cost carrier Wizz Air, to ensure that routes can be replaced if necessary.
The rapid growth in passenger traffic has placed significant strain on the existing airport infrastructure. The current terminal was designed to handle up to three million passengers, meaning the current volume is already causing operational friction, including baggage wait times that can reach an hour.
Major expansion of the Tallinn airport ongoing
To address these bottlenecks, the airport is planning a major physical expansion. Tuvike said that while new check-in kiosks have already been installed, the main construction work is scheduled to begin early next year. The project aims to expand the passenger terminal by 50 percent by the first half of 2029, with a specific focus on enlarging the overcrowded baggage claim and border control areas.
Regarding flight destinations, Tuvike emphasized that major hubs remain the most critical connections for Estonian travelers because they open access to the rest of the world. Currently, Warsaw has emerged as the number one destination, with Frankfurt, Riga, and Helsinki also making up the majority of flights.
Tuvike mentioned that while direct flights largely dictate where Estonians go on vacation, his future target destinations for direct flights from Tallinn include London Heathrow and Madrid.
"London Heathrow is definitely a place where we really want to go, because there are so many flight opportunities and it contributes strongly to Estonia's connection," Tuvike said.
Tuvike also addressed the future of Estonia's regional airports, noting that while airports on the country's islands are fully justified due to the lack of fast land transport, the future of mainland facilities like Pärnu Airport is less certain. He pointed out that once the Rail Baltica railway is completed, Pärnu will be just a 45-minute journey from Tallinn, making the local airport's role highly questionable.
--

WSJ: Russian military held drills to prepare for mobilization
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
12:23:09 UTC
21:23:09 KST

Military exercises rehearsing mobilization procedures were held in Russia’s Kaliningrad region in July, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing Western intelligence officials.
According to the newspaper’s sources, the drills tested the military’s readiness to carry out mobilization measures in the region, including its ability to house mobilized personnel and supply them with provisions and weapons.
Western intelligence officials said similar exercises are being held in other Russian regions as well, though they did not specify where.
The drills are specifically meant to prepare for a possible new wave of mobilization, the newspaper’s sources said, though no such decision has been made yet. Mobilization is unlikely to be announced before the September parliamentary elections, they added.
Experts interviewed by the newspaper said it is unclear what practical effect a fall mobilization announcement would have, since fighting typically slows in winter due to difficult weather conditions. But military analyst Michael Kofman said a new wave of mobilization could affect the situation at the front as early as 2027.
Sources have told Meduza and other outlets since late June that a new wave of mobilization is possible. The most common theory holds that mobilization could be announced after the September elections.
Russian authorities officially deny any plans for a new wave of mobilization. They did the same before announcing mobilization in September 2022, and no official decree has ever ended it.
Amid rumors of a new mobilization wave in August, the human rights organization Kovcheg recorded a sharp rise in inquiries about emigrating from Russia.

Yordan Alvarez’s Triple Crown bid will have to survive a major challenge from the AL East
As the season winds down, Houston slugger Yordan Alvarez will have to worry about two sets of spoilers.
The first is the more traditional type — teams that will try to beat the Astros in key games and deny them a spot in the postseason.
The other includes individual spoilers — players who could prevent Alvarez from making history as baseball’s next Triple Crown winner.
Alvarez currently leads the American League with a .320 average, 36 home runs and 90 RBIs. If he holds onto the top spot in all three categories, he’d be the first batter to win the Triple Crown since Miguel Cabrera in 2012. The biggest threats Alvarez faces all come from the AL East.
The next-highest batting averages in the AL both belong to Tampa Bay players — Chandler Simpson at .310 and Yandy Díaz at .306. Fortunately for Alvarez, there aren’t any stealth candidates — players with high averages who don’t currently have enough plate appearances to qualify, but would by the end of the season.
The home run race is currently the tightest, with Tampa Bay’s Junior Caminero just one behind with 35. Ben Rice of the New York Yankees has 34. There are times when Alvarez seems like Houston’s only major threat offensively, and he’s been intentionally walked 28 times — way more than Caminero (10) and Rice (four). Those lost opportunities could matter in a close race.
Alvarez’s closest competition in RBIs is Baltimore’s Pete Alonso, who has 85. Alonso recently went on a 14-game hitting streak. Caminero is also in the mix with 83 RBIs.
When Cabrera pulled off the Triple Crown in 2012, he had to hold off Hall of Famers Joe Mauer and Adrian Beltre in batting average, as well as likely Hall of Famer Mike Trout. He finished one homer ahead of Josh Hamilton and Curtis Granderson.
Trivia time
Alvarez broke Jeff Bagwell’s franchise record for intentional walks in a season. Bagwell drew 27 in 1997. Who is in third place on that list for Houston?
Performance of the week
Pete Crow-Armstrong hit a leadoff homer in the bottom of the first and a walk-off shot in the 10th to give the Chicago Cubs a 7-5 win over the White Sox on Monday night.
The Cubs then won in walk-off fashion again a night later against the White Sox, but were beaten via the walk-off twice in a row by Seattle later in the week. The Cubs have 13 walk-off wins this year, the most in baseball, but the White Sox and Mariners aren’t far behind with 11.
Comeback of the week
Philadelphia was down 4-0 with two outs in the bottom of the ninth Sunday before rallying for a 6-4 victory over St. Louis. Edmundo Sosa hit a three-run double, and Bryan De La Cruz hit a single that tied the game. Then Kyle Schwarber won it with his major league-leading 39th homer of the season.
It was the ninth straight victory for the Phillies, who now trail first-place Atlanta by only three games in the NL East. The Braves were 9 1/2 games up less than two weeks ago.
It’s been a bizarre season for Philadelphia, which was 8-18 by late April, then went 48-27, then lost eight of its last games in July before going 16-5 so far in August.
Team of the week
Kansas City was the lone team to go 7-0 over the past week, although the Phillies and Los Angeles Dodgers both went 6-0. The Royals took advantage of four games against the dreadful Athletics before sweeping three in a row from a Detroit team that’s chasing a playoff berth.
Last-place Kansas City is actually 36-30 at home this year but has gone 22-44 on the road.
Trivia answer
Rusty Staub drew 24 intentional walks for the Astros in 1968.

JOHANNESBURG (AP) — Four suspects in the killing of former world champion boxer Zolani Tete were arrested, South African police said Monday.
Tete was in his car outside his home last week when men wearing balaclavas opened fire, police said. A woman who was in the vehicle was injured and has since been hospitalized.
The shooting took place at Mdantsane, Eastern Cape, according to the police. Tete was arriving at his residence and waiting for the gate to open when he was ambushed by two armed suspects.
Police said one of the suspects arrested two days ago was expected to appear in court on Monday, while the other three would appear on a later date.
Tete held the World Boxing Federation flyweight title from 2007 to 2008 and the World Boxing Organization bantamweight title in 2017 and 2019.

AP Decision Notes: What to expect in Georgia’s special congressional runoff
WASHINGTON (AP) — Residents of Georgia’s 13th Congressional District outside of Atlanta will get a new representative to Congress after a special election runoff Tuesday to replace the late Democratic U.S. Rep. David Scott, who died April 22.
The contest between two Democrats will further reduce an already thin Republican majority in the U.S. House.
The finalists for the seat are former Gwinnett County School Board Chair Everton Blair and Marcye Scott, daughter of the late congressman. They were the top two vote-getters among five contenders in the July 28 all-party special election. Scott received about 46% of the vote, compared to about 38% for Blair.
The winner will serve out the remaining few months of David Scott’s final term. Neither candidate is running in for the next full term in this seat, which begins on Jan. 3, 2027.
Blair was the only candidate in the special election who also ran for the full-term seat. He placed third in the May 19 Democratic primary with about 12% of the vote. State Rep. Jasmine Clark won the primary with 56% of the vote and will face Republican Jonathan Chavez in November. Chavez, who ran unopposed for the GOP nomination, challenged David Scott in the 2024 general election and received about 28% of the vote.
Clark did not file to compete in the special election. Doing so would have required her to resign from her seat in the state Legislature just as Republican Gov. Brian Kemp was calling for a special session to redraw the state’s congressional boundaries in time for the 2028 elections. The state constitution bars state officeholders from seeking a different office with a start date more than 30 days before the end of the officeholder’s current term. The special session did convene, but Republican leaders opted not to take up redistricting.
In recent years, Congressman Scott had faced questions over his age and health. At the time of his death at age 80, he was facing a tough primary challenge from Clark and others as he sought a 13th term.
Georgia’s 13th Congressional District is east and southeast of Atlanta and includes parts of six heavily Democratic counties: Clayton, DeKalb, Gwinnett, Henry, Newton and Rockdale. Of the six, the district’s portion of Gwinnett County has the lion’s share of voters, with about 46% of the district electorate in the 2024 general election.
Blair’s best performance in the July 28 special election was in his home base of Gwinnett County, where he received 56% of the vote. Marcye Scott, who lives outside the district in Fulton County as her father did, carried the other five counties in the district, scoring her highest totals in DeKalb, Clayton and Henry.
David Scott won his 2024 reelection bid with about 72% of the vote. In the presidential election that night, Democratic then-Vice President Kamala Harris received about 71% of the vote in the district, compared with about 28% for Republican Donald Trump. Trump had his best performance in the district in Gwinnett County, although that still only amounted to about 35% of the vote.
Here are some of the key facts about the election and data points the AP Decision Team will monitor as the votes are tallied:
When do polls close?
Polls close at 7 p.m. ET.
What’s on the ballot?
The Associated Press will provide vote results and declare a winner in the special runoff in the 13th Congressional District.
Who gets to vote?
Any voter registered in the 13th Congressional District may participate in the special runoff.
How many voters are there?
As of Friday, there were about 585,000 registered voters in the 13th Congressional District. Georgia voters do not register by party.
How many people actually vote?
A total of 20,510 votes were cast in the July 28 special election. Turnout in a runoff election tends to be lower than in the election that preceded it.
How much of the vote is cast early or by absentee ballot?
About 47% of the total vote in the July 28 special election was cast early in-person or by mail.
As of Friday, about 5,200 ballots had already been cast in Tuesday’s election, with by far the largest share coming from Gwinnett County, followed by Clayton and Rockdale counties.
When are early and absentee votes released?
All six counties in the 13th Congressional District tend to release most or all of their results from early in-person and mail voting in the first vote update of the night, usually before any in-person Election Day results are released.
How long does vote-counting usually take?
In the July 28 special election, the AP first reported results at 7:05 p.m. ET, or five minutes after polls closed. The last vote update of the night was at 10:05 p.m. ET with about 99.9% of total votes counted.
When will the AP declare a winner?
The AP does not make projections and will declare a winner only when it’s determined there is no scenario that would allow a trailing candidate to close the gap. If a race has not been called, the AP will continue to cover any newsworthy developments, such as candidate concessions or declarations of victory. In doing so, the AP will make clear that it has not yet declared a winner and explain why.
How do recounts work?
There is no automatic recount provision in Georgia, but a losing candidate may request a recount if the margin is less than or equal to 0.5% of the total vote. The AP may declare a winner in a race that is subject to a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.
Are we there yet?
As of Tuesday, there will be 70 days until the 2026 midterm elections.

US strikes another boat in eastern Pacific, killing two, Pentagon says
U.S. forces have struck another vessel in the eastern Pacific, killing two people the Pentagon says were trafficking drugs.
The U.S. Southern Command announced the strike in a social media post early Monday. The death toll from the Trump administration’s campaign of bombing boats off Latin America’s Caribbean coast and in the eastern Pacific now exceeds 210 after more than 60 strikes.
The Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere “executed a lethal kinetic strike on a low-profile vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Eastern Pacific.” Intelligence confirmed the vessel was carrying illegal drugs, the statement said.
“We are committed to imposing total systemic friction on narco-terrorists -- disrupting their operations, dismantling their leadership, and eliminating cartel terror across the region,” said Gen. Francis Donovan, who leads U.S. Southern Command.
The latest strike comes days after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that the U.S. would extend its offensive to land across multiple Latin American countries. The secretary said during a visit to Panama that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to allow the U.S. to carry out joint military operations against criminal groups on their soil. Guatemala denied reaching such an agreement.
Ecuador launched similar missions with the U.S. in March.

IN BRIEF: Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan on EU membership bid, CSTO withdrawal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
12:22:09 UTC
21:22:09 KST

YEREVAN, August 24. /TASS/. Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said he supports Yerevan’s expulsion from the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) and would welcome the move.
He also said in the parliament that Armenia would soon begin the process of applying for EU membership.
TASS has compiled the key points from the Armenian prime minister’s statements.
Preparing EU membership bid
- Armenia will soon begin the process of applying for EU membership, Pashinyan said, adding that Yerevan would at least heed calls from its Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) partners.
- He said Armenia could hold a referendum on EU membership or remaining in the Eurasian Economic Union once discussions reach a turning point and it can prepare a roadmap.
- Yerevan must first formally apply for EU membership before holding such a referendum, he said.
- Pashinyan described the process as requiring extensive work.
Armenia’s CSTO membership
- Pashinyan said he would be very pleased if the CSTO decided to expel Armenia, noting that the organization’s charter provides for such a measure.
- This would free Yerevan from the dilemma of whether to leave the organization, he said.
- Pashinyan said Armenia’s 2026-2031 government program does not envisage stepping up its CSTO activities over the next five years, adding that Yerevan’s interest in the organization has run out.
Reaction
- Armenia may leave the CSTO if Yerevan no longer needs its membership, Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
- Peskov urged to remember the experience of Turkey and other countries whose EU membership bids have remained unresolved for years.
Armenia’s EAEU and CSTO membership
- On March 26, 2025, the Armenian parliament passed a law launching the process of joining the EU.
- Russian President Vladimir Putin has said EU integration would automatically end Armenia’s cooperation with the EAEU and cause it to lose all related benefits.
- At the May 29 EAEU summit in Astana, the leaders of Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan adopted a joint statement supporting a nationwide referendum in Armenia on joining the EU or remaining in the EAEU.
- On August 11, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin told TASS that Armenia should decide whether to hold a nationwide referendum on joining the EU or retaining EAEU membership by December, when EAEU leaders are due to discuss possible further steps toward Yerevan.
- In September 2024, Pashinyan said Yerevan had frozen its participation in CSTO activities.
- He declared that the organization had created threats to Armenia’s sovereignty.
- In October 2024, Armenian Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan said at an international security forum in Warsaw that Yerevan was assessing all risks associated with a possible decision to leave the CSTO.
- In December 2024, the Armenian prime minister said relations between Armenia and the CSTO had reached a point of no return.
- On June 10, 2026, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said CSTO members agreed to consider applying a charter provision to Armenia over two years of unpaid membership fees.
- On August 11, Galuzin told TASS that the CSTO summit on November 11 could consider stripping Armenia of its voting rights in the organization.

EU unlocks new tranche of €90 billion loan to Ukraine for weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24

EU unlocks new tranche of €90 billion loan to Ukraine for weapons
The European Commission has approved €6.1 billion ($7.1 billion) in new weapons purchases for Ukraine, the commission said on Monday. The tranche is part of a €90 billion loan allocated by Brussels for budgetary and military aid to Kiev earlier this year.
Facing mounting battlefield pressure, Kiev is increasingly pushing for faster aid disbursements as it relies heavily on foreign funding to plug a widening budget gap and sustain its war effort against Russia. Moscow has argued that Western military aid to Ukraine, which comes at the expense of ordinary taxpayers, only serves to prolong the conflict.
In April, the EU approved a €90 billion ($105 billion) emergency loan for Ukraine that allocates €30 billion for budget support and €60 billion for military aid in 2026-2027. The loan, backed by joint EU borrowing and repayable only if Kiev receives war reparations from Russia, was pushed through after plans to seize Russian sovereign assets frozen in the West failed. Hungary, the Czech Republic, and Slovakia have secured exemptions from the scheme.
The latest tranche came on top of €16 billion of previously approved procurement plans, of which €8.35 billion has already been transferred to Kiev. The €6.1 billion disbursement is expected to finance air and missile defense systems, missiles, ammunition, and radars, according to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
In February, the European Council set “strict conditions” for Ukraine to secure the funds, specifying that Kiev is obliged to purchase weapons and military equipment only from companies based in the EU, Ukraine, the European Economic Area, and the European Free Trade Association. Purchases from third countries are allowed in cases of urgent need, including when a defense product is not available in the EU.
The EU’s financial and military aid to Ukraine has drawn criticism from current and former officials in and outside the bloc. Earlier this month, former Ukrainian Prime Minister Nikolay Azarov said the West will never recover its loans to Kiev.
German MEP Fabio De Masi warned that the funds will enrich “corrupt oligarchs.” Former Austrian Foreign Minister Karin Kneissl told RT earlier this year that the EU is shifting from its traditional focus on trade toward an increasingly geopolitical and defense-oriented agenda.
In July, Russian President Vladimir Putin accused Kiev and the “so-called European pseudo-peacekeepers” of seeking to prolong the conflict. He said their goal is “not peace, but the continuation of the war with Russia to the last Ukrainian.”

Man in Bristol convicted over bid to join Islamic State
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
13:16:57 BST
21:16:57 KST

A 22-year-old man living in Bristol has been convicted of preparing acts of terrorism after travelling to Somalia with the intention of joining Daesh, following an investigation by Counter Terrorism Policing South East.
A 22-year-old man living in Bristol has been convicted of preparing acts of terrorism after travelling to Somalia with the intention of joining the proscribed terrorist organisation Daesh, the UK Defence Journal understands.
Mohamed Mohamoud, of Francombe Grove in Horfield, Bristol, was found guilty by a unanimous jury following a three-week trial at Winchester Crown Court. According to a Counter Terrorism Policing news update, Mohamoud was convicted of preparation of acts of terrorism contrary to Section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006. The verdict was returned on 18 August, with details of the investigation published on 24 August.
Investigators said Mohamoud, a security guard who was born in Somalia, travelled there intending to join Daesh, which is proscribed in the United Kingdom. He purchased a ticket on 13 January 2025 for a journey from Heathrow to Somalia via Ethiopia, leaving the UK on 30 January and returning on 3 March. Counter Terrorism Policing South East later used evidence from his electronic devices, travel history and communications to establish the purpose of the journey.
Officers attended Mohamoud’s home on 20 January 2026 and arrested him, seizing a number of digital devices including a Samsung Galaxy mobile phone. Examination of location data from the handset showed that it had been present at various locations in Somalia between January and March 2025. Investigators also recovered a Telegram conversation in which Mohamoud asked for assistance travelling to Somalia so that he could join the “Mujahedeen”. In another message, police said, he expressed an ambition to become a “martyr”.
Further examination of the phone uncovered Daesh propaganda including battlefield footage, executions and beheadings, as well as material produced in a news-style format by the terrorist organisation. Counter Terrorism Policing said the material demonstrated that Mohamoud had adopted an extremist Islamist ideology. Messages recovered following his return to Britain also recorded what investigators described as his continuing intention to commit himself to jihad.
Detective Chief Superintendent Oliver Wright, Head of Counter Terrorism Policing South East, said, as quoted in the news update: “Mahmoud had become radicalised to adopt an extremist Islamist ideology and travelled to Somalia with the intention of joining Daesh.”
Wright added: “It is important to note that Mahmoud communicated to others about his intentions to travel to commit jihad and become a ‘martyr’.” The spelling of the surname in the quoted police remarks differs from the spelling used elsewhere in the Counter Terrorism Policing account, which identifies the defendant as Mohamed Mohamoud.
The conviction centres on preparation for terrorism rather than an allegation that Mohamoud carried out an attack in the UK. The prosecution case concerned his journey to Somalia, his stated intentions and the digital evidence recovered during the subsequent investigation. Daesh maintains an affiliate in Somalia, while the organisation itself remains proscribed under British terrorism legislation.
Mohamoud was charged in connection with the offence on 26 January 2026, six days after his arrest. He was subsequently tried at Winchester Crown Court, where the jury returned a unanimous guilty verdict after hearing evidence concerning his travel, communications and extremist material.
Wright also urged members of the public to report concerns where individuals appear to be moving towards extremist violence. He said: “If you become aware of anyone whose behaviour may have changed, who has adopted extreme views and is expressing similar intentions, please ensure you report this to police. Reporting can save lives.”

Facebook, TikTok promoted Colombian armed groups’ content to recruit children: NGO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
12:15:00 UTC
21:15:00 KST

Facebook, TikTok promoted Colombian armed groups’ content to recruit children: NGO
BOGOTA – Facebook and TikTok failed to prevent the spread of content produced by Colombian armed groups to recruit children, and in some cases even “appeared to promote these posts”, Human Rights Watch (HRW) reported on Aug 24.
HRW said the circulation of social media content by armed groups “glorifies life in armed group ranks” and promotes “deceptive job offers”.
Since 2021, around 1,500 children have been recruited by armed groups, according to HRW.
Armed groups use children for combat, handling weapons, drones and explosives, and intelligence gathering, the HRW report said.
In some cases, it said, children without combat training are used as “cannon fodder”.
According to the report, almost half of child recruits are indigenous children, despite indigenous people representing only around four per cent of the population.
Girls account for around 40 per cent of child recruits, and are “particularly exposed to sexual violence”.
In the report, HRW described social media posts showing members of armed groups flaunting wads of cash and jewellery.
In other posts, they appear in training camps or listening to “narcocorridos” – a Mexican music genre that celebrates the exploits of infamous drug traffickers.
In the comments sections, some users asked how they could join.
HRW said dissident groups that emerged from the now-defunct Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) have been responsible for 74 per cent of child recruitment cases documented between 2021 and 2025.
HRW said it had informed Meta, Facebook’s parent company, and TikTok’s owner ByteDance of the problem. Both said they had removed the specific content mentioned.
Meta said it “constantly strives to refine (its) approach to combating it across (its) platforms”.
TikTok said it “proactively (prevents) illegal armed groups and organised criminal groups from using TikTok, including to target, exploit or recruit minors”.
The historic 2016 peace agreement ended a half-century of war between the government and the FARC guerrilla group, but remaining armed groups continue to control large swathes of territory in remote parts of the north-east and south.
Newly inaugurated President Abelardo de la Espriella has vowed to crack down on armed groups and plans to forge a military alliance with the US and Israel. AFP

Russian troops liberate three communities in Ukraine operation over past day — top brass
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
12:13:22 UTC
21:13:22 KST

MOSCOW, August 24. /TASS/. Russian troops liberated three communities in the Sumy and Zaporozhye Regions and the Donetsk People’s Republic over the past 24 hours in the special military operation in Ukraine, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"Battlegroup North units took control of the settlement of Pershe Travnya in the Sumy Region through decisive operations. <…> Battlegroup Center units liberated the settlement of Kucherov Yar in the Donetsk People’s Republic through active operations. <…> Battlegroup East units advanced deep into the enemy’s defenses and liberated the settlement of Dolinka in the Zaporozhye Region," the ministry said in a statement.
Kiev loses 1,400 troops along engagement line in past day - latest figures
The Ukrainian army lost roughly 1,400 troops in battles with Russian forces in all the frontline areas over the past 24 hours, according to the latest data on the special military operation in Ukraine released by Russia’s Defense Ministry.
The latest figures show that the Ukrainian army lost roughly 235 troops and 11 motor vehicles in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup North, over 220 troops and three artillery guns in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup West and more than 255 troops, a German-made Leopard tank and two armored combat vehicles in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup South.
During the last 24-hour period, the Ukrainian army also lost roughly 330 troops and six armored combat vehicles in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center, over 315 troops and three armored combat vehicles in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup East and about 45 troops and two jamming stations in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup Dnepr, the latest figures show.
Russia’s Battlegroup North inflicts 235 casualties on Ukrainian army in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup North inflicted roughly 235 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 11 enemy motor vehicles in its areas of responsibility over the past day, the ministry reported.
During the last 24-hour period, Battlegroup North units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of a mechanized brigade of the Ukrainian army and a territorial defense brigade in areas near the settlements of Kiyanitsa and Pisarevka in the Sumy Region," the ministry said.
In the Kharkov direction, Battlegroup North units inflicted losses on formations of two mechanized brigades of the Ukrainian army in areas near the settlements of Veliky Burluk and Prikolotnoye in the Kharkov Region, the ministry reported.
The Ukrainian army lost an estimated 235 personnel and 11 motor vehicles in those frontline areas over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup West inflicts over 220 casualties on Ukrainian army in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup West inflicted more than 220 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed three enemy artillery guns in its area of responsibility over the past day, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup West units gained better lines and positions and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of a mechanized brigade, an assault brigade of the Ukrainian army and a marine infantry brigade in areas near the settlements of Izyumskoye, Selishche and Chervony Oskol in the Kharkov Region and Svyatogorsk in the Donetsk People’s Republic," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 220 personnel, 25 motor vehicles, three artillery guns and three electronic warfare stations in that frontline area over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicts over 255 casualties on Ukrainian army in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicted more than 255 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed a German-made Leopard tank and two armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the past day, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup South units improved their forward positions and inflicted losses on formations of two mechanized brigades and a mountain assault brigade of the Ukrainian army in areas near the settlements of Kondratovka, Semyonovka and Vasilyevskaya Pustosh in the Donetsk People’s Republic," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 255 personnel, a German-made Leopard tank, two armored combat vehicles, 29 motor vehicles and four field artillery guns in that frontline area over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicts 330 casualties on Ukrainian army in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicted roughly 330 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed six enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the past day, the ministry reported.
During the last 24-hour period, Battlegroup Center units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of a mechanized brigade, an assault brigade of the Ukrainian army, a marine infantry brigade and two National Guard brigades in areas near the settlements of Belozerskoye, Verovka, Dobropolye, Novotroitskoye and Sergeyevka in the Donetsk People’s Republic and Ivanovka in the Dnepropetrovsk Region," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost an estimated 330 personnel, six armored combat vehicles, eight motor vehicles and two artillery guns in that frontline area over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicts over 315 casualties on Ukrainian army in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicted more than 315 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed three enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the past day, the ministry reported.
During the last 24-hour period, Battlegroup East units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of an assault brigade, an air assault brigade, two assault regiments of the Ukrainian army and a marine infantry brigade in areas near the settlements of Vasilkovka in the Dnepropetrovsk Region, Barvinovka, Nikolskoye and Omelnik in the Zaporozhye Region," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 315 personnel, three armored combat vehicles and five motor vehicles in that frontline area over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminates 45 Ukrainian troops in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminated roughly 45 Ukrainian troops and destroyed two enemy jamming stations in its area of responsibility over the past day, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup Dnepr units inflicted losses on formations of a mechanized brigade of the Ukrainian army and a territorial defense brigade in areas near the settlements of Malokaterinovka and Orekhov in the Zaporozhye Region," the ministry said.
"Up to 45 [Ukrainian] military personnel, 11 motor vehicles and two electronic warfare stations were destroyed," it said.
Russian troops strike Ukrainian military-industrial site, port facilities over past day
Russian troops struck a military-industrial enterprise, port facilities used in the Ukrainian army’s supplies and enemy deployment areas over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Operational/tactical aircraft, attack unmanned aerial vehicles, missile troops and artillery of the Russian groups of forces struck a military-industrial enterprise, port, energy and transport infrastructure facilities in Ukraine and logistics centers used by the Ukrainian army, a workshop producing long-range unmanned aerial vehicles, and also temporary deployment areas of Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries in 142 locations," the ministry said.
Russian air defenses intercept 988 Ukrainian UAVs, 17 smart bombs over past day
Russian air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 988 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and 17 smart bombs over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Air defense capabilities shot down 17 guided aerial bombs, three rockets of the US-made HIMARS multiple launch rocket system, 11 Flamingo long-range cruise missiles and 988 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said.
Tally of Ukrainian army’s losses
Overall, the Russian Armed Forces have destroyed 674 Ukrainian combat aircraft, 284 helicopters, 218,809 unmanned aerial vehicles, 669 surface-to-air missile systems, 30,710 tanks and other armored combat vehicles, 1,775 multiple rocket launchers, 36,255 field artillery guns and mortars and 70,068 special military motor vehicles since the start of the special military operation, the ministry reported.

Indonesia quake death toll rises to 100 as thousands remain displaced
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
20:13:06 CST
21:13:06 KST

JAKARTA, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- The death toll from the 7.7-magnitude earthquake that struck Indonesia's Flores region on Aug. 15 has risen to 100, with 1,603 people injured and over 180,000 still displaced, the National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) said Monday.
BNPB chief Suharyanto said many of the additional deaths were people who had initially suffered serious injuries and later died while receiving treatment.
He said 6,409 aftershocks have been recorded, including 33 with a magnitude of at least 5.0. The strongest measured 6.2.
Suharyanto urged residents not to believe false information about stronger earthquakes or another tsunami, saying aftershock activity has shown a declining trend in recent days.
Authorities said aftershocks could continue for three to four weeks after the main quake, with their frequency and intensity expected to decline.
The government continues to deliver aid to displaced residents, including those in remote areas. ■

Namibia names squad for T20I tri-series with South Africa, Zimbabwe
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
20:12:57 CST
21:12:57 KST

WINDHOEK, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Cricket Namibia on Monday named a 16-player squad for an inaugural men's T20 International tri-series featuring Namibia, South Africa and Zimbabwe from August 28 to September 6 in Windhoek.
Also known as the FNB Eagles, Namibia will be captained by veteran all-rounder Gerhard Erasmus, who was named the ICC Men's Associate Cricketer of the Year for 2024.
Head coach Craig Williams said the tournament would give Namibia an opportunity to test itself against two strong African sides and called on local supporters to rally behind the Eagles.
The tournament will mark the first time Namibia, South Africa and Zimbabwe have competed in a multi-team T20I event on Namibian soil. Each team will play the other two twice, with the top two advancing to the final.
Cricket Namibia said the series would serve as an initial step toward the planned launch of an Africa Cup in 2027, aimed at providing regular high-level competition among leading African cricket nations.
Following the tri-series, Namibia will host South Africa for three ODIs on September 9, 11 and 13. The matches will make up the first bilateral ODI series between the countries and Namibia's first home ODI series against South Africa. ■

20:12:50 CST
21:12:50 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- The past week has been busy and fruitful for China's humanoild robot industry, which is qucikly racing from lab demos toward real-world deployment.
On Wednesday, as the 2026 World Robot Conference (WRC) opened in Beijing, drawing more than 300 exhibitors from 26 countries with over 3,000 products, Unitree Robotics became the first humanoid robot maker to list on China's A-share market.
On Saturday, the second World Humanoid Robot Games kicked off at the "Ice Ribbon," the 2022 Winter Olympics venue, with 666 teams and 2,056 robots from 16 countries.
ROAD TO PROFITABILITY
Unitree debuted on the Shanghai Stock Exchange's STAR Market on Aug. 19, opening at 1,100 yuan (about 162 U.S. dollars) per share -- a 629-percent premium. As of Monday's opening, although it had pulled back significantly, it still remained at a high level.
The sell-off from the opening high was a sobering signal. Financial observers noted that the sector will enter a digestion period that may last for months, predicting investors will shift their focus from rewarding "the only listed robot stock" to its actual business performance.
Still, Unitree's listing marks a watershed moment for China's humanoid robot industry.
The listing will transition the industry from "technological validation" and "narrative-driven hype" into an era of "commercial value verification," where profitability is the ultimate test, said Tian Lihui, a finance professor at Nankai University.
Unitree has already delivered a compelling answer. Established in 2016, the company shipped over 5,500 humanoid units in 2025 to secure the top spot worldwide. Its revenue surged to nearly 1.7 billion yuan in 2025, and the momentum continued into the first half of 2026, with revenue reaching approximately 1.15 billion yuan, up 48.54 percent year on year.
Unitree's success is underpinned by its strong emphasis on independent R&D and technological innovation. The company has achieved vertical integration by developing proprietary core components -- including motors, reducers, controllers, and LiDAR -- alongside high-performance perception and motion control algorithms. This in-house approach is backed by a portfolio of over 200 patent applications.
The company's founder Wang Xingxing attributed its growth to independent innovation, pragmatic execution and long-termism. He emphasized that, because the humanoid robotics industry remains in its dawn phase, navigating its significant challenges requires collective effort and sustained investment from the entire sector.
TECH LEAP IN PITCH
While the IPO measured progress in valuation, the robot games measured it in velocity, endurance and raw athleticism -- taking the technology off the lab bench and onto the pitch.
In the 100-meter heats, the Beijing-based humanoid robot Tien Kung Ultra crossed in 9.39 seconds, faster than Usain Bolt's 9.58-second human world record. Tien Kung Ultra also posted a standing high jump of 2.88 meters, well above the human mark.
The games also featured a dazzling array of human-machine showdowns: robots traded shots with Olympic table tennis champion Ding Ning and tennis Grand Slam winner Zheng Jie, and went toe-to-toe with former national football player Yang Chen.
Robot football offered a special glimpse of how far the technology has come. Beijing-based Booster Robotics' newly developed bipedal robot, Booster T2, is the star player in the large size group of the football tournament at this year's games. Beyond its taller stature and greater strength, the robot can kick balls at over 100 km/h, and its end-side computing power is 10 times that of the previous generation, with the system latency dropping from 10 milliseconds to 4 milliseconds.
Many events at the games were run fully autonomously, with no remote controls, testing robots' ability to perceive and decide independently. "Every centimeter higher, every kilogram heavier, reflects engineers' optimization of joint motors and reducers," said Jiang Guangzhi of Beijing's Bureau of Economy and Information Technology.
REAL-WORLD APPLICATIONS
As China's robots demonstrate formidable technological prowess, the industry is now focusing on expanding robots' real-world applications -- a widely recognized challenge within the industry.
The World Robot Conference serves as a resounding testament to China's pragmatic shift and its global resonance. At the event, Beijing Galbot Co., Ltd. drew crowds with robots folding clothes, fetching goods, and making breakfast. The company says its pharmacy sorting robots are already deployed in nearly 100 stores across more than 10 cities, including Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen.
At the Galaxea AI display area, visitors could scan a QR code to place an order and then watch a wheeled robot pick, pack and label items they ordered in real time. The company's robots will be rolled out to unmanned warehouses and supermarkets this year, and has already partnered with JD.com for warehouse sorting and shelving.
Practical robots took center stage, just as the Spanish news agency Agencia EFE reported on the conference, Chinese companies are transitioning robots from mere "attention-grabbers" to genuine "workers and practical consumer goods."
Xiong Youjun, CEO of the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Center, said this year's conference showed an industry clearly transitioning from mere technological showmanship to industrial implementation. He added that the sector is currently on the "eve of the ChatGPT moment" regarding embodied intelligence, with companies across the board accelerating the deployment and validation of their technologies.
A recent Morgan Stanley report draws a striking parallel between the current trajectory of China's humanoid robotics industry and the electric vehicle sector a decade ago. The investment bank predicts that over the next five to ten years, humanoid robots are poised to become the next major driver of China's machinery exports.
BOOMING INDUSTRIAL LANDSCAPE
The rapid ascent of the robot industry perfectly aligns with China's national strategic blueprint for future development.
"Embodied intelligence" was first written into China's government work report in 2025. Furthermore, China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) calls for a forward-looking layout of future industries, including embodied artificial intelligence, alongside mechanisms to boost funding and share risks in these emerging sectors.
Data underscores this momentum. Among companies currently queuing for an IPO on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange alone, 46 are robotics-related, highlighting China's systematic industrial advantage in embodied AI. As Bloomberg noted, the surge in robot IPOs "reflects the rapid rise of China's AI ecosystem."
This wave of listings comes amid China's robotics sector securing unprecedented global prominence. China is now home to over 140 humanoid robot manufacturers. With an annual shipment volume of 14,400 units, the country now accounts for eight out of every ten humanoid robots produced globally.
Global shipments of humanoid robots reached approximately 19,100 units in the first half of this year, with China accounting for over 97 percent of the global total, industry data shows.
According to Xi Yue, co-founder of Beijing-based leading robot maker Robotera, the nation's robotics industry now stands firmly in the first tier globally, boasting the world's largest application market, the most comprehensive supply chain, and a leading edge in embodied AI algorithms. ■

Feature: In Hong Kong, global ecologists restore biodiversity by putting together healthy forest
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
20:12:16 CST
21:12:16 KST

by Xinhua writer Liu Yinglun
HONG KONG, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Restoration ecologist Fernanda Cardoso grew up hearing grim stories about forest degradation in her home country Brazil and other places worldwide, which got her interested in studying plant ecology and forest restoration. Now she is trying to piece together a fully functional and diverse subtropical forest on the hillsides of Hong Kong's highest mountain Tai Mo Shan.
The forest restoration site Cardoso works on is a part of Kadoorie Farm and Botanic Garden (KFBG), a 70-year-old local non-profit organization dedicated to natural conservation. In 2013, it launched a project to turn its degraded grassy slopes into a diverse native forest that can support a wide variety of wildlife.
So far, over 50,000 seedlings representing hundreds of native species have been planted. Mammals, birds and insects are returning, including rare species like the butterfly Burmese Bush Blue.
MAXIMUM DIVERSITY
"A good forest is one that's alive at every level," said Cardoso. It is not just a canopy of trees, but the constant exchange of energy between hundreds of species -- different plant life forms, animals, fungi, pollinators and seed dispersers.
Unfortunately for the restoration site, hundreds of years of agricultural history as well as frequent wildfires had eroded the soil and deprived it of enough seed dispersers to restore biodiversity naturally, said Zhang Jinlong, senior ecologist at KFBG's Flora Conservation Department.
The missing links have to be reconstructed artificially, and ecologists at KFBG are doing it by mimicking the end result of natural succession. Based on extensive flora surveys on local natural forests and some others in south China, they drew up plans to plant diverse life forms including trees, shrubs, epiphytes, herbs, and climbers to recreate the structure of the best south China-Vietnam subtropical evergreen forest.
A big part of the restoration plan is nurturing seedlings of native plant species in KFBG's nursery, for which the Flora Conservation Department's fieldwork teams scour wild areas of Hong Kong to collect seeds under local government permission. To preserve genetic diversity, they make a special effort to source seeds from diverse mother trees from as many populations as possible.
"Hong Kong is incredibly rich in species, many of which have rarely if ever been cultivated," said Craig Williams, horticultural manager who used to work at botanic gardens in Britain and Singapore. The metropolis is home to over 2,200 documented plant species.
Williams and his team make it their mission to propagate and conserve rare and threatened species. Sometimes the job entails huddling with co-workers on a small pink boat, or "Barbie's boat," as Williams called it, on a field trip to a tiny island to take cuttings of the only known wild Lofty Strangling Fig (Ficus altissima) mother trees in Hong Kong. Now the fig tree is growing in the KFBG nursery.
When the seedlings become strong enough, they are taken from the nursery and planted in the restoration site, where arborists have developed practical tools to overcome the substandard conditions of degraded land.
The team strengthens the soil with a mixture of biochar, dead branches and fallen leaves and uses tree guards made from plastic mesh and steel poles to protect seedlings from over-foraging by animals, said Cyrus Cheung, senior arborist at KFBG's Flora Conservation Department.
BACK WITH LIFE
Over a decade of efforts has helped bring wildlife back to the slopes. KFBG's Fauna Conservation Department has detected activities of almost all native mammal species, as well as the chirping of over 50 kinds of birds.
Zhang expects the canopy on the restoration site to keep expanding over the next five to ten years while self-regeneration begins for some species. To completely restore the function and structure of natural forests, however, is a matter of at least a century.
The Forest Declaration Assessment 2025 found that 8.1 million hectares of forest were lost in 2024, a level of destruction 63 percent higher than the trajectory needed to halt deforestation by 2030. Ecologists worldwide are calling for more restoration efforts.
"Conservation directly benefits everyday living. Just look at how much Hong Kong residents enjoy hiking and spending time outdoors," said Cardoso. She appreciates that local residents make full use of their country parks, which cover about 40 percent of the city's expanse, to maintain a healthy lifestyle.
Williams called his job a "privilege" because it is a rare opportunity to focus on growing native plants as well as participating in ecological restoration.
"The seedlings we plant will grow into massive trees that, long after I pass away, I wouldn't even get my arms around. It feels great to imagine that," said Williams. ■

ISTANBUL, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- A stone artifact inscribed with the name of Prophet Muhammad has been unearthed at the ancient archaeological site of Ani in eastern Türkiye, offering fresh insight into the region's history, authorities said Monday.
In a post on the social media platform X, Turkish Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said the name appears six times in Kufic script on the stone, which is believed to have come from a Seljuk tomb tower.

The site was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016. ■
