Feature: Afghan gemstones seek new luster through global trade
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
20:12:09 CST
21:12:09 KST

KABUL, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Behind the glass counters of Kabul's antique sellers' street, blue lapis lazuli, green emeralds, red rubies and multicolored tourmaline reflect the light of a market that has long connected Afghanistan's mineral-rich mountain regions with buyers across the globe.
For traders and jewelry designers in the capital, the stones represent more than valuable commodities. They are part of Afghanistan's cultural heritage and, potentially, a source of employment, export income and international recognition.
"Most customers, especially those who come from outside Afghanistan, are interested in emerald, ruby and tourmaline," said Khalid Haidari, who has worked in the city's antique market for 18 years.
"For many buyers, however, the appeal of Afghan jewelry extends beyond the stones themselves. Traditional designs remain especially popular."
Local merchants said that Afghan gemstone jewelry has gained rising popularity in overseas markets, with China serving as a key export destination. Online platforms have provided local sellers and designers with new ways to present their products to customers abroad and arrange exports without relying entirely on physical stores or international exhibitions.
Yet Afghanistan's natural gemstone wealth has not automatically translated into a mature domestic industry.
"The stones from Afghanistan are of very high quality," Haidari said. "The main problem is that the equipment and standards needed for extraction and shaping are not sufficiently available."
This presents a major bottleneck for the industry, as a gemstone's commercial value is largely created after extraction. Cutting, polishing, design, certification, packaging and marketing can transform a raw mineral into a high-value finished product.
Nader Khan, who has worked in the gemstone trade for 30 years and has operated on antique sellers' street for 15 years, said Afghan stones remain highly competitive in foreign markets.
"Afghan lapis lazuli, emeralds and rubies are of a quality that is difficult to find elsewhere," Khan said.
He said customers also attach great importance to handmade work and domestic designs. In his view, processing more stones inside Afghanistan would help preserve their original character while creating employment opportunities for local workers.
"We process the stones here with the machinery available to us and turn them into different designs," Khan said.
Khan also cautioned that sending stones abroad for additional modern processing could raise costs and risk affecting the stones' original quality. Developing local processing capacity, he said, would allow Afghan producers to retain more value while preserving the distinct cultural identity of their products.
The future of Afghanistan's gemstone trade is closely linked to access to international customers.
"International exhibitions had previously provided important opportunities for sellers to display their products and expand sales. The decline in such events has reduced direct contact," Khan said.
"Chinese customers remain among the most active buyers in Kabul's gemstone market, particularly for lapis lazuli and nephrite," Khan added.
At the same time, online sales are creating a new route to consumers. Afghan sellers and designers are using digital platforms to display jewelry, communicate with buyers and send products overseas.
The shift has opened opportunities for small businesses, but it also requires reliable product photography, accurate information about gemstones, secure delivery and consistent quality.
"I am very satisfied with my work, and most of my customers are particularly interested in lapis lazuli, emeralds and rubies," Ahmad, an online seller, said.
The charm of Afghan gemstones goes beyond their market value. For buyers, these precious stones carry unique emotional and cultural significance.
A piece of jewelry may serve as a souvenir, a gift, a symbol of cultural identity, or a reminder of a particular journey. Such associations add meaning to a product whose value begins in the earth but is completed through human workmanship.
"Customers use gemstones with a good design at home to improve their mood and to overcome some health problems because seeing the stone gives them a feeling of calmness and happiness," Ahmad told Xinhua.
Sula, a customer visiting the market to buy a gift for a friend, chose tourmaline bracelets, describing them as attractive, memorable and valuable.
The gemstone trade also unlocks profound cultural development potential. Distinctive traditional Afghan designs stand out in the competitive global jewelry market. Combined with high-quality local gemstones, these handcrafted pieces are both commercially competitive and closely connected to the country's profound history. ■

Ukraine at 35: Can the Strategic Partnership With the US Survive?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
12:12:00 UTC
21:12:00 KST

In 2008, I took part in drafting the first Charter on Strategic Partnership between Ukraine and the US. At the time, it was difficult to imagine that less than two decades later I would be seriously asking whether Ukraine is in danger of losing its principal strategic partner – and at the most critical moment in our country’s modern history.
To be sure, warning signs appeared long before Russia’s full-scale invasion. One of them was the Obama administration’s weak response to Russia’s aggression against Ukraine in 2014. Barack Obama proceeded from the assumption that Ukraine will always be “vulnerable to military domination by Russia no matter what we do.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Joe Biden made important adjustments to the Democratic Party’s approach, arguing that supporting Ukraine was in the US’ “vital national interest.” Ukraine managed to withstand the initial stages of Russia’s full-scale invasion largely thanks to the assistance provided by the anti-Putin coalition created and led by the US. (Biden’s inconsistency and his obvious miscalculations are a subject for a separate discussion.)
Serious doubts about the future of our strategic partnership emerged with Donald Trump’s second presidential term, although the roots of his skeptical – and at times openly negative – attitude toward Ukraine can be traced back to his first administration. That period was marked by his unsuccessful attempts to obtain compromising information about Joe Biden and by the political trauma of his first impeachment.
Does Ukraine Still Have Hope?
Despite Trump’s undisguised admiration for the Russian dictator, military cooperation with Ukraine continued during his first term, and Kyiv received its first lethal defensive weapons. This happened largely because Trump’s administration still included what were often described as the “adults in the room” – military leaders and experienced policymakers who clearly understood the threat Russia posed to US national security.
Such people are no longer needed for Trump to pursue the objectives of his second presidency.
Expert advice and institutional assessments have been replaced by the president’s instincts, his intuition and his belief in his own ability to strike deals on virtually any issue. The US has witnessed an unprecedented personalization of foreign policy, with decisions increasingly determined by whether the anticipated outcome serves Donald Trump’s personal interests, those of his inner circle, and his own preferences and inclinations.
As a result, US policy toward individual countries is increasingly shaped by Trump’s personal relationship with their leaders.
From the very beginning of Trump’s return to office, Ukraine and its political leadership found themselves under maximum pressure – something that could have been anticipated from his campaign rhetoric. His hostility toward Ukraine, and toward President Volodymyr Zelensky, personally, was reinforced by his efforts to portray Joe Biden as the president who had squandered American resources on supporting Ukraine.
This tendency reached its peak during the now infamous Oval Office meeting.
Despite Trump’s volatility and frequent emotional swings, the fundamental principles underlying his policy toward Ukraine have remained consistently unfavorable for our country.
First, Trump wants to end the Russia-Ukraine war as quickly as possible, regardless of the conditions and with little regard for Ukraine’s national interests or the fact that Russia is the aggressor. In Trump’s worldview, these considerations are of secondary importance.
His so-called peace initiatives cast him as a mediator rather than Ukraine’s partner. Whether presented as “28 points” or “20 points,” these proposals are not designed to deliver either a just or a lasting peace for Ukraine.
Can we expect the current US administration to come forward with proposals that are more acceptable to Ukraine as negotiations evolve? Time will tell, but there are ample reasons for skepticism.
Second, Ukraine is neither important nor particularly interesting to Donald Trump – neither personally nor from the standpoint of US security or economic interests, at least as he understands them.
Perhaps the only tangible interest he sees in Ukraine is the so-called minerals agreement, which, despite subsequent revisions, he still appears to view primarily as a mechanism for extracting maximum benefit: “We’ll go in whenever we want and take practically whatever we want.”
Third, despite Vladimir Putin’s brazen behavior, his broken promises, and even actions as scandalous as assisting Iran during its confrontation with the US, Trump remains determined to preserve the possibility of dealing with him as a partner. He appears to hope for the realization of grandiose – and largely illusory – economic projects, as well as a radical revision of the rules governing world politics, under which “strong” and “weak” states would be subject to different standards.
Keeping these realities in mind helps explain why every expectation that Trump might eventually shift toward a policy more favorable to Ukraine has repeatedly ended in disappointment. Time and again, his administration has returned to positions that clearly contradict both the letter and the spirit of the Charter on Strategic Partnership.
The current US administration regards one of its greatest achievements as ending military assistance to Ukraine and replacing it with commercial arms sales.
One can only hope that, even under these new circumstances, the Presidential Drawdown Replacement and Replenishment (PURL) mechanism will continue to function, and that the Graham-Blumenthal sanctions bill will not only be adopted, but also fully implemented. In both cases, however, the decisive word belongs to the President of the US.
We must be prepared for the possibility that this situation is unlikely to change fundamentally before January 2029. Until then, US support for Ukraine may well depend on the emotions, priorities and intentions of a single individual occupying the world’s most powerful office.
That said, the prospects for renewing and restoring the strategic partnership between Ukraine and the US will ultimately depend on more than the occupant of the White House. They will also be shaped by the consistency of support for Ukraine among American policymakers, by the attitudes of the American public, and by the condition in which Ukraine emerges from this phase of its struggle against Russian aggression.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

Ukraine holds world’s first all-drone military parade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
12:09:29 UTC
21:09:29 KST

- Ukraine held what was described as the world's first all-drone military parade in Kyiv on August 24, 2026, its 35th Independence Day.
- Ground, aerial, and naval unmanned systems, including interceptor, reconnaissance, strike, and kamikaze drones, took part across three domains.
Ukraine held what organizers described as the world’s first military parade composed entirely of unmanned systems on August 24, 2026, marking the country’s Independence Day with a display of ground, naval, and aerial drones instead of traditional manned formations.
Dozens of ground robotic systems moved down Kyiv’s main street, built for logistics, reconnaissance, and combat missions. Overhead, interceptor drones designed to shoot down incoming aerial attacks flew above the capital alongside reconnaissance drones used to monitor the battlefield and strike drones. On the Dnipro River, Ukraine’s naval kamikaze drones, already known internationally from their use against Russia’s Black Sea Fleet, took part alongside reconnaissance versions and naval drones equipped with anti-aircraft missiles.
The event follows Ukraine’s move to formalize its Unmanned Systems Forces as a dedicated branch of the military. President Volodymyr Zelensky signed a decree in June 2024 establishing the branch, and later designated June 11 as an annual Day of Unmanned Systems Forces. Ukrainian officials have said the country was the first in the world to stand up a dedicated military branch built specifically around drone warfare.
Independence Day fell on Ukraine’s 35th anniversary of statehood this year, the fifth marked since Russia’s full-scale invasion began.
Kyiv had not held a conventional military parade since 2022, instead using Khreshchatyk Street in recent years to display destroyed Russian military equipment as a symbol of resistance.

Russia launches new military spacecraft (VIDEO)
Russia has successfully placed a new military spacecraft into orbit aboard a Soyuz-2.1b rocket launched from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome in Arkhangelsk Region, the Defense Ministry has said. The type and specific mission of the spacecraft have not been disclosed.
A combat crew of the Russian Space Forces launched the medium-class rocket at 5:40 AM Moscow time on Monday. The spacecraft was sent up “in the interests of the Russian Defense Ministry,” according to an official statement.
The spacecraft reached its designated orbit and was taken under the control of ground-based Space Forces systems.
“Stable telemetry communication has been established and maintained with the spacecraft, its onboard systems are functioning normally,” the ministry said. The flight and deployment proceeded as planned.
After the launch, the Soyuz-2.1b and its payload were tracked by the ground-based automated control complex of the German Titov Main Test Space Center, which is responsible for controlling and monitoring Russian military spacecraft.
The Soyuz-2.1b is a disposable three-stage medium-lift launch vehicle that has frequently been used to deploy both military and civilian satellites.
The mission comes after several military launches from Plesetsk earlier this year. On April 17, a Soyuz-2.1b carried several spacecraft into orbit for the Defense Ministry. Six days later, an Angara-1.2 light rocket was launched from the cosmodrome with military satellites.
Plesetsk is Russia’s northernmost major launch facility. Its high latitude makes it suited to place spacecraft into polar orbits, which are widely used for Earth observation and military missions. The facility began as a Soviet intercontinental ballistic missile base before being converted for space launches in the 1960s.
The cosmodrome’s first satellite launch took place in March 1966, when a Vostok-2 rocket carried the Kosmos-112 reconnaissance spacecraft into orbit. Plesetsk subsequently became a major launch site for Soviet and Russian military spacecraft and has hosted numerous versions of the R-7 family from which the modern Soyuz launch vehicle was developed.

"In recent years, diplomatic relations have been more informal, often conducted through special representatives such as Cardinal Matteo Zuppi for Ukraine. He further elaborated that the agenda extends beyond humanitarian mediation to encompass critical issues in the Middle East, Africa, and Ukraine. "There is a clear commitment to seeking solutions across these regions, and previous efforts have laid the groundwork for meaningful dialogue," he added. Don Caprio also recalled the initiatives proposed by Pope Francis and Pope Leo XIII for the Catholic Church to serve as a mediator or platform for negotiations. While Russia has rejected such a platform, he noted that this does not equate to a rejection of dialogue altogether. "The Holy See continues to play a moral role, fostering an environment conducive to diplomacy," he remarked.
In Don Caprio’s view, Gallagher’s visit exemplifies the Vatican’s reaffirmation of its diplomatic stance, including the Pope’s intention to restore functions to the Secretariat of State. This is noteworthy given that Pope Francis has largely assumed these responsibilities, whereas Leo XIII previously managed them directly.
Vatican analyst Pietro Schiavazzi commented that Gallagher’s visit would resonate far beyond the local Catholic community. "This trip carries much broader implications," he stated. "Pope Leo XIII’s actions may still surprise us."

Iran denies receiving invitation to join Mecca defense pact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
12:03:37 UTC
21:03:37 KST

Iran denies receiving invitation to join Mecca defense pact
Iran has denied reports that it has been invited to join the Mecca defense pact comprising Saudi Arabia, Türkiye. and Pakistan, while confirming that proposals have been made for talks with the three countries on regional security.
The clarification comes after Mehdi Rahimi, the head of the Iranian parliament’s Khaneh Mellat news agency, told Al Mayadeen on Saturday that Tehran had received an invitation to become a member of the Mecca pact and was considering it.
On Monday, however, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei rejected the claim, stating that no formal invitation had been received in Tehran. At the same time, he said that discussions with the pact members concerning broader regional security have been proposed and are under consideration.
The three founding members of the pact had previously repeatedly said the alliance could eventually expand to include other regional states, with Egypt being publicly mentioned as a possible candidate. Pakistan has also said it would have no objection to Iran joining.
The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, which was signed on August 7, brings together Türkiye, which possesses one of NATO’s largest militaries and a rapidly growing defense industry, Saudi Arabia, which features enormous financial resources and ambitions to shape the Arab political order, and Pakistan, a nuclear-armed state with one of the largest militaries in the Muslim world.
The pact stipulates that an armed attack on one member would be regarded as an attack on all three, and also calls for closer military coordination, joint exercises and defense-industry cooperation.
Tehran initially said it had “no reason for concern” over the agreement, with spokesman Baghaei noting that its creation reflected a growing desire among regional states to develop their own security mechanisms.
Some observers have dubbed the new grouping an “Islamic NATO,” although experts have cautioned against treating it as a fully-fledged military bloc. Gulf Research Center chairman Abdulaziz Sager has said the pact could strengthen the members’ combined diplomatic and defense weight and contribute to a more regionally driven security system.
Israel, meanwhile, has responded to the pact with alarm, raising concerns that a bloc built around Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and nuclear-armed Pakistan could emerge as a counterweight to its own military dominance in the region.
The Mecca pact members, however, insist that the agreement is defensive, is open to other countries in the region, and is not directed against any other states.

The physiological reasons the human brain struggles to process information in extreme heat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
12:00:42 UTC
21:00:42 KST

Ever feel that the arrival of summer sun makes you feel a bit dopey? You wouldn’t be the only one. Soaring temperatures are known for their ability to slow our thought processes, making even everyday tasks seem like a baffling ordeal.
But what is actually happening inside our heads when the heat is on? The explanation appears to lie in the extra work our brain and body have to do to keep us cool.
The brain and body are in constant conversation. When outdoor temperatures change, thermoreceptors which sit near the surface of the skin send signals to the hypothalamus – the brain’s temperature regulation centre.
When things become too hot or cold, the hypothalamus co-ordinates a series of responses to bring body temperature back towards normal (around 37°C). Keeping the core temperature at this level is critical for metabolism, activity of enzymes and many other essential body functions.
Being commander-in-chief of temperature regulation means that the brain becomes rather occupied when having to consistently regulate your temperature.
In hot weather, this means cooling the body down by switching on mechanisms that allow heat to radiate from the surface. This includes diverting blood to the skin, flattening skin hairs and sweating.
These responses are governed by nervous pathways that link the brain to blood vessels and sweat glands. This allows it to fine-tune the amount of heat the body sheds.
But the additional demand that keeping cool places on the brain may therefore leave less capacity for it to perform cognitive tasks which require sustained thought and attention.
This becomes particularly noticeable if you’re also exercising or exerting yourself at the same time. This is because working muscles and metabolism generate heat, which places additional strain on the body and brain’s cooling mechanisms.
Our neurons (nerve cells) may also start to function differently with rising heat. Neurons rely on the flow of electrical currents and the release of chemical neurotransmitters to function. These processes depend upon enzymes, proteins and the movement of charged ions in and out of the neuron – all of which are sensitive to temperature.
Although the brain is normally able to compensate and keep up with these demands, past a certain point the finely controlled balance becomes disrupted. This alters the way neurons fire and communicate with each other, which can affect processes such as memory, decision-making and concentration.
Another potential complication to consider is dehydration, which commonly occurs in hot weather as we lose more fluid in sweat. Failing to replace fluid losses adequately means additional strain is placed on the cardiovascular system as it tries to supply the skin and organs – including the brain – with blood.
Like many other organs, the brain is over 70% water. Even modest dehydration can result in impairment to attention, reaction times and short-term memory.
This is because dehydration can affect the brain in several ways. It can reduce cerebral blood flow, alter the way that neurons function and even affect the delicate balance of electrolytes needed for normal activity – all of which impact how well our brain works.
Another important consideration is not just how brain and body respond to heat in the moment, but also in the aftermath when they rest and recuperate – namely, through sleep. In hotter weather, it can become increasingly difficult to sleep. And, if you do manage to doze off, the time spent in deeper, restorative sleep may also be short-lived.
In disrupting sleep, hot weather adds another contribution to brain fog: inadequate sleep impairs attention, memory and thinking – furthering the effects of heat on cognitive performance.
Keeping cool
The degree to which the heat affects our thinking will probably vary between people. Some may cope well, whereas others may find difficulty in doing complex cognitive tasks or simple, everyday activities. This will be due in part to individual differences in physiology and heat tolerance.
Perception matters, too. Even a relatively small dip in attention or processing speed can feel much more dramatic when we notice ourselves struggling with something that would usually come easily.
Try not to be hard on yourself if this happens. Take a moment to chill, rehydrate and reclaim your thoughts.
You can fend off some of this summer brain fog by keeping yourself cool as best as you can. Simple measures such as cool clothing, bedding and taking regular breaks from heat exposure do work wonders. Good fluid intake is also paramount to making sure both body and brain stay hydrated.
While it’s frustrating when our brains just don’t feel like they’re firing on all cylinders on hot days, just remember that it’s only a temporary blip. And one that should start to ease off as we cool down.
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Georgina Hayden’s quick and easy recipe for charred corn, jalapeño and black bean nachos | Quick and easy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
12:00:32 UTC
21:00:32 KST

Corn is a late-summer staple in our house, but its arrival often leaves me feeling a little blue (end of summer and all that). So, instead, I like to entertain more and make the most of the warm, light evenings. These nachos are a great snack for adults and kids alike (just adjust the chilli for younger palates), and a solid base that can be tweaked any which way. Have some lovely ripe tomatoes to hand? Chop them up and throw them in, too. Avocados at their peak? A side of guacamole would be a dream. Got a well-stocked spice cupboard? Add a little sweet smoked paprika and even some crushed coriander seeds to the fried beans. Make it to your liking and pantry, and enjoy with friends, ideally in the evening sun.
Charred corn, jalapeño and black bean nachos
Prep 10 min
 Cook 20 min
 Serves 4-6
2 ears of corn, kernels cut off the core
2 tbsp vegetable oil
200g tinned black beans, drained and rinsed (net weight)
½ tsp cumin seeds, lightly ground
  Sea salt and black pepper
  2 limes
  ½ bunch coriander, finely chopped
2 jalapeños, or green chillies, stalks, pith and seeds removed, flesh finely chopped
200g tortilla chips
  75g grated mozzarella
  100g mature cheddar, grated
Soured cream, to serve
Put a large frying pan on a high heat, add the corn and fry for five to 10 minutes, until the kernels start to char. Transfer to a large bowl.
Pour the vegetable oil into the pan, then add the black beans and ground cumin, and season well. Fry on a high heat for about five minutes, until the beans start to crisp up and pop a little, then tip into the bowl of charred corn.
Finely grate in the zest of one of the limes, and squeeze in the juice of one and a half limes. Add most of the chopped coriander and chilli, then toss well. Tweak and adjust the seasoning to taste, adding more lime juice or salt as required.
Meanwhile, heat the grill to high. Spread out the tortilla chips on a baking sheet or tray, and cover with both grated cheeses. Pop under the grill for a couple of minutes, until the cheese turns oozy – if if starts to catch, turn off the heat and leave it to finish melting in the residual heat.
Transfer the cheesy nachos to a platter and dot with the corn salsa. Dot with the soured cream and finish with the remaining coriander and chillies scattered over the top.

How growing up in ‘Chemical Valley’ inspired lawyer to sue industry she used to work for
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
12:00:32 UTC
21:00:32 KST

The factories were just part of the landscape for Hélène Duguy growing up in the heart of an area known as France’s “Chemical Valley”.
“Those factories are visible from my mother’s apartment,” says Duguy, 34, whose mother still lives in St-Genis-Laval, south of Lyon.
Until recently, her mother did not accept that there might be any danger associated with living in close proximity to chemical factories. “She just trusted the municipalities to do their job,” Duguy says. “I think it remained something quite remote for her – she understood there was a problem, but Pfas is invisible, so it’s very hard to understand the reality of it and what it could mean for you.”
It was only after a warning was issued about the safety of homegrown food and locally produced eggs that the scale of the contamination became more tangible. “She’s now even considering selling her flat,” Duguy says. “I was with her last weekend and I told her that for me, the contamination she is exposed to continuously is extremely worrying […] Here I feel very close to people who I was raised with, so this makes the issue very relatable, very tangible, and also it makes the fight more concrete.”
Today, as an ambitious young lawyer, Duguy is part of a team taking the companies running the factories to court.
“I have a very deep sense of justice and law has really become the way for me to express that,” says Duguy, who joined the ClientEarth legal team six years ago.
The NGO, which describes itself as “one of the world’s most ambitious environmental organisations”, has brought legal action against some of the biggest and most polluting companies in the world, from the fossil fuel firm Shell to the agricultural company Cargill.
Now it has set its sights on the chemical industry, and Duguy has been appointed to lead the charge. ClientEarth is challenging the EU’s reapproval of one of the most controversial pesticides – glyphosate. It also recently filed a complaint to the European Committee of Social Rights arguing the Belgian government has violated its residents’ rights to protection and health by failing to prevent widespread Pfas pollution.
Pfas are a class of thousands of chemicals used in a wide range of household products. They have been linked to cancer, birth defects, decreased immunity and other serious health problems. They are often described as “forever chemicals” because they do not break down in the environment.
Their use and production are associated with widespread environmental contamination, with pollution recorded at an estimated 17,000 sites across the UK and Europe. “We’re creating sacrifice zones for the sake of a toxic industry that has no place in a European society,” says Duguy. “Our goal is not just to get compensation, but to force regulators to act, and that’s why this litigation path is very strategic.”
As well as working on these cases, Duguy advises and supports lawyers across Europe. She advised lawyers on the Miteni case in Italy, in which 11 former executives from the chemical company received jail sentences of up to 17 years after they were found guilty of polluting the water and soil in a 100 sq km area with Pfas.
She is also supporting lawyers in France who are taking the chemical companies Arkema France and Daikin Chemical France to court for allegedly causing widespread pollution in St-Genis-Laval, at the heart of “Chemical Valley”.
The scale of the pollution in the valley has unravelled over several years after journalistic investigations revealed the extent of the problem. Investigations have found Pfas in the air, soil and water, and in the blood of local people.
Residents in towns around these factories, including in St-Genis-Laval, have been advised not to consume locally produced eggs or poultry meat. And yet despite these risks, locally led environmental campaigns have faced barriers over concerns the cost of the cleanup could affect jobs. This is a narrative Duguy believes has been “built by the industry”.
“When you think about creating a toxic-free environment or a toxic-free society, you need to look at everything holistically. If you have less jobs in those toxic industries, you could create new jobs in safe industries. While we keep providing opportunities for those toxic industries to thrive, we prevent other safe industries from really becoming important for the economy,” she says.
Still, Duguy acknowledges the argument can be hard to make when jobs are on the line. “I think NGOs often don’t really understand what’s happening at the local level,” she says, remembering the pride she herself felt at coming from somewhere that felt like a “hub of innovation”.
It is not just her personal background that Duguy believes makes her well placed to work on these cases. Before she joined ClientEarth, she worked at the law firm Squire Patton Boggs, providing advice to the very companies she is now seeking to hold to account.
In this role, Duguy was part of the firm’s public policy division, where she advised the industry on chemical and environmental law and how they could “limit the impact of those requirements on their businesses”.
While clearly conflicted by the time she spent doing this work, Duguy says the experience gave her an insight into why corporate actors think the way they do.
After one year in the role, she moved to ClientEarth and has set up a network of some of Europe’s best environmental lawyers. “We support each other, find synergies and collaborate,” she says. “It’s incredibly rich and also shows how much people are looking to access justice and to change things at all levels.”
For Duguy, the goal is simple: turn complex legal battles into real-world accountability before the damage becomes irreversible. “The problem with Pfas is that it’s something that you cannot grasp, but hopefully those actions that we’re launching will trigger some kind of emotion that can lead to action,” she says. “If not, we will just continue to face really awful consequences and then try to think of solutions when it’s too late.”

China’s advanced chip supply to surge by 2035 despite equipment bottlenecks, Goldman says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
12:00:13 UTC
21:00:13 KST

China’s advanced chip supply to surge by 2035 despite equipment bottlenecks, Goldman says
The increase will be driven by aggressive capacity expansion at SMIC, China’s largest contract chipmaker, as well as improving yields
China is on track to dramatically slash its deficit in advanced chips over the next decade as domestic foundries rapidly scale up production, though the weak link of lithography threatens to keep full semiconductor independence out of reach, according to US investment bank Goldman Sachs.
The supply of wafers made using 7-nanometre and below advanced processes is projected to grow at a compound annual rate of 46 per cent between 2025 and 2035, far outpacing the 17 per cent growth expected in domestic demand, Goldman analysts said in a report on Monday.
That would narrow the gap between domestic supply and demand to 34 per cent by 2035, from 92 per cent in 2025, according to the investment bank. China’s advanced-node wafer supply is expected to reach 410,000 wafers per month by then, compared with demand of 619,000 wafers.
Goldman’s model assumes SMIC adds monthly capacity of between 30,000 and 50,000 advanced-node wafers each year from 2026 to 2031, before adding another 20,000 wafers per month annually through 2035. It also assumes yields rise from 23 per cent in 2026 to 50 per cent in 2030 and 75 per cent by 2035.
The world’s No 1 foundry, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which started mass-producing 7nm chips in 2018, achieves yields that can exceed 90 per cent, depending on chip design and die size.

Taiwan unveils Strong Bow anti-ballistic missile specs in push for US$1.13 billion funding
Developers disclose details of Chiang Kung hypersonic interceptor with active radar to convince lawmakers to approve funding
The disclosure comes as the government prepares another attempt to secure funding after the system was excluded from a pared-back special defence spending package approved by the opposition-controlled legislature in May.
The defence ministry plans to resubmit Strong Bow and other programmes through a supplementary budget, which the cabinet could consider as early as Thursday before sending it to lawmakers.
The ministry has proposed spending NT$36.1 billion (US$1.13 billion) to produce two Strong Bow systems and 128 interceptor missiles.
Strong Bow, also referred to as Tien Kung (Sky Bow) IV, is a land-based mid-tier anti-tactical ballistic missile system designed to intercept incoming missiles at altitudes of at least 70km (43 miles) – higher than Taiwan’s existing Patriot and Tien Kung III systems.
According to NCSIST, the vertically launched missile can reach hypersonic speeds and uses a two-stage solid-fuel rocket motor. It relies on inertial guidance and radar uplink corrections during midcourse flight before switching to an active seeker in the terminal phase.

Trade between India and Russia growing – Moscow
Bilateral trade turnover between India and Russia grew 8% in the first half of the year, Russian First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov said in Moscow on Monday, adding that both exports and imports showed expansion.
“Our goal is not only to increase the volume of trade turnover, but also to diversify its structure,” Manturov said at the 27th Session of the India-Russia Inter-Governmental Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technological and Cultural Cooperation, which he is co-hosting with visiting Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar.
India and Russia are pursuing a bilateral trade target of $100 billion to be reached by 2030, which was set by President Vladimir Putin in December when he visited New Delhi.
Jaishankar said bilateral trade has increased more than fourfold in the last four years, from around $13 billion in 2021-22 to over $60 billion in 2025-26. He also noted, however, that the rapid expansion has increased the trade imbalance. The Indian foreign minister said progress on market access, removal of tariff and non-tariff barriers, and strengthening payment mechanisms will be critical in addressing the imbalance.
Manturov said the free trade agreement (FTA) that the Russia-led Eurasian Economic Union has been negotiating with India since August last year will be a new driver for sustainable trade growth. “Its preparation is in an active stage and it is important to maintain a high pace of negotiations,” he added.

Agriculture ministry reports NT$10.29 million in losses from torrential rain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:56:09 UTC
20:56:09 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of Agriculture said Monday that heavy rain in late August caused NT$10.29 million (US$323,000) in agricultural losses in southern Taiwan as of 5 p.m.
CNA had earlier reported that losses totaled NT$6.15 million as of 11 a.m., with Tainan accounting for 95% of the total.
The updated figures showed that Tainan suffered NT$7.19 million in losses, accounting for 70% of the total. Yunlin recorded NT$1.18 million, Pingtung NT$1 million, and Kaohsiung NT$920,000 in losses, according to an updated Ministry of Agriculture report.
The rain damaged 203 hectares of crops, with an average damage rate of 20%. The ministry said this was equivalent to the complete loss of 42 hectares of crops.
Watermelons suffered the largest financial loss at NT$3.69 million. Other affected crops included asparagus, non-heading Chinese cabbage, green onions, and water spinach.
The ministry reported no losses to livestock, fisheries, forestry products, or private agricultural facilities.
The figures were based on reports from local governments as of 5 p.m. Monday. The ministry said it would continue updating the agricultural damage report as more information became available.

After 100 days of the deadliest Ebola outbreak, it can be stopped. Here’s how | Jean Kaseya and Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:54:08 UTC
20:54:08 KST

Each time we travel to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), we go first to listen. In Bunia, we have met dozens of community representatives: survivors, women, young people, local organisations, health workers and leaders from affected areas.
Their message was direct: involve us. We know our communities. We know where families seek care, how information moves and why trust is breaking down. Give us the means to help drive the response. They were right.
Ebola spreads through communities – and communities hold the knowledge required to stop it.
They can identify illness early, alert health teams, help trace contacts, challenge dangerous rumours and support families through treatment and safe, dignified burials. The response will move faster when communities lead alongside national authorities and health workers.
The government of the DRC declared its 17th Ebola outbreak 100 days ago after confirmation of the Bundibugyo virus.
The outbreak has since become the deadliest ever recorded, with about 2,500 deaths.
Behind this unprecedented toll are families grieving and communities confronting Ebola alongside conflict, displacement and fragile access to care.
At the centre of it all are the people who show up every day. Health workers care for patients. Laboratory teams identify the virus. Contact tracers follow its path. Community health workers build trust where fear and misinformation have taken hold. Burial teams help families honour their loved ones safely and with dignity.
They are working under extraordinary pressure, often in insecure areas.
Some have contracted Ebola in the line of duty; some have paid with their lives.
Their service must be met with action: protection, training, reliable equipment, timely payment, psychosocial support and access to vaccination, testing and treatment. Their safety is central to stopping transmission.
The response has made progress. Under the leadership of national authorities, Congolese responders, WHO, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) and partners have expanded surveillance, deployed laboratories, supported treatment centres, reinforced infection prevention and delivered essential supplies.
Uganda has interrupted transmission and declared the end of its outbreak, proving the Bundibugyo Ebola virus can be stopped. Decisive national leadership and close cooperation with communities broke the chains of transmission.
The emergency continues in the DRC. Cases are still being detected outside known contact lists. Each one points to a chain that has not yet been found. Every delay gives the virus another opportunity to spread.
The next phase must reach the village.
The DRC’s village-centred strategy takes the response to the places where transmission occurs. Surveillance, testing, treatment, vaccination, infection prevention and community engagement must operate together, close to affected families. Teams need the authority and resources to act quickly.
This is how we stop Ebola at its source: identify infection early, isolate and care for patients safely, follow every contact and prevent the next transmission.
Community leadership will determine whether this works. Women’s groups, young people, religious leaders, traditional healers, survivors and community health workers know where families seek care, how information moves and where trust is weakening. They can identify concerns early, challenge dangerous rumours and help response teams reach people who may otherwise remain invisible.
Their knowledge must shape the response. When they raise concerns, they must see action.
Trust is earned through delivery. A family that reports a suspected case needs safe transport and immediate care. A community that supports vaccination needs clear information about what the vaccine can do. Families who lose loved ones need dignity, compassion and support through safe burial procedures.
Health facilities also require urgent protection. As of 18 August, 163 health workers have been infected and 47 have died in the DRC, while Uganda has recorded four health worker infections. Every facility needs trained staff, protective equipment, clean water and sanitation.
An infection in a health facility places workers, patients and families at risk. A protected health facility becomes a centre for early detection, safe care and public confidence.
Financing remains a decisive test. Governments and partners have made commitments that must now reach the response.
National and local teams need predictable funding for surveillance, laboratories, treatment, vaccination, logistics, infection prevention and community engagement. Frontline workers must be paid on time. Supplies must arrive before stocks run out.
Delayed financing costs lives; fragmented financing leaves gaps. Ebola exploits both.
Cross-border coordination must remain strong. People move to trade, work, study, seek care and support families. Countries need rapid information-sharing, aligned surveillance and prepared health facilities along major routes.
The first 100 days have made the priorities clear: find every case; follow every contact; protect every frontline worker; bring testing, treatment and vaccination closer to every affected community. Turn every pledge into action.
Africa CDC will continue working with the DRC, alongside neighbouring countries, communities and partners, to bring the full strength of international and continental cooperation behind the nationally led response.
This outbreak can be ended. Uganda has shown what focused leadership and community action can achieve. The DRC can do the same.

Iran vows to retaliate against countries that cooperate with fresh US sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:53:10 UTC
20:53:10 KST

Tehran has vowed to retaliate against any country that cooperates with the US attempt to impose fresh sanctions against Iran in what the Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has billed as “the single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary”.
In advance of the US announcement, the United Arab Emirates, Iran’s single biggest trading partner in the Middle East, announced it was ending all trade with Iran, a move Tehran believes was coordinated between Washington and the UAE.
The US has said it will impose sanctions on any country or entity trading with Iran – what is known as secondary sanctions.
The test of the US rhetoric is likely to rest on whether countries such as India, China and Russia believe continued trade with Iran would lead to credible US reprisals against their economies. China has for decades been the main importer of Iranian oil.
In May, the US threatened sanctions against Chinese refiners and the banks funding them, but the Chinese commerce department directed Chinese firms to ignore US warnings over Iranian oil imports, saying the threats were illegitimate and deploying for the first time a government statute designed to render US sanctions ineffective in Chinese jurisdictions.
The US had imposed sanctions on Hengli Petrochemical (Dalian) Refinery Co in April but Washington largely backed off as Donald Trump realised he was risking a wider trade and tariff war with China that the US was likely to lose.
This time the Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson, Lin Jian, again said China opposed unilateral sanctions that lacked basis in international law and China believed that military means, sanctions and pressure tactics were not the solution.
However, unlike in May, Iran’s oil shipments to Asia have already all but ended due to the effectiveness of a US naval blockade of Iranian ports, driving the cost of those cargoes to the highest levels in years. Last week, Iran’s central bank governor, Abdolnaser Hemmati, admitted his country’s crude exports had “virtually stopped” due to the US blockade.
The White House believes the Iranian economy is as a result once again on the brink of collapse due to hyperinflation and lack of foreign exchange income caused by the US blockade of oil exports. The rial was trading at 1.992 million per dollar on the unregulated market on Monday, down 4.5% since the US president announced a “crushing economic operation” against Tehran last week.
But Iran has been under some kind of US economic maximum pressure campaign for more than 20 years and so far survived.
Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, said Tehran would respond with an “earthquake-like” retaliation if Washington proceeded with the proposed measures. He also warned Iran’s Gulf neighbours against joining the US sanctions campaign.
“If the countries surrounding Iran join the Americans in their economic war, not a drop of oil will leave the Persian Gulf and the strait of Hormuz,” Rezaei said, adding that Iran would also target other oil export routes from the Gulf.
Shipping through the strait remained severely disrupted over the weekend, putting further pressure on global energy markets.
Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, dismissed the expected sanctions as a sign of US desperation, arguing that the measures would fail to defeat Tehran. He said the US had shifted from military operations to what he described as “the same old plans”.
Reza Nasri, an international lawyer with links to the Iranian foreign ministry, said: “The announcement is not a measure against Iran. It is a claim of jurisdiction over the world, and every sovereign state on Earth is its real addressee. Iran is merely the occasion. The demand that no country allow its own banks, businesses, airports or ship registries to engage in lawful trade with another country is aimed at everyone else. Sovereignty itself is the target.”
Esmail Baghaei, the Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson, said: “Repeating methods that have previously proven to fail will not produce any different results, except that it shows the extent to which America is hostile and spiteful towards each and every Iranian, because it knows very well that the effects of these sanctions will affect ordinary Iranian citizens.”
He added: “Obliging or intimidating other countries to stop or limit their trade relations with another country means violating the most important foundation of international relations and the most fundamental pillar of the United Nations charter, which is respect for the national sovereignty of countries.”
Hassan Ahmadian, a professor of west Asian studies at the University of Tehran, said: “There isn’t a single new sanction. Everything in Iran has been under primary and secondary sanctions since 2018. Since these sanctions failed to achieve the goals the US and Israel wanted, both sides turned to military action. The big fanfare about an ‘economic war’ is really just a public admission of a major step backward. After failing militarily, Washington is clearly stepping back to square one – the economy.”
He said Iran had been signalling in recent weeks that US economic warfare was no longer an acceptable option for Tehran and it would prefer going to war rather than standing idly by in the face of the US implementing the blockade. He said this involved “Iranian calculations related to military capabilities, the American domestic situation, and the Iranian domestic situation”.
Last Thursday Bessent claimed in an interview with CNBC that “the US will lead the Islamic Republic of Iran to collapse with the toughest sanctions in history”.
The Treasury secretary claimed “the US government is asking its allies and the rest of the world to stop trading with Iran”. He added that the US “will use all its power against anyone who does not comply with this demand”.
“Either the countries are with us or against us,” Bessent said. “It is time for our allies and the rest of the world to decide, and we will destroy the economy of this regime.” Writing in the Financial Times on Sunday, he said: “Total financial isolation can obviate the need for American force while enlarging the sphere of freedom for our allies. Those who sever Iran’s remaining financial and commercial connectivity will reinvigorate their own. They will deepen their access to global capital, reinforce confidence in their markets and attain the standing they seek in the world economy.”
But China and Russia have so far shown no interest in succumbing to US pressure.
By coincidence, Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, flew to Tehran on Monday where he will explore the opportunity to revive talks on the stalled memorandum of understanding signed in June, but not implemented either by Iran or the US largely due to a dispute about whether the memorandum granted Iran interim control over shipping in the strait of Hormuz.

Dutch broadcaster to boycott Eurovision for a second year, calling it a ‘platform for division’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:53:02 UTC

Dutch broadcaster to boycott Eurovision for a second year, calling it a ‘platform for division’
THE HAGUE, Netherlands (AP) — A Dutch broadcaster announced Monday it is boycotting the Eurovision Song Contest for a second year, calling it a “platform for division” because of tensions over Israel’s involvement.
The decision by AVROTROS comes after broadcasters in the Netherlands, Iceland, Ireland, Slovenia and Spain refused to take part in this year’s contest because of Israel’s participation.
“AVROTROS will not participate in the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027 because the event can no longer be considered neutral, with a participating country still involved in a large-scale military conflict,” it said.
The Dutch broadcaster, which has a long history of involvement with the competition, said it was leaving it up to the public network NPO to decide on any Dutch involvement.
“The Eurovision Song Contest was originally created to bring people and countries together. It is undeniable that international conflicts are increasingly affecting the contest, undermining its neutral character,” AVROTROS director-general Taco Zimmerman said in a statement. “The Eurovision Song Contest has therefore become a platform for division.”
Eurovision Song Contest Director Martin Green said in a statement that the organization regretted the move, but respects the views of member broadcasters. The contest is run by the Geneva-based European Broadcasting Union (EBU) — a group of public broadcasters from 56 countries.
“The Eurovision Song Contest has always been a place to bring people together, celebrate diverse communities, and show that a better world is possible even in the most difficult times,” Green said in a statement sent to The Associated Press.
“We will now continue our dialogue with NPO, the umbrella organization for Dutch public service media, regarding the opportunities for another broadcaster to participate. We very much hope that audiences and artists in the Netherlands can continue to be represented in the Eurovision Song Contest,” he added.
In a statement, the NPO said it recognized that “geopolitical tensions are having a divisive effect. That’s why this hasn’t been an easy decision for our colleagues. We will reflect on the upcoming edition and will come back to this at the right moment.”
NPO said it was “too early to comment on the next steps at this point; we’re currently deliberating on that.”
AVROTROS said it has called on the EBU to establish transparent rules for the participation of countries involved in military conflicts. “However, the recently announced changes by the EBU do not provide sufficient confidence that the independent and neutral character of the Eurovision Song Contest has been restored,” it said.
While AVROTROS did not mention Israel by name, it said the network will boycott Eurovision in 2027 “because the event can no longer be considered neutral, with a participating country still involved in a large-scale military conflict.”
It added: “The severe humanitarian suffering in Gaza and the ongoing restrictions on press freedom have contributed to increasing divisions surrounding the Eurovision Song Contest in recent years.”
The contest was founded in 1956, in part to help unite a shattered continent after World War II. It pits acts from dozens of countries against one another for the continent’s musical crown. Bulgarian singer Dara won the event this year with her infectious party anthem “Bangaranga.”
A number of performers and countries have called for the exclusion of Israel, which has taken part in Eurovision since 1973, one of a few non-European countries to compete.
___
Associated Press journalist Jamey Keaten in Geneva contributed.

AP Decision Notes: What to expect in South Carolina’s special U.S. Senate primary runoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

AP Decision Notes: What to expect in South Carolina’s special U.S. Senate primary runoff
WASHINGTON (AP) — South Carolina Republicans will return to the polls Tuesday for the fourth time since June to replace the late U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham on the fall general election ballot.
Graham won the June 9 Republican primary for renomination to the seat he first won in 2002, but his unexpected death on July 11 from an aortic tear created a vacancy not only for his current U.S. Senate seat but also as the party’s pick to compete for another six-year term.
The finalists for the Republican nomination are Graham’s sister, U.S. Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to serve out the remainder of her brother’s current term, and U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman, a five-term congressman who ran for governor earlier in the year and placed third in the primary.
Darline Graham placed first in the Aug. 11 special primary but fell shy of the vote majority needed to avoid Tuesday’s runoff. She received about 33% of the vote, compared to about 25% for Norman. U.S. Rep. Russell Fry placed third with about 20% of the vote.
Graham swept the counties across central South Carolina, including the Columbia area, as well as the state’s Low Country region, which includes Charleston. She scored her highest percentages in counties along the Georgia border.
Norman performed best in the state’s Piedmont and Upcountry regions, including the Greenville area. Fry did best in the eight counties in the Pee Dee and Waccamaw regions that he represents in Congress.
Fry endorsed Graham after he lost the primary. She also has key backing from Republican U.S. Sen. Tim Scott and President Donald Trump, who was an early proponent of Graham and held a campaign rally with her Friday in Myrtle Beach.
Greenville County is the most populous in the state and typically contributes the most votes in statewide Republican primaries. It also has bucked against the front-runners in recent Republican primaries. Norman also carried Greenville County in the gubernatorial primary, and it was one of the only counties Lindsey Graham lost in his final election.
Democratic-leaning Richland and Charleston counties have the next-largest populations and contribute a sizable number of votes in Republican primaries, but they tend to be more influential in Democratic contests.
Horry, Lexington and Spartanburg counties are also large counties that have big impacts on Republican primaries. Spartanburg was the only other county Lindsey Graham lost in the June primary.
The winner will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, a Charleston pediatrician who challenged Republican U.S. Rep. Nancy Mace in the 1st Congressional District in 2022.
Lindsey Graham last won reelection in 2020 with 54% of the vote. Trump carried the state in 2024 with 58% of the vote.
Here are some of the key facts about the election and data points the AP Decision Team will monitor as the votes are tallied:
When do polls close?
Polls close at 7 p.m. ET.
What’s on the ballot?
The Associated Press will provide vote results and declare a winner in the special Republican primary runoff for U.S. Senate.
Who gets to vote?
Voters who participated in the Democratic primary on June 9 may not participate in the special Republican primary runoff on August 25. Only Republican primary voters or registered voters who did not participate in any party’s primary on June 9 may cast ballots in Tuesday’s election.
How many voters are there?
As of Friday, there were about 3.4 million registered voters in South Carolina. Voters in South Carolina do not register by party.
How many people actually vote?
About 465,000 voters cast ballots in the June 9 Republican U.S. Senate primary when Lindsey Graham was renominated. About 336,000 voters participated in the Aug. 11 special Republican U.S. Senate primary.
How much of the vote is cast early or by absentee ballot?
About 19% of the vote in Aug. 11 Republican special primary was cast early in-person or by mail.
As of Friday, about 45,000 ballots had already been cast in Tuesday’s election.
When are early and absentee votes released?
Nearly all of South Carolina’s 46 counties release all or almost all of their early in-person and mail voting results in the first vote update of the night, usually before releasing any results from in-person Election Day voting.
How long does vote-counting usually take?
In the Aug. 11 special primary, the AP first reported results at 7:13 p.m. ET, or 13 minutes after polls closed. The last vote update of the night was at 11:25 p.m. ET with more than 99% of total votes counted.
When will the AP declare a winner?
The AP does not make projections and will declare a winner only when it’s determined there is no scenario that would allow a trailing candidate to close the gap. If a race has not been called, the AP will continue to cover any newsworthy developments, such as candidate concessions or declarations of victory. In doing so, the AP will make clear that it has not yet declared a winner and explain why.
How do recounts work?
In South Carolina, recounts are automatic if the margin between the winning and losing candidates is 1% of the total vote or less. The AP may declare a winner in a race that is subject to a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.
Are we there yet?
As of Tuesday, there will be 70 days until the 2026 midterm elections.

DAKAR, Aug 24 - A mission to observe implementation of a ceasefire between Congolese forces and Rwandan-backed rebels began on Monday in eastern Congo, the first field deployment under a monitoring mechanism established by a Qatari-mediated peace deal signed last year.
• The deployment of the mission is the latest sign of incremental progress under the Qatar-mediated talks, which began last year after AFC/M23 staged a lightning offensive in eastern Congo, seizing the region's two largest cities.
• The two sides signed a peace deal in November 2025 that established a framework for a comprehensive peace agreement and the implementation of ceasefire monitoring arrangements.
• The mission is taking place in the town of Minembwe, South Kivu province, which has seen a surge in fighting in recent weeks between AFC/M23 rebels and government forces, with each side accusing the other of ceasefire violations.
• AFC/M23 accused government forces on Monday of shelling a village near Minembwe, causing civilian casualties and displacing residents. A spokesperson for Congo's armed forces did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
• Congolese government and AFC/M23 representatives met in Switzerland last week and agreed on a new roadmap for negotiations, pointing to renewed momentum in the Doha peace process after months of stalled talks.
• The Doha process is running parallel to U.S.-mediated talks between Congo and Rwanda that Washington hopes will fuel Western investments in eastern Congo's minerals sector.
• Earlier this month, Congolese authorities released 15 prisoners and handed them over to AFC/M23 rebels, in the first known transfer of prisoners under the deal.
• The rebels control large swathes of eastern Congo after staging their offensive last year. REUTERS

Eastern Libya executes 10 convicted on 'terrorism' charges

Breadcrumb
Eastern Libya executes 10 convicted on 'terrorism' charges, sparking rights outcry
Authorities in eastern Libya said they executed 10 people after their conviction by military courts on terrorism-related charges.
The executions, announced Sunday, triggered condemnations by rights groups in the North African country that is divided between rival administrations, each backed by a set of militias and foreign governments.
The office of the military prosecutor in eastern Libya said the 10 people were executed by firing squad after yearslong trials. The office is overseen by the self-styled Libyan National Army, which is commanded by powerful Gen. Khalifa Hifter and controls the eastern and southern parts of Libya.
The people were convicted of charges ranging from joint terrorist groups to assassinations of military personnel and civilians, the office said in a statement.
The statement didn't provide further details about the charges, and when or where the executions took place, but said they were executed after "all legal procedures" were concluded.
Local media reported that the executions took place in the notorious Qarnada military prison in the northeastern town of Shahat, and that their families were notified to receive their bodies from a hospital in the city of Benghazi.
Rights groups condemned the executions and questioned the trials. The National Institution for Human Rights in Libya said military trial of civilians "raises fundamental questions concerning jurisdiction, judicial independence, and guarantees of a fair trial."
The group called for Libya's chief prosecutor and judicial authorities to investigate the executions and all procedures taken through their trials.
It cited a Constitutional Court ruling that said the trial of civilians before military courts for terrorism-related offenses and crimes against the state was unconstitutional.
International rights groups have repeatedly criticized the detention and sometimes execution of people after unfair trials. Amnesty International has said that Libya has retained the death penalty for a wide range of offenses, with courts in both eastern and western Libya continuing to impose death sentences for murder following "grossly unfair trials."
Libya was plunged into chaos and division after a NATO-backed uprising that toppled and killed its longtime autocrat Moammar Gadhafi in 2011.
The county has been divided for years between rival administrations in the east and west, each backed by armed groups and foreign governments.

'Monstrous, mindless': Chidambaram criticises 'One Nation, One Election' plan at House panel meet

Former union minister P Chidambaram opposes the proposed ‘One Nation, One Election’ framework. Photo credit: ANI
NEW DELHI: Former union minister P Chidambaram has opposed the proposed ‘One Nation, One Election’ framework before a joint parliamentary committee, calling the initiative “unconstitutional”, “monstrous” and “mindless”.Chidambaram, who appeared before the panel examining the Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024, and the Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2024, argued that synchronising Lok Sabha and state assembly elections could violate the constitutional framework governing elected legislatures.Sources, quoted by news agency PTI, said the former home and finance minister told the panel that since legislatures are elected for five-year terms, curtailing their tenure would amount to a violation of the basic structure of the Constitution.Chidambaram also said his conscience did not allow him to support the proposed legislation and argued that the government does not have the required two-thirds majority to pass the bills, sources told PTI.The Congress leader described the proposal to hold nationwide elections simultaneously as a “mindless” exercise and strongly opposed the government’s push for simultaneous polls.Trinamool Congress (TMC) MP Sagarika Ghosh, who is also a member of the committee, separately opposed the bills.
Ghosh said the proposal could give “unbridled” power to the Election Commission, sources said.The joint committee, headed by BJP MP PP Chaudhary, also heard representations from around 10 Padma awardees, including Tarlochan Singh, Navin Khanna, Meenakshi Jain and Niru Kumar. While some supported simultaneous elections, others opposed the proposal, warning that it could lead to “chaos” in the country.
The two bills were introduced in the Lok Sabha in December 2024 and subsequently referred to the joint committee for detailed examination.The proposal followed recommendations from a high-level committee headed by former president Ram Nath Kovind, which suggested holding Lok Sabha, state assembly and local body elections simultaneously in a phased manner. Union Home Minister Amit Shah was also a member of the panel.India had earlier held Lok Sabha and state assembly elections together from 1951-52 through 1967. The cycle was disrupted after premature dissolutions of some state assemblies in 1968 and 1969, followed by the early dissolution of the Fourth Lok Sabha in 1970 and fresh general elections in 1971.Since then, staggered election cycles have become the norm, with several Lok Sabha and state assembly terms ending before their full five-year tenure.

Pluto still isn’t a planet—unless Earth’s moon is, too
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:39:26 UTC
20:39:26 KST

Twenty years ago Pluto lost its planethood, and I’m partially to blame.
“Blame” is a strange word to use for what seems like a matter of mere semantics; after all, Pluto exists as an intriguing world worthy of study and exploration, regardless of labels. But after two decades in the rearview, Pluto’s demotion still stirs anger and controversy, and many people regard its change in status as a very bad thing.
To everyone upset about this: I’m truly sorry, but Pluto had it coming.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
To understand why, do one thing: gaze up at the moon during a long summer twilight, note the dark patterns of ancient volcanic flows mottling its surface, and ask yourself a simple, sincere question: Is the moon a planet? I think that you, like me, will agree that the obvious answer is no. And that means that you, like me, think that Pluto isn’t a planet either.
You might object that your opinion of the moon has no effect on your feelings for Pluto, but equating these two objects is unavoidable for anyone seeking to manufacture a philosophically consistent reason for Pluto’s planethood. The main argument, these days, for why Pluto’s status should be restored boils down to an astrophysical version of what’s best known as “the duck test”: if something looks, walks and quacks like a duck, it’s probably a duck. In Pluto’s case, the idea is that “geophysically” it’s a planet, which simply means it looks like a planet (it’s round!) and acts like a planet (it probably once had active volcanoes, albeit of water!). Earth’s moon—which also has the advantage of being 50 percent larger than Pluto and of having volcanoes that once spewed actual lava instead of mere water—fully deserves planethood by these very same metrics.
Yet, according to the current formal definition from the International Astronomical Union, which was so controversially set on August 24, 2006, Pluto’s “problem” is its failure to “clear the neighborhood around its orbit” rather than anything intrinsic to the world itself. This phrase is a complicated way of simply acknowledging the fact that Pluto sits within the Kuiper Belt, a vast swarm of bodies that go around the sun in similar orbits beyond Neptune. Astronomers call this way of looking at a population a “dynamical” classification. What matters is not just the body itself but also its relationship to the solar system around it. Simply remove the dynamical classification part of the definition, critics say, and Pluto reverts to its former lofty status!
And they’re entirely correct. The trouble is that Pluto would not be alone.
The reason the moon doesn’t qualify as a planet is dynamics—where and how the body orbits. When you acknowledge that you don’t think the moon is a planet, you are acknowledging that dynamics actually matter, too. And it’s not just Earth’s moon that would suddenly join the elite “planetary” club. There are many round, massive, geologically interesting objects in our solar system that, viewed in isolation, look and act somewhat like planets. By one count, if we removed the dynamical part of the classification, we would make planets out of one asteroid, four moons of Jupiter, seven of Saturn, five of Uranus, one of Neptune, and then maybe 10 (or maybe 200!) objects in the Kuiper Belt, where Pluto also lies.
I arguably have more to gain by this looser, more flexible accounting than anyone: I discovered seven of those most distant bodies, so I would instantly become the most prolific planet discoverer in solar system history. This could be nice, I guess, but instead I’d feel somewhat embarrassed. Every time I looked up and saw the moon in the sky, I would be reminded that my newfound historical stature would require me to accepti something that seemed obviously wrong: if I had discovered multiple planets, then our moon definitely would be a planet—which it is not. Surely you’d agree.
I can already anticipate the vociferous boos from Pluto’s proplanetary contingent. But what is the true nature of our disagreement? Why would any scientist—or anyone, really—support a definition of the word “planet” that goes against 500 years of common usage and that seems obviously wrong to most people?
Yes, it could be a strongly held belief that the geophysical definition of what makes a planet is of great importance. But, if true, these strongly held beliefs are suspiciously recently formed. No hint of the importance of this definition was even mentioned prior to the discussions that led to Pluto’s demotion, though the evidence of the geophysical nature of the moon has been evident to our eyes for centuries. Whether discussing the past of NASA’s moonwalking Apollo astronauts or the future of the crewed landings planned for the agency’s Artemis program, no one talks about these missions as voyages to another planet.
Similarly, we have sent spacecraft to visit every single one of the moons of the other planets that are on the upgrade list; never, in the previous decades of those visits, did anyone suggest that we were instead visiting planets. We found active volcanoes on Jupiter’s moon Io, vast lakes of liquid methane and ethane on Saturn’s moon Titan, geysers and a nitrogen atmosphere on Neptune’s moon Triton. But as fascinating as each of these bodies was found to be, no one felt that they suddenly deserved planethood.
The real reason for the attempt to promote all of these new bodies, it seems evident, is nostalgia—not just for Pluto but also for a time when our conceptions of the solar system and the universe at large were simpler (and less informed).
You might consider scientists immune to nostalgia, but they were children once, too—and some of them grew up in a solar system with nine planets, no less. A few of them then spent years of their lives studying Pluto—and even built and launched a spacecraft to go there, waiting a decade for its arrival and the spectacular images of that world’s nitrogen glaciers, suspiciously volcanolike mountains and bizarre system of moons. After all of this, having Pluto suddenly stripped of planetary status must feel like a betrayal. Even I feel it. I, too, had a solar system poster on my wall as a kid and stared at Pluto’s odd and distant orbit out on the edge. I could never imagine that someday there would be posters without it—or that I would help to make that happen.
Nostalgia is powerful, for schoolchildren and eminent scientists alike. But nostalgia is not a particularly strong argument in a scientific discussion, so it has to be hidden behind something that sounds dispassionate and scientific, such as a newly minted geophysical definition. And if your argument must seem scientific, it must certainly also be internally consistent. Tragically, the sole scientific-sounding definition of “planet” that allows Pluto to hang on must, for consistency’s sake, encompass all of these other bodies. If Pluto is to be a planet, then the moon—and many others—must be planets, too. Such is the price of your nostalgia.
A better choice is to admit what we all know in our minds, if not our hearts: the moon is not a planet. That acknowledgement comes with the corollary of letting Pluto’s planethood go. Something can be beloved, complex, and captivating and still not be a planet; there is liberation—redemption, even—in realizing this world remains undiminished.
To the scientists and to the former schoolkids and to the NASA administrators who are sad when they think about Pluto’s exclusion, we should extend our sympathy. It’s hard. But we can also offer them a consolation: the sight of the moon hanging in the sky, majestic and battered, unencumbered by the collateral damage of misplaced nostalgia, footprints and tire tracks still preserved on its dusty surface, waiting for our return. Best of all, a day will come, finally, when the moon is no longer the lone holder of such hallmarks of humanity. Someday humans could possibly land on Mars. Let’s let them feel joy and awe to be the first to walk on another planet. Let’s not pretend that we already did that more than a half-century ago.
This is an opinion and analysis article, and the views expressed by the author or authors are not necessarily those of Scientific American.

Photos: Towering landfill collapse kills 30 in Guinea’s capital, Conakry
A landfill collapse in Conakry kills 30, injures six, and destroys homes after heavy rains in Guinea’s capital.
At least 30 people have been killed after a towering heap of rubbish collapsed at the largest landfill in Guinea’s capital, Conakry, following heavy overnight rains, authorities said.
The landslide struck shortly after 2am (02:00 GMT) on Sunday at the Dar es Salam open-air dump, sending a mountain of waste crashing onto nearby shacks.
Rescue workers dug through debris to reach survivors as six critically injured people were taken to hospital and several homes were reported destroyed.
The main dumping ground for the city of two million people had been scheduled for closure on Sunday, officials said.
Residents had received eviction notices, but many families were still in the area when the collapse happened. “We will ensure that the remaining families are relocated elsewhere,” said Territorial Administration Minister Dienabou Toure who was at the scene.
Despite vast mineral wealth, including the world’s largest bauxite reserves, Guinea remains one of West Africa’s poorest countries, with nearly half the population living below the national poverty line.
