Hong Kong to offer free dental check-ups to preschoolers from September
More than 70 per cent of kindergartens join scheme bringing screenings and fluoride treatment to campuses
Hong Kong preschoolers will be offered free dental check-ups starting next month, with more than 70 per cent of the city’s kindergartens already signed up for the new government initiative.
The Department of Health announced on Monday the launch of the Outreach Oral Health Programme for Preschool Children on September 1, aimed at fostering oral hygiene habits and preventing tooth decay at an early stage.
Under the scheme, dental teams from 23 participating service providers will visit kindergartens across all 18 districts once each academic year, offering pupils aged 32 months or older free oral screenings and risk assessments.
“Children usually have a full set of milk teeth by the age of three. The period between the ages of three and six is the most crucial time to protect these teeth,” said Dr Kitty Hse Mei-yin, consultant in charge of the dental service at the department.
“At this stage, children love to eat, which makes reinforcing dental care and oral hygiene extremely important.”
Hse said that conducting examinations in a familiar school environment helped ease young children’s anxieties.

Israel recovers gun-running boat whose 1948 sinking caused deep divide that persist to present
Israel announced on Monday it had recovered the wreckage of the Altalena, an arms-smuggling boat whose sinking by the Israeli military in 1948.
The Altalena had set sail from France loaded with weapons packed for the Irgun, the militant Zionist force considered a "terrorist organisation" that conducted attacks against the British colonial authorities and civilian Palestinian population to forcibly establish Israel.
In June 1948, Israeli forces opened fire and sank the boat in waters off Tel Aviv on the orders of David Ben Gurion, Israel's first prime minister. He wanted to exert his authority and prevent the emergence of any paramilitary rival to the Israeli military in the month-old state, which was in the throes of committing ethnical cleansing of the Palestinian population and attacking neighbouring Arab countries.
"At 12:30 am, at a depth of 503 metres, west of the coast of Israel, the Altalena ship was located intact -- 78 years after that painful and seminal event that shook the young State of Israel," Heritage Minister Amihai Eliyahu said.
Sixteen Irgun members and three Israeli soldiers were killed. Irgun chief Menachem Begin asked his fighters to surrender to Israeli authorities with words that would become famous: "There will be no civil war with the enemy at our gates."
The conflict pitted against each other the two political blocs that would define Israel. Begin became prime minister in 1977, ushering in the rise of right-wing nationalists and sweeping out the supposedly socialist movement launched under Ben Gurion.
Eliyahu, who announced the salvaging of the Altalena, hails from the far-right, which has taken power as part of a government led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
He called the Altalena "the story of a deep national wound, and the story of the historical responsibility that Menachem Begin showed when he prevented a civil war".
"A country that is not afraid to touch on the painful chapters of its history is a stronger country," he said.
Israel erected a monument to the fallen Altalena militants in 2008 on the Tel Aviv seafront and has been searching for the wreckage for years, with crews often working in secrecy.
It was not immediately known what would happen to the ship's wreckage.

Former Hong Kong teacher gets 18 months in prison for molesting student twice

Former Hong Kong teacher gets 18 months in prison for molesting student twice
Judge Gary Lam describes defendant Cheng Hon-sze’s case as serious and says there is no room for a reduced sentence
A Hong Kong court sentenced a former teacher on Monday to 18 months in prison for molesting a student, aged 15 at the time, on two occasions in 2020.
District Judge Gary Lam Kar-yan described defendant Cheng Hon-sze’s case as serious and said there was no room for a reduced sentence, even if it was a first offence.
Cheng, now 32, was sentenced at Tsuen Wan Court after being found guilty of two counts of indecent assault for groping the student and making her perform an obscene act in May and October 2020.
He was cleared of seven other counts of indecent assault as the court ruled the girl on those occasions had not expressly refused the defendant’s advances or that the acts involved were not considered inherently indecent.
The defendant earlier admitted to having repeatedly engaged in intimate acts with the victim in the school’s music storage room and other locations.
Lam sentenced Cheng to one year in jail for each count of indecent assault, while ordering that the prison terms be served as a partially consecutive sentence, bringing the overall period down to 18 months.

'Insult to 4cr people of Telangana': CM Revanth Reddy flays Centre over US visit block

Telangana CM Revanth Reddy (File photo)
NEW DELHI: Telangana chief ministerRevanth Reddy on Monday accused the Centre of "insulting" 4 crore people of the state by declining permission for his visit to the United States.Reddy claimed that the move showed the "Centre's discrimination" against Telangana and said that the issue would be raised in Parliament."The ministry of external affairs examined my proposal and declined clearance from the political angle. I want to ask Prime Minister Narendra Modi: if there was nothing political about my foreign tour, why was permission granted for England but denied for the US?"He also questioned why Gujarat chief minister Bhupendra Patel was allowed to visit the US and Canada from August 17 to 24 as part of the Vibrant Gujarat 2047 initiative to attract investments, while his proposed US visit under Telangana Rising 2047 was rejected."Not just America but any country in the world. If they are going to come and invest in my state, whatever regulations are made by the government of India, we want to welcome everyone, we want to protect their investment, we will make sure to get profit from Telangana, so this is very simple. This is the only political reason Narendra Modi has refused to let me travel to the US to promote Telangana," Reddy added.
Reddy's remarks came days after the ministry of external affairs denied him permission to visit the United States, saying that the programme submitted for the trip was not considered appropriate to the office he holds and the purpose of the visit.
MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal, in a briefing, said that visits by chief ministers and other dignitaries are assessed by the ministry before political clearance is granted."Let me say that the visit of chief ministers, as indeed of other dignitaries, are assessed by the ministry of external affairs in order to accord political clearance," Jaiswal said."The programme proposed, in such cases, should be appropriate to the office held and the purpose of the visit. In this particular case, that was not so in respect of the United States, and therefore the clearance was denied," he said.

Birdfy Nest Duo Review: My Own Private Nature Documentary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

Even though I've been a bird-watcher most of my life, nothing prepared me for the experience of witnessing—on my phone—the entire process of birds being born in my own backyard.
I’ve maintained a regular “dumb” nest box for years, the birthplace of generations of black-capped chickadees. I’ve seen them going in and out, but I always wondered what was happening in there, especially the year I opened up the box in the fall and found five deceased fledglings at the bottom. How could this have happened? I wondered.
Thanks to the Birdfy Nest Duo smart nesting box and its built-in thermometer and hygrometer, I now at least have an educated guess. (The poor things likely overheated during an early season heat wave.) Being able to watch the entire nesting operation from all angles, starting with excavation and egg-laying and ending in hatching and fledging, has been one of the most educational and entertaining bird-watching experiences I have ever had, and something I'd recommend to anyone interested in birds, nature, or just life science in general.
Eye Spy
Birdfy makes three smart nest boxes in addition to the Duo. The original, the Birdfy Nest, has one camera—located inside the box—and can only hang from an eye hook screwed into the top. There's also a version made out of solid fir in contrast to the others’ lightweight bamboo. I have also tested Birdfy’s artful Polygon, but persistent connection issues prevented me from using it this season.
I have not tested the first two single-camera versions, but I can't imagine not having a second camera outside the hole to see who's unexpectedly poking their head in. (At one point in my testing, it was a confused flicker; another, a curious starling—this is when I learned chickadees can hiss). It's also critical to be able to pole-mount the box to keep it away from predators.
The Nest Duo is substantial—16 inches tall and about 8 pounds—with one 1080p HD camera facing the nest entry hole on the exterior and another tucked discreetly inside the nest box itself. There's also an internal hygrometer (humidity) and thermometer (temperature) that show readings on the live view in Birdfy's easy-to-use app. There are four easy-to-install, screw-on entry hole sizes for different species, from 0.9 inches for wrens up to 2 inches for starlings or bluebirds, along with corresponding metal predator guards to prevent chewing. The entire side of the box opens with a latch for easy cleaning and access.
In the app, each screen capture appears as a split-screen image, which you can tap to view 20-second videos (with audio) of both the inside and the outside of the box. The videos are immediately downloadable and shareable—no subscription is needed.
The screen captures work much like one of Birdfy's smart bird feeders, but with images shunted to sections labeled “Prelude,” “Nesting,” “Brooding,” “Nestling,” “Fledgling,” and “End.” There seemed to be no rhyme or reason for what process the app thought was happening at the time (for example, if a nestling was simply turned around, the app asked if it should label it as “Fledgling”), but this story format was easy enough to ignore onscreen.
House Hunters
In March of this year, at the beginning of nesting season on the West Coast, I installed the Duo with the 1-inch entry hole on a pole stand and mounted the included solar panel below the box with hose clamps. Black-capped chickadees were consistently interested, popping in and looking around, but something was preventing them from staking a claim. It took me a while to realize they were looking askance at the holes on the metal tray “floor,” which is perforated for drainage. The idea is that this tray can be inserted into one of a series of slots to increase or decrease the nest cavity depth, depending on your local species' preference.

AfD turns 'Vespa of East Germany' into election campaign vehicle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:28:56 UTC
20:28:56 KST

AfD turns 'Vespa of East Germany' into election campaign vehicle
QUEDLINBURG, Germany, Aug 24 - The sound of thousands of engines filled the festival grounds of the medieval German village of Quedlinburg on Sunday as Ulrich Siegmund, the far-right AfD's charismatic candidate in a key vote next month, led out a motorcade atop a blue moped.
Nearly 5,000 people turned out for the Alternative for Germany (AfD) campaign event-cum-motorcycle show ahead of elections in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt on September 6, in which it could become the first far-right party to take power at a state level since the Nazi era.
The AfD has seized onto "the Vespa of East Germany," the beloved Simson brand, to appeal to the strong sense of East German identity that lingers 35 years after reunification, even as a significant number of young people, including Siegmund, never experienced a divided Germany themselves.
SIMSON BRINGS BACK POSITIVE MEMORIES
"My parents instilled in me an understanding of everything that happened back then. Not everything was wonderful," the 35-year-old Siegmund told the crowd on Sunday.
"But this Simson culture represents individual freedom of movement. It stands for a time when we in this country stuck together," he said.
The AfD's manifesto "Vision 2026" argues that eastern Germany should be seen as a model for the rest of the country rather than a disadvantaged region.
Based on the 2025 federal election, their strategy is working. Among Saxony-Anhalt voters aged roughly 18-34, AfD support rose to 40% from about 25% in the previous election in 2021.
Julian, who declined to give his last name, said it was great the AfD was organising meet-ups for fans.
"If someone else had done it, we obviously wouldn't have taken part," said the 24-year-old from the neighbouring eastern German state of Thuringia who, along with his brother, attended Sunday's event with his green Simson motorcycle.
BRAND WITH HISTORY
The Simson company began as a weapons manufacturer run by two Jewish brothers in the mid-19th century whose family was forced to flee as the Nazis rose to power.
After World War Two and the separation of Germany, the company focused on motorcycles and mopeds, with their distinctive Schwalbe, known as the "Vespa of East Germany," and sporty S50 becoming particularly popular models with young people by letting them bypass the often years-long waiting period for cars.
The Simson family, who now live in the United States, have publicly criticised the AfD's use of their namesake.
"The threats against immigrants, people of other skin colours and sexual minorities are something we want no part of," said descendent and family spokesperson Dennis Baum at an anti-AfD rally in Germany last month.
The AfD has rejected allegations of racism, saying it just wants stricter controls over immigration.
The Center for Intercultural Understanding Dresden (ZVID) is running an online petition with nearly 24,000 signatories calling on the current trademark holder to protect the brand's reputation by sending a cease-and-desist letter to the AfD.
Roughly 100 counter-demonstrators at Sunday's event were cordoned off by police in a lot whose view of the grounds was obscured by trees and throngs of supporters.
ROOTS OF EAST GERMAN IDENTITY
East German identity emerged mainly after reunification, shaped by the experience of adapting to West German political, economic and cultural structures and by feelings of disadvantage, according to sociologist Daniel Kubiak from the Humboldt University of Berlin.
This shared feeling of structural disadvantage and unequal opportunities, which young people learned through their parents' experiences, has often been neglected by mainstream politics, creating space for the AfD to appeal to eastern voters through identity politics, he added.
While eastern Germany has largely caught up in terms of living standards, many young people still report concerns about financial security: A 2024 government-commissioned survey found 67% of respondents from the east considered it most important, versus 62% of their western peers.
However, Kubiak described the AfD's version of East German identity as vague and inconsistent, arguing the party mainly uses feelings of devaluation and marginalisation to mobilise support rather than offering a coherent East German identity.
"The AfD's identity narrative can always adapt very well to where they are," he said. REUTERS

China Focus: Chinese micro-dramas race onto global stage
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
19:25:43 CST
20:25:43 KST

CHONGQING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- By 10 a.m., a film and animation park in southwest China's Chongqing Municipality is already buzzing with activity. Crews are scattered across their respective sets -- interrogation lights snap on inside a "police station" soundstage, while upstairs in a "hospital ward," a nurse slowly pushes a medicine cart down the corridor.
Repurposed from a disused commercial property, the park in the Liangjiang New Area now hosts nearly 300 realistic filming sets and accommodates about 1,000 productions a year, turning out more than 700 short-form dramas annually. A 40-episode micro-drama can be wrapped up in as little as four days.
"You can literally show up with just a script," said Zeng Li, head of the park. The facility provides lighting, equipment, costumes, props and extras, alongside accommodation and catering, a turnkey package that allows crews to hit the ground running. With everything under one roof, productions can move seamlessly between scenes, significantly boosting overall efficiency.
"Micro-dramas are all about emotional resonance," director Bao Yinfei said, noting that unlike traditional TV series, micro-dramas feature fewer setups, more plot twists and faster pacing, allowing them to grab viewers' attention in a matter of seconds. "This storytelling style transcends language and geographical boundaries. If the story resonates, it can travel."
"This production model has pushed every link in the chain, from filming and editing to acting, to pick up the pace, giving rise to a standardized and streamlined ecosystem for micro-drama production in China," Bao added.
What's happening in Chongqing is not an isolated case -- it reflects a broader phenomenon reshaping the global entertainment landscape. Made-in-China micro-dramas, with their cliffhanger-packed storytelling and hyper-efficient shoots, have evolved from a domestic craze into a full-blown cultural export powerhouse.
According to a 2025 white paper on the development of China's micro-drama industry, the overseas micro-drama market generated a total revenue of over 1.52 billion U.S. dollars between January and August of 2025, marking a year-on-year increase of 194.9 percent. Global downloads of micro-drama apps surged 370.4 percent to approximately 730 million over the same period.
Chinese companies dominate the overseas micro-drama market, with 90 percent of the top 20 revenue-generating apps worldwide backed by Chinese origins or investment.
Beijing and south China's tech hub Shenzhen have taken the lead in micro-drama exports, housing a cluster of companies spanning content production, platform operations and overseas distribution. Other cities, including Chongqing, Hangzhou in east China, and Chengdu in southwest China, are rapidly catching up by leveraging their strengths in online literature, internet technology and cultural resources. A micro-drama shot at a Chongqing studio and polished through distribution platforms in Beijing or Shenzhen can end up on phone screens in Tokyo, Los Angeles or Jakarta.
But winning these markets takes more than just dubbing or subtitling. "Previously, we mostly translated successful domestic shows and sent them out," Zeng said. "Now, more projects are being developed with overseas audiences in mind right from the script stage."
In Japan, for instance, Zeng noted that local audiences have shown a strong appetite for stories about women's empowerment and workplace dynamics. As a result, Chinese producers have taken genres already validated in the domestic market and adapted them for Japanese viewers, weaving local social nuances and emotional cues into the narratives.
"Going global is no longer just about translating subtitles," Zeng said. "It's about reimagining the entire production chain, from scripts and casting to shooting, post-production workflows and even distribution strategies."
"We're moving toward telling stories in a way that local audiences can truly connect with," she added.
As high-speed production becomes the industry norm, leading players are moving the competition to a new level. Maiya Media, a digital culture and technology company based in Chongqing, is now seeking to layer its micro-dramas with deeper cultural substance. Its overseas platform, NetShort, has already reached more than 40 countries and regions.
To sustain this momentum, the company has also partnered with Sichuan International Studies University in Chongqing to establish a multilingual translation and production base for micro-drama exports, supporting international distribution through talent training in translation and overseas content operations.
"We respect local cultures and leverage technology to promote the translation and localization of premium micro-dramas overseas," said He Yunchang, founder and chairman of Maiya Media. "Meanwhile, we hope that overseas audiences will also be able to learn about China's rich culture and contemporary vitality through the characters, scenes and stories in our dramas." ■

Third time the charm? Democrat Christina Bohannan tries again in pivotal US House race in Iowa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:23:01 UTC
20:23:01 KST

Third time the charm? Democrat Christina Bohannan tries again in pivotal US House race in Iowa
COLUMBUS JUNCTION, Iowa (AP) — It may have seemed out of place for a university professor from the liberal enclave of Iowa City to be holding court at a roadside bar and grill in a rural county where Republican Donald Trump won overwhelmingly two years ago.
But that’s part of Christina Bohannan’s long learning curve as a Democratic candidate for Congress.
“It’s a big district. It takes a lot of time to get around, get people to know you and trust you,” Bohannan told a couple dozen voters in the tiny Louisa County town of Columbus Junction on a recent Sunday afternoon.
She would know. It’s her third crack at it.
Bohannan lost to Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks in Iowa’s 1st Congressional District in 2022 and 2024. Now she’s banking on Trump’s sagging popularity, healthcare struggles and economic concerns to put her over the top in a race that could help Democrats regain control of the U.S. House.
Miller-Meeks is digging in for a difficult campaign, describing Bohannan as a “radical progressive.” If Bohannan pulls off a victory this time, it could be the first ripple of what Democrats see as a potential national wave.
The Democrat is reaching into rural counties to shave the Republican edge
That’s why Bohannan was in Louisa County, a place she did not visit in the months leading up to the 2024 election, when she lost to Miller-Meeks by only 799 votes.
It was the second-closest House race that year, and far closer than Bohannan’s loss in 2022, when she fell short by 23,000 votes.
Iowa’s 1st District is a microcosm of the state, largely rural with urban and suburban pockets. A geographic area larger than Massachusetts, more than half of its 20 counties have populations of less than 20,000 residents.
Cindy Starr and her husband Tim Knutson had never met Bohannan before they made the drive from nearby Wapello to see her at 92 Roadside, a Louisa County social hub named for the highway that runs past it.
“We’d never heard of any campaign event for her before,” said Starr, a 62-year-old retired social worker.
“Somebody rang our doorbell,” said Knutson, a 60-year-old retired meatpacking plant manager. “That’s never happened before.”
Two years ago, she lost the county by almost 1,400 votes.
This time, Bohannan has a more aggressive ground game, reaching out in rural counties she lost, but also beginning her canvassing in January as opposed to April. Her campaign’s door-knockers travel with a letter from Bohannan introducing herself.
Pushing against the image of a left-wing college professor
Bohannan’s day job — University of Iowa law professor — can be tricky in a district where Trump won by 8.4 percentage points in 2024 and where the school is often parodied by Republicans as a haven for left-wing liberals.
“I’m not some radical,” said the 55-year-old former environmental engineer whose legal scholarship has focused on intellectual property, business innovation and copyright law.
She portrays her low-income upbringing in rural central Florida, her father’s nomadic life as a construction worker and her family’s healthcare crises during her youth as experiences that echo across the Mississippi Valley district where union manufacturing jobs have been declining for decades.
“Iowa is just a really good, common-sense state full of fair-minded, common-sense people,” she told The Associated Press. “Sometimes the Republicans have a point. I think tax dollars are precious. I think sometimes we do tend to stifle economic growth with maybe unnecessary regulation.”
Miller-Meeks did not agree to an interview.
Bohannan has been gaining ground in the district
Along with trying to shave the Republican advantage in the district’s dozen-plus rural counties, Bohannan is also trying to gain a foothold in its more urban and suburban hubs.
Johnson County, with Iowa City and its teeming suburbs, and Scott County’s economically diverse cities of Davenport and Bettendorf help make the district among the most competitive in the country.
Bohannan won more than 70% of the vote in Johnson County in 2022 and 2024. She also improved her performance in Scott County, losing in 2022 but winning narrowly there in 2024.
Those gains in a high-turnout presidential year, combined with the very narrow final margin — after a recount — made the decision simple for Bohannan to sign up a third time.
“That was a big part of it. That means tens of thousands of Trump voters split their ballot and voted for me,” she told The Associated Press after a stop at a Scott County Democrats’ picnic in Bettendorf. “It’s not always easy to get people, especially in this toxic political environment, from the other party to support you. But we’re taking the time. We’re going to every corner of the district.”
Now, she is trying to hold the edge in Scott County, hoping the recent move of more independent voters into the Democrats’ ranks continues.
In another potential boost to Bohannan, Democratic voter registration in Iowa rose more than Republican registration ahead of the June primaries.
In Scott County, the district’s most populous, the trend has continued since the primary, said Terry Olsen, vice chairman of the Scott County Democrats and a former Republican.
“Every month it’s been moving,” Olsen said, though Democrats still narrowly trail Republicans and independent voters in the county. “But it’s a different strategy than 2024, trying to grab more of that rural vote and still boost turnout in the cities. That’s the hope, at least.”
Trump’s agenda could drag down Miller-Meeks
Bohannan believes that Trump’s failure to curb inflation since returning to the White House will drag down Miller-Meeks, who was first elected in 2020.
Miller-Meeks voted for measures blocking Congress from challenging Trump’s emergency tariff actions, and the trade war has cut U.S. soybean sales. She has voted in support of Trump’s ability to continue U.S. military operations against Iran, as drivers in her district pay nearly $4 per gallon for gas and farmers pay $5 per gallon for diesel fuel.
And Miller-Meeks last year supported Trump’s signature tax-break and spending cuts bill, which is expected to reduce federal Medicaid spending over the coming years. Hospitals and other healthcare providers have warned that the changes could put additional financial pressure on rural facilities that rely heavily on Medicaid reimbursements.
Miller-Meeks, a physician, defended her record in a statement by saying “I’ve spent my career on the side of patients, not the big insurance companies and bureaucrats standing between them and the care they need.”
She said the legislation included “common sense provisions the majority of Americans support,” and she said Bohannan “would have kept subsidies flowing straight to big profitable insurance companies that deny claims, jack up premiums, and restrict which doctors you can see.”
Healthcare funding pressures have surfaced in Miller-Meeks’ district. MercyOne Clinton Medical Center announced it would end its obstetrics, labor and delivery services in 2026, citing rising costs, staffing shortages, inadequate reimbursement, and changes to Medicaid policy among the factors.
“In the past, when I ran the last couple of times, people weren’t entirely clear on what Miller-Meeks had been up to,” Bohannan said. “And now people know what they are paying at the grocery store. They know what they are paying at the gas pump.”

AP Decision Notes: What to expect in Oklahoma’s state primary runoff

Unknown Publisher

AP Decision Notes: What to expect in Oklahoma’s state primary runoff
WASHINGTON (AP) — Oklahoma Republicans will return to the polls Tuesday to settle an expensive nomination fight for governor, while Democrats will pick a nominee for U.S. Senate. Voters will also decide two statewide ballot measures, including one that would add a voter identification requirement to the state constitution.
The outcome of the gubernatorial primary to replace term-limited Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt has major implications for the fall general election, as Democrats haven’t won the Oklahoma governorship in 20 years. It will also further test President Donald Trump’s endorsement power.
State Attorney General Gentner Drummond and former state Sen. Mike Mazzei were the top vote-getters among nine candidates in the June 16 primary, with Drummond just edging Mazzei, 26.25% to 25.97%. Both fell far short of the majority needed to avoid Tuesday’s runoff.
Drummond narrowly carried Oklahoma and Cleveland counties in the Oklahoma City area, while Mazzei edged Drummond in Tulsa County. The two split most of the counties in the Tulsa area.
The two have poured millions from their personal fortunes into the race, with Mazzei loaning his campaign more than $11 million, compared with $3 million for Drummond, according to state campaign finance records. Mazzei has spent $12.3 million in the race overall, while Drummond has spent about $9.1 million. Loans aside, Drummond has far outraised Mazzei in campaign contributions, $7.1 million to about $1.5 million.
Trump endorsed Mazzei ahead of the primary, while also lobbing insults at Drummond. Trump’s picks overall in 2026 have had a strong record at the ballot box, but his endorsement is not a guarantee of victory, especially in gubernatorial primaries. The president’s picks for Iowa governor and Georgia governor lost their nomination bids, while his pick for South Carolina governor was forced to a runoff and ultimately lost the nomination after the president also endorsed her opponent.
The Oklahoma winner will face Democratic state House Minority Leader Cyndi Munson in the general election.
In the U.S. Senate race, nurse N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas received about 45% of the Democratic primary vote, short of the majority required to avoid a runoff. Attorney and minister Jim Priest placed second with about 24% of the vote, despite a massive fundraising advantage. He raised almost six times more than Thomas heading into the primary and increased his advantage heading into the runoff. As of Aug. 5, the Thomas campaign reported having only $455 in the bank, compared to about $56,000 for Priest.
The winner will face Republican U.S. Rep. Kevin Hern, who won the five-way primary with about 70% of the vote. The state last elected a Democrat for U.S. Senate in 1990.
Also before voters is State Question 846, which would amend the state constitution to require voters to provide proof of identity in order to cast a ballot, which is already required under state law.
State Question 844 would affect the reimbursements that local governments receive from the state for lost property tax revenue under an incentive program for manufacturing companies.
Here are some of the key facts about the election and data points the AP Decision Team will monitor as the votes are tallied:
When do polls close?
Polls close at 7 p.m. CT, which is 8 p.m. ET.
What’s on the ballot?
The Associated Press will provide vote results and declare winners in primary runoff elections for U.S. Senate, governor, state school superintendent, labor commissioner, insurance commissioner, state Senate and state House, as well as for the two statewide ballot measures.
Who gets to vote?
Voters registered with a political party may participate only in their own party’s primary runoffs. Democrats may not vote in a Republican primary runoff or vice versa. Independent or unaffiliated voters may not participate in either party’s runoff elections. All registered voters may cast ballots on the statewide ballot measures.
How many voters are there?
As of July 31, there were about 2.4 million registered voters in Oklahoma, including about 1.3 million registered Republicans, 616,000 registered Democrats and 500,000 independents not registered with any party.
How many people actually vote?
Roughly 403,000 votes were cast in the June 16 Republican primary for governor and 169,000 votes in the Democratic U.S. Senate primary.
How much of the vote is cast early or by absentee ballot?
In the June 16 state primaries, about 11% of Republican primary ballots and about 12% of Democratic primary ballots were cast early in-person or by mail.
As of Friday, about 32,000 ballots had already been cast in Tuesday’s election.
When are early and absentee votes released?
Almost every county in Oklahoma releases all or almost all of its results from early in-person and mail voting in the first vote update of the night, usually before any results from in-person Election Day voting are released.
How long does vote-counting usually take?
In the June 16 state primary, the AP first reported results at 8:14 p.m. ET, or 14 minutes after polls closed. By 10:19 p.m. ET, more than 90% of the vote had been counted. The last vote update of the night was at 12:14 a.m. ET with about 99.9% of total votes counted.
When will the AP declare a winner?
The AP does not make projections and will declare a winner only when it’s determined there is no scenario that would allow a trailing candidate to close the gap. If a race has not been called, the AP will continue to cover any newsworthy developments, such as candidate concessions or declarations of victory. In doing so, the AP will make clear that it has not yet declared a winner and explain why.
How do recounts work?
Oklahoma does not have automatic recounts for elections involving candidates, but candidates may request and pay for one regardless of the vote margin. The state does require automatic recounts for statewide ballot questions if the margin is 0.5% or less of the total votes cast. The required margin is larger for state constitutional amendments. The AP may declare a winner in a race that is subject to a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.
Are we there yet?
As of Tuesday, there will be 70 days until the 2026 midterm elections.

Preservationists are working to extend the life of a rare Revolutionary War ‘witness tree’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:23:01 UTC
20:23:01 KST

Preservationists are working to extend the life of a rare Revolutionary War ‘witness tree’
EUTAW SPRINGS, S.C. (AP) — Standing beneath the spreading branches of a massive live oak, historian Garrison Marcoux tries to imagine what this scarred, struggling tree saw 245 years ago.
Did one of the British soldiers encamped at this South Carolina crossroad near the end of the Revolutionary War sit in the oak’s shade to recuperate from the series of attacks in American Maj. Gen. Nathanael Greene’s “war of posts?” Did he or his comrades take cover behind its then slender trunk and fire at the onrushing Continental Army?
Perhaps a soldier took his last breath beneath its canopy, watering its roots with his blood.
“I’m a spiritual person,” Marcoux, with the South Carolina Battlefield Preservation Trust, said as workers clamber among the limbs above. “To say that a place that experienced a lot of violence and intense emotion and things like that doesn’t hold some kind of energy is probably not likely. I think that energy exists where something like this happened.”
This is a “witness tree.” And it now faces its own fight for survival.
After multiple attempts to stave off its death over the decades, it is being choked by the chains and cables meant to support it. Preservationists are working to save this unique, living reminder of an oft-overshadowed chapter in U.S. history.
What the oak witnessed during the Revolutionary War
Arborists estimate that the tree was about 50 years old on Sept. 8, 1781, when British and colonial forces clashed during the Battle of Eutaw Springs — considered by historians to be the last open field engagement of the American Revolution.
“It’s very rare to have a witness tree, especially from the Revolutionary War,” Marcoux said on a recent sultry morning as gnats and mosquitoes buzzed around his head. “To have the tree that witnessed this battle and still standing is short of a miracle.”
Among the officers were famous names like Lt. Col. Henry “Light-Horse Harry” Lee and Brig. Gen. Francis Marion, better known as the “Swamp Fox.”
About 2,500 Americans attacked the roughly 2,000 British and Loyalist troops camped around a fortified brick house. Greene, who had a horse shot out from under him during the battle, called Eutaw Springs “by far, the hottest action I ever saw, and the most bloody for the numbers engaged.”
Lt. Col. Alexander Stewart, the British field commander that day, later wrote to Gen. Charles Lord Cornwallis, “I assure you the Action was bloody and obstinate.”
There were 1,461 killed, wounded, captured or missing. Both sides would claim victory.
“That tree probably took a few lead balls itself,” says arborist Aron Landsaw.
The combatants would move on. The oak remained — and faced several more battles of its own.
The supports to help the tree are now choking it
Hung with swaying Spanish moss, its branches festooned with bright-green resurrection fern, the tree reaches 45 feet (13.7 meters) into the sky, its canopy spreading about 130 feet (40 meters). Its trunk is 72 inches (1.83 meters) in diameter at breast height.
The twin springs that gave the Revolutionary War battle its name are no more, inundated by the 1940s project that flooded the Santee River basin for hydroelectric power and flood control. Development in the 1960s swallowed up much of what the lake project spared.
The tree survived it all.
Then, about 50 years ago, lightning struck the oak’s crotch, splitting the tree nearly in two. Workers lashed the broad branches together with steel cables and chains.
But the mechanisms that saved the oak are now slowly killing it.
As the tree grew, the metal bands cut into the trunk and branches, in some places disappearing beneath a scar-like covering of bark.
“The chains and cables are actually choking it out,” says Landsaw. “It can’t pull nutrients up from the soil.”
Preservationists hope to reverse that.
A super
sonic air tool and a kelp mixture offer a lifeline
South Carolina 250 and the American Battlefield Trust joined forces to hire New York state-based SavATree for the project as the U.S. marks the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence.
Crews recently used a supersonic air tool to de-compact the ground around the tree’s roots, then injected a kelp mixture to add nutrients to the soil. The day of Marcoux’s visit, SavATree workers hammered little blunt lightning rods into the main branches, connecting them with shiny copper cables that converge on a longer copper rod pounded deep into the ground about 10 feet (3 meters) from the trunk.
“If lightning does hit it, it’ll run down the copper cables and dissipate into the ground,” says Landsaw, a consulting arborist with SavATree.
Next, workers will install new cables, bolted into the five main branches, to stabilize the tree before removing the old supports.
“There’s going to be a center hub in the middle that connects all these cables and allows the tree to sway with the wind and move around when it needs to,” Landsaw explains.
Landsaw says this is the most significant project he’s ever worked on.
While he can’t promise the tree will live another three centuries, Landsaw is confident it will be around to inspire new generations of Americans.
“We’re focusing on another 100 years at least,” he says. “Hopefully longer.”
___
The story has been updated to correct that SavATree is based in New York state, not Maryland.

Iran warns of a harsh response to anticipated US sanctions and other Middle East news
Iran warned that U.S. sanctions set to be announced Monday would not bring peace to the region. Meanwhile, Israeli and Syrian officials met less than a week after Israeli strikes in Syria. And Israel said it killed a Hamas commander in Gaza.
Here’s a look at the latest developments in the Iran war and the wider Middle East on Monday. Full coverage can be found here.
Iran threatens response ahead of US sanctions announcement
Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson warned that Tehran would respond harshly to expanded U.S. sanctions, including measures against countries it sees as cooperating with Washington.
“Any escalation of this situation will undoubtedly bring about consequences,” Esmail Baghaei said. “Our hands are not tied.” The new head of Iran’s top security body warned Sunday that Tehran will see any country’s support for the sanctions as an “act of war.”
The expanded sanctions come after weeks of impasse. The United States has not dislodged Iran’s grip on the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s traded oil passed before the war started nearly six months ago.
Iran’s demands for reopening the strait include lifting the U.S. naval blockade, withdrawing U.S. forces from the region and reparations for damages sustained in the war. It has held separate talks with Oman, on the other side of the strait, on jointly managing the waterway regardless of whether a new deal is brokered with the U.S.
Sanctions have historically raised prices of basic goods in Iran, but after decades of withstanding them, Iran’s economy has adapted through finding new trading partners and building domestic industries.
Ahead of the expected U.S. announcement, the country’s currency hit a record low on Monday.
Israeli and Syrian officials meet following an Israeli airstrike
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani met over the weekend with a high-level Israeli delegation in Jordan to try to defuse tensions after Israel last week struck an air base in northern Syria, Syrian state news agency SANA reported.
The U.S.-mediated discussions on Sunday focused on restarting negotiations for a future security agreement, SANA said.
Israel struck the Abu Duhur air base in Idlib province, saying it aimed to stop Turkey — which has supported the new Syrian government’s efforts to rebuild its armed forces after 14 years of civil war — from establishing a presence there.
Syrian officials during the talks asserted the right to develop an army and freely forge alliances with any country, SANA said.
They also called for the withdrawal of Israeli forces from a buffer zone in southern Syria they have occupied since December 2024, and reiterated Syria’s stance that the Golan Heights — which Israel captured in the 1967 Mideast war and later annexed — is Syrian territory.
Israeli officials didn’t immediately comment on the meeting.
Israel says it killed another Hamas militant
Israel’s military said it killed a militant affiliated with Hamas’ special forces unit in an overnight airstrike, the latest targeted killing announced since U.S. officials met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu last week hoping to push last year’s ceasefire deal forward.
Israel says it targets and kills Palestinian militants it says participated in the Oct. 7, 2023, attack that sparked the war.
Israel has announced targeted strikes on six of the seven days since U.S. negotiator Jared Kushner’s meeting with Netanyahu.
At least 1,288 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire took effect last October, according to Gaza’s health ministry, part of the Hamas-run government. Its numbers are generally considered reliable by the international community.
Palestinian American says he can’t freely leave West Bank home
The Palestinian American homeowner whose residence was besieged this month by Israeli settlers said he remained unable to move freely in the village of Qusra in the occupied West Bank. Loui Ridi traveled from Ohio to join his relatives defending his home a week ago.
The Israeli military declared the area a closed zone to restore order in Qusra. Ridi said settlers returned throughout the week to the hill above his house.
Since Israeli settlers surrounded the house more than two weeks ago, preventing occupants from leaving, Israeli soldiers have encouraged them to leave but Israel’s police have not announced arrests.
The siege and Israel’s response have sparked condemnation from Israeli rights groups and foreign officials, including U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, who called the violence terrorism.
Palestinians consider the West Bank, home to some 3 million Palestinians and 560,000 Israeli settlers, the heart of any future state and have condemned Israel’s expansion there. This year has seen a dramatic spike in violence carried out by Israeli settlers against Palestinians.

Some 60 earthquakes hit Iran in a week
TEHRAN – A total of 59 earthquakes have been recorded across the country in a week from August 15 to 21, according to the seismological networks of the Institute of Geophysics of the University of Tehran.
Statistically, 54 earthquakes with magnitudes smaller than 3, three earthquakes with a magnitude between 3 and 4, and two earthquakes with a magnitude between 4 and 5 have occurred in the country, irsc reported.
Of the total quakes, one had a magnitude of 4.2 on the Richter scale, which occurred on August 19th in Kermanshah provinces.
Among the provinces of the country, Khorasan Razavi experienced the highest number of earthquakes with 13, followed by Kermanshah and Kerman each with 7, and Semnan with 6 earthquakes.
During the same period, no earthquakes were recorded in Tehran, East Azarbaijan, West Azarbaijan, Ardabil, Alborz, South Khorasan, Zanjan, Fars, Qom, Qazvin, Kordestan, Gilan, Kohgiluyeh-Boyerahmad, Markazi, and Hormozgan provinces.
A total of 2,380 earthquakes with a magnitude of more than 2.5 on the Richter scale were recorded across the country over the past calendar year (March 2025–March 2026), according to the Seismological networks of the Institute of Geophysics of the University of Tehran, Mehr news agency reported.
Out of recorded earthquakes, 910 had a magnitude greater than 3, 130 had a magnitude greater than 4, and 15 had a magnitude greater than 5 on the Richter scale.
The Iranian plateau is located in a very seismically active region of the world and is known not only for its major catastrophic earthquakes but also for the disasters relating to natural hazards, especially earthquakes.
About 2 percent of the earthquakes in the world occur in Iran, but more than 6 percent of the victims of the world’s earthquakes during the 20th century are reported from Iranian earthquakes.

US police in Omaha halt use of shock gloves in schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:20:42 UTC
20:20:42 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
Police in Omaha, located in the US state of Nebraska, have recently agreed to stop carrying gloves capable of delivering electric shocks to students in most middle and high schools after concerns from educators, students and residents.
The decision came after media reports about Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s alleged plan to equip officers with the devices, known as G.L.O.V.E.s (Generated Low Output Voltage Emitters). Some jails have also used them in recent years.
Omaha Public Schools Superintendent Matthew Ray requested on Aug. 18 that school resource officers stop using the gloves. Omaha police agreed two days later, according to The Guardian.
The move followed a school board meeting where about 30 people spoke against the devices. No one spoke in favor.
“I can’t even imagine walking down the hallway and seeing a peer of mine being electrocuted in a place that is supposed to be a safe space for students,” said Nora Wessel, a senior at Omaha Central High School.
Omaha police used the gloves twice during the 2025-26 school year, including once on a student at a special education learning center after police said the student threatened and assaulted a security guard.
Ray said continued use of the devices “would be counterproductive to our work together” with law enforcement.
While the Omaha Police Department has agreed to comply with the decision, the Bellevue Police Department, which patrol two schools in Omaha, announced that they will continue carrying the gloves. Bellevue Police Chief Ken Clary said he was not comfortable giving up a tool he considers “safe, effective and less harmful than the alternatives.”
Omaha police said most of its 34 school resource officers had been trained to use the gloves. The department said officers will still carry stun guns, batons, pepper spray and firearms.
In 2025, Omaha police agreed to pay Compliant Technologies LLC about $66,000 for 40 gloves. Officers were expected to issue a warning before using them and could apply the shock for up to 15 seconds.
Ken Trump, president of National School Safety and Security Services, said schools should carefully consider how such technology would be used with students who have disabilities or medical needs.
“Less than lethal doesn’t mean low risk,” Trump said.

Iran proposes BRICS to establish network centered on children’s human capital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24

Iran proposes BRICS to establish network centered on children’s human capital
TEHRAN – Iran's representatives at the BRICS Child Futures Forum have proposed developing a BRICS knowledge network focused on children’s human capital.
Hosted by the Observer Research Foundation (ORF) in partnership with the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), the event was held on the sidelines of the 18th BRICS Academic Forum (BAF), held on August 23 in Lucknow, India.
The forum, titled ‘Investing in Children, Securing the Future: Human Capital for the Next BRICS Decade’, brought together policymakers, researchers, development practitioners, experts and youth representatives to discuss priorities for advancing child and adolescent wellbeing across BRICS. Discussions focused on investing in children as a foundation for human capital, alongside themes of health and nutrition, climate resilience, technology and innovation, youth leadership, and partnerships.
Addressing the forum, Iranian officials, Morteza Daman-Pak Jami, Senior Research Fellow, Institute for Political and International Studies (IPIS), and former Ambassador to Lisbon, and Omid Babelian, Diplomat and Research Fellow, Institute for Political and International Studies, detailed Iran’s perspectives and experiences in safeguarding children and strengthening human capital during crises, IRNA reported.
Daman-Pak Jami suggested that BRICS member states use available capacities, foster collaboration in education, health, youth, universities, science, technology, and social development, and then leverage them to forge a coherent approach to human capital.
Highlighting the importance of the life-cycle approach to human capital development, he stated that investment in human capital must begin in the early years of life and persist through early childhood development, education, skills training, and entry into the labor market.
He also elaborated on the country’s achievements in health and children’s education.
 
 Referring to illegal US-Israel attacks against Iran, he said the war was a blatant violation of international humanitarian law, and highlighted the need for upholding children’s right to education amidst war and crises.
“The attacks on Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab, Hormozgan province, are a typical example of the humanitarian consequences of aggression and violation of children’s right to education and safety.
Schools must be safe environment for the education and upbringing of the next generation under all circumstances. The global community must not remain indifferent to attacks on children and educational institutions,” he further noted.
For his part, Babelian said protection, empowerment, and integration are three principles to strengthen human capital. Children and young people must retain access to education, healthcare, social protection, and essential services during crises, while also having the opportunity to participate meaningfully in shaping their own futures, he added.
“When we speak of human capital, I can no longer think of numbers and charts. For me, human capital has a face: the face of a child sitting in a classroom, a young person in a laboratory trying to discover a better medication, a student dreaming of building a better future, and families that—despite all hardships—still pin their hopes on their children’s tomorrow.
Protecting human capital should not be limited to saving their lives during crisis; it should ensure a future in which they can thrive.”

National Youth Population Award slated for November

‘Aging rate in Iran exceeds global average’
The rate of aging in Iran is growing faster than the global average, so that the country will be among the oldest countries in the world in 25 years, the head of the Welfare Organization said in January.
Based on the World Health Organization (WHO) age classification in 2025, the elderly population constitutes those aged 60 and older. Accordingly, 14 percent of the country’s population is old now, ISNA quoted Seyed Javad Hosseini as saying.
A population is considered to be young, with seven percent of people being 60 or older; when seven to 14 percent of people are over 60, the country is said to be aging. Countries with 14 to 21 percent and 21 to 27 percent of people aged 60 or over are aged and super-aged, respectively, the official said.
In the Iranian year 1395 (2016 – 2017), only 9.5 percent of the population was aged over 60, and the global average aging rate was about 12 and 13 percent. In the Iranian year 1415 (2036 – 2037), the figure will rise to 15 percent in Iran and 16.5 percent in the world. However, in 1430 (2051 – 2052), the figure will reach 31 percent in Iran, and 21.5 percent in the world. The life expectancy in Iran has increased, but the birth rate has lowered, Hosseini stressed.
According to the latest census, the number of aged citizens in the country is growing by 3.62 percent, which is five times faster than the total population growth rate, which is 1.24 percent. For the time being, elderly women account for 52.3 percent of the total population, outnumbering men (47.7 percent), ISNA quoted Saber Jabbari, an official with the health ministry, as saying.
Despite offering incentives to encourage childbearing in line with the youth population law, the desired growth in the youth population has not been accomplished yet. It is one of the most important challenges facing the country.
“At best, Iran’s population with a total fertility rate of 2.5 will reach 102,890,000 by the next seven years,” IRIB quoted Mohammad-Javad Mahmoudi, an official with the Civil Registration Organization, as saying.
The official noted that the fertility rate has remained stable at around 1.6 over the past two years. This trend has heightened concerns about a continued decline in population growth in the coming years and the growing likelihood of Iran becoming one of the world’s oldest countries.

CUHK academic who allegedly hid marital status cleared of indecent assault
Peng Peng, 38, walked free from Sha Tin Court on Monday, where he had previously pleaded not guilty to two counts of indecent assault
An associate professor at the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) has been acquitted of indecently assaulting a woman who reported him upon discovering he was married, after a court found the pair had been mutually attracted and that the man may have wrongly believed she had consented to being touched.
Magistrate Raymond Wong Kwok-fai acquitted Peng Peng, 38, at Sha Tin Court on Monday, following hearings that began in July.
Peng had pleaded not guilty to two counts stemming from alleged incidents on May 21, 2025, when he and the complainant – a fellow scholar from mainland China – visited CUHK’s art museum before dining in Ma On Shan.
The court earlier heard that the two met in April after a conference and went hiking on CUHK’s campus, but the complainant said Peng never mentioned he was a married man or a father.
Peng later emailed her, calling the hike an “unforgettable adventure on the campus.” She replied she was “very happy” and looked forward to meeting again in summer. Peng responded: “The views at CUHK are beautiful, but nothing compares to the sight of you beside me.”
They later moved their conversations to WeChat. On May 20, the woman invited Peng to campus but he said he was busy and would see her the next day. She replied: “Nothing, talk to you when we meet.” When Peng asked, “why so mysterious?”, she sent a “doll” emoji and wrote, “keep smiling”.
During their museum visit, the court heard, their conversation included sexual innuendo – remarks about her outfit and the colour of her toenails – and Peng patted her on the back.

Singapore launches world-first data center powered by human brain cells
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:14:03 UTC
20:14:03 KST

Singapore launches world-first data center powered by human brain cells
Singapore has launched the world’s first independently operated data center using living human brain cells for some computing tasks, the medical school of the National University of Singapore (NUS Medicine) has said. The system consumes a fraction of the power of traditional computing hardware. The neurons are fed every three days and sustained by dedicated life-support equipment.
NUS Medicine announced the prototype earlier this month in partnership with Singapore-based data center operator DayOne and Australian biotech firm Cortical Labs. Housed at the university, the system is described by its developers as the world’s first independently operated biologically integrated server rack.
The facility comprises 20 CL1 biological computers, each containing at least 200,000 lab-grown human neurons on an electrode-fitted silicon chip. Derived from blood cells reprogrammed into stem cells, the neurons exchange electrical signals with conventional hardware, turning their activity into computing power.
Cortical Labs founder and CEO Hon Weng Chong said the prototype moves biological computing “from research to commercial application,” arguing it could complement AI where “data is sparse” and conditions change. He pointed to potential uses in drug discovery, humanoid robotics, cybersecurity and fraud detection.
Unlike conventional data centers packed with power-hungry servers and cooling systems, biological computers could operate on a fraction of the electricity by harnessing the natural processing capabilities of living neural networks.
Keeping the “computers” running looks more like maintaining a laboratory than a server room. Technicians feed the cells a mixture of sugar, micronutrients and pH buffers every three days, while a gas system supplies carbon dioxide, oxygen and nitrogen.
Each CL1 draws around 30 watts including its life-support equipment, according to Chong. Nvidia’s H100 SXM AI processor can consume up to 700 watts under heavy workloads, while a server fitted with eight such chips can draw around 10,200 watts including supporting hardware.
The power difference is particularly relevant for Singapore, which temporarily halted construction of new data centers in 2019 because of concerns over their electricity and water consumption. Data centers accounted for around 7% of the country’s electricity use in 2020.
The technology is not intended to replace silicon, which Chong said remains “far superior” for the fast, repeatable calculations behind large language models such as ChatGPT. Biological systems, however, can learn from fewer examples and adapt to changing conditions.

Roche snags rights to South Korean obesity treatment
Genentech, the Californian subsidiary of Swiss pharmaceutical giant Roche, has secured worldwide rights to develop, manufacture and market an experimental treatment for obesity from the South Korean company Hanmi Pharmaceuticals.
The agreement excludes South Korea, Hanmi stated in a press release issued today.
+ Can Swiss pharma giant Roche reshape the obesity market?
Hanmi stands to receive a total of $2.3 billion under the agreement, a figure largely contingent upon the achievement of clinical, regulatory and commercial milestones. The initial payment amounts to $190 million.
The product in question – HM17321 – is currently the subject of a Phase I clinical trial, which Hanmi must complete. If all goes well, Genentech will take over for Phase II and subsequent stages of development.
The experimental treatment is based on a mechanism of action different from that of GLP-1-type products, which is expected to promote weight loss whilst preserving muscle mass.

The parties are expected to discuss the outcomes of cooperation in the first half of 2026 and outline projects for the near future. The Brest Free Economic Zone and the Special Economic Zone of Irkutsk Oblast are set to sign an agreement on cooperation.

The delegation includes representatives from processing industry enterprises, Svetopribor of BelTIZ, and our industrial flagships MAZ and MTZ. Israel freaks out over children's kites in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:07:56 UTC
20:07:56 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel puts its military on 'high alert' over children's kites in Gaza
Nine-year-old Arkan Radi sat inside his family's tent in a displacement camp in Al-Zawayda in the central Gaza Strip, carefully making a small kite.
He cut the paper, attached thin wooden sticks, tied the string and chose colours resembling those of the Palestinian flag. He imagined it rising above the rows of tents as he and his friends ran after it.
For Arkan, it was supposed to be nothing more than a summer game and a brief escape from the tents, rubble and fear that have defined much of his childhood.
But when he finally stepped outside carrying the kite, his parents stopped him. At first, Arkan could not understand why.
"I made it to play with my friends," he told The New Arab. "I spent days working on it. I wanted to fly it and chase it after it, but my parents told me not to go out with it. I don't understand why they're afraid of it. It's just paper and string."
Wiping away his tears, he added, "I don't want to hurt anyone. I just want to play like children everywhere. We're even afraid of playing now."
Radi, his father, told TNA that "I would never have stopped Arkan from flying a kite if it were not for recent Israeli threats to target people launching kites from Gaza."
For days, Israel's concern over kites and balloons launched from Gaza has intensified, turning children's toys into a "security issue".
Israeli media claimed that several kites from Gaza had landed near areas surrounding the besieged coastal enclave.
In statements concerning some of the incidents, the Israeli military acknowledged that no suspicious materials or explosives were found and that the kites posed no danger to the public.
Israeli Defence Minister Yisrael Katz ordered the military to act "very forcefully and immediately" against kites and balloons launched from Gaza, treating them like drones.
"A balloon is like a kite, and a kite is like a drone, whether it carries explosives or not," Katz boasted.
Netanyahu and Katz warned that ongoing launches could lead to wider war, including targeted killings and evacuations.
They claimed they had warned Hamas that "if the launches toward Israel do not stop immediately, the army will increase targeted killings of those responsible", while also threatening to "evacuate residents from areas from which kites, drones, and balloons are launched."
Thus, the kites made of paper, string and wooden sticks have become entangled in a security narrative involving targeted killings, military raids and evacuation threats.
In Gaza, however, the question is far simpler: how did a children's toy become a source of fear?
"My son doesn't know anything about politics or what Israel is saying," Radi said. "He sees a kite and wants to play with it. But we adults know what it means when Israel threatens to target those who launch these kites, so we stopped him."
"We're afraid for him of anything that might attract attention. In Gaza, a child can't know where the danger is coming from. He might go out to play, and suddenly the whole area becomes a target," he added.
What hurts him most, however, is that kites were never a form of resistance for Gaza's children. They were simply a familiar summer pastime.
"Children here used to make and fly kites during the summer. It's perfectly normal for us. What's wrong with a child flying a kite? Why should a child be afraid of the sky too?" he asked.
A summer game turns into a source of fear
In another displacement camp in central Gaza, 13-year-old Mohammed made a kite with the help of his older brother. He chose several colours and attached a long tail, hoping it would rise high above the camp.
"Every year when summer comes, we make kites and go to an open space to fly them," Mohammed told TNA. "This isn't the first time I've done this, but this year my mother was very scared."
"She told me the Israelis could see us and shoot us. I don't want to die because of a kite. So, I kept it with me and didn't fly it," he said.
His mother, Ruba, said her fear was not of the kite itself, but of what could happen if Israeli forces saw her son carrying one.
"My son doesn't understand what's going on around him. He sees other children playing and wants to join in. But we've lived through war, and we know that anything can become a reason for bombing," she added.
"We want our children to laugh, even for just one hour. We don't want them to grow up afraid to play, but at the same time, we can't risk their lives," she explained.
Meanwhile, Hamas has rejected the Israeli narrative, describing the focus on kites as an attempt to create new justifications for escalation against Gaza.
Hamas spokesperson Hazem Qassem said the kites being discussed by Israel were essentially "children's toys in displacement camps", warning of the consequences of Israeli threats to target those who launch them.
"These threats, based on fabricated pretexts, are an attempt to justify the continuation of aggression and violations against our people, even going so far as to threaten children in the Gaza Strip," Qassem said.
He called on the US administration and mediating and guarantor states to pressure Israel to halt what he described as its "unbridled aggression" and not use the issue to undermine the ceasefire process.
Turning a toy into a pretext
For Gaza-based Palestinian political analyst Mustafa Ibrahim, the controversy over kites cannot be understood solely by whether they pose a physical threat.
"Rather," he told TNA, "it reflects the broader political and military context surrounding Gaza."
"When an unexploded kite becomes a security issue that warrants threats of assassination and evacuation, it means the issue transcends the actual danger posed by this tool," Ibrahim said.
"Israel is trying to portray everything coming from Gaza as a potential security threat, even when it involves children's toys. The danger here is not in the kite itself, but in its use as a pretext to broaden the scope of targeting," he added.
Ibrahim also linked the rhetoric to Israel's domestic political environment and the pressures facing Netanyahu.
"Israel's security rhetoric serves Netanyahu at a sensitive political moment because it allows him to appear as a leader who confronts any threat, no matter how small, and diverts attention from larger political and security issues," he explained.
He warned that turning incidents involving kites into grounds for military action could have serious consequences for civilians in Gaza, particularly amid the fragility of the ceasefire and the territory's continuing humanitarian crisis.
"The problem is that this rhetoric could quickly escalate from political threats to military action," he said. "Then the price won't be a kite that landed somewhere, but entire neighbourhoods are facing evacuation orders or airstrikes."
For children like Arkan and Mohammed, politics seems distant and incomprehensible. They see only a paper kite, summer wind, and fleeting childhood they try to reclaim. But in Gaza, even the sky is fearful.

Lebanon abolished the death penalty. Can it now deliver justice?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:06:18 UTC
20:06:18 KST

Breadcrumb
Lebanon abolished the death penalty. Can it now deliver justice?
Beirut, Lebanon - Lebanon became the first state in the Middle East to abolish the death penalty following a parliamentary vote on 11 August, formalising a two-decade moratorium on capital punishment in the country.
The achievement caps a nearly 30-year national campaign for nonviolence and has implications for Lebanon’s pursuit of justice in connection with other countries.
“It is a clear and firm commitment to strip the law and political authority of the power to kill,” Ogarit Younan, co-founder of the national abolition campaign, told The New Arab. “The death penalty kills, and I cannot accept being a citizen of a state of gallows.”
Lebanon last executed three men in 2004 at Roumieh Prison. Since then, death sentences have still been handed down but not carried out.
The abolition reverses a regional trend that has seen other states resume executions, pronounce death sentences or pass new death penalty laws.
In June, Jordan hanged six men in its first executions since 2017, and Syria sentenced nine men, including former dictator Bashar Al-Assad in absentia, to death earlier this month.
In March, Israel adopted a discriminatory death penalty law mandating executions for “terrorism-related” offences and applied exclusively to Palestinians.
“The Lebanese authorities, the judiciary, will not be resorting to this cruel and irreversible punishment,” Ramzi Kaiss, Lebanon researcher at Human Rights Watch, told The New Arab, hailing the new law as a step in the right direction.
According to Minister of Justice Adel Nassar, abolition in Lebanon can set an example for other states.
“Historically, Lebanon was known to be a country that has modern laws, that is keen to protect fundamental rights, to be a pioneer in the region,” Nassar told The New Arab.
“Because of what we lived through here, I think we can give the proper message to the world. We are providing a counterexample.”’
Removing a barrier to justice?
Abolishing the death penalty in Lebanon opens a path toward resolving one of the most sensitive justice issues in the country: accountability for the 2020 Beirut port blast.
Lebanese authorities have previously sought extradition of Russian-Cypriot Igor Grechushkin, former owner of the Rhosus container ship allegedly carrying the ammonium nitrate that detonated at the port, in connection with the investigation into the explosion.
In September, Bulgarian authorities detained Grechushkin on an Interpol notice, but a Bulgarian court rejected Lebanon’s extradition request. Grechuskin’s lawyer had argued Lebanon’s laws on capital punishment put her client’s life at risk.
“Under international human rights law, individuals should not be extradited to areas where the death penalty is used,” Kaiss said. “In Lebanon, there have been several obstacles to justice as a result of the death penalty being in effect.”
With this obstacle removed, Lebanese authorities may be able to move forward with the investigation and potential prosecutions of those deemed responsible for the port blast.
The same principle, however, could complicate efforts to hold accountable Syrian members of the Assad regime accused of committing atrocities.
In February, Lebanon and Syria signed a judicial cooperation agreement providing for the transfer of convicted Syrians held in Lebanon to serve out their sentences in Syria.
Lebanon has also arrested former regime officials and received an extradition request from Syria; the transfer of Syrian officials who fled the country after Assad’s fall has previously been a subject of discussion between the neighbouring countries’ authorities.
“Lebanon will not pursue extradition without assurances that an individual will not be subject to the death penalty,” Nassar said, once the law enters into force upon its publication in the official gazette.
If Syrian authorities carry out the death sentence against former security chief Atef Najib and the death penalty remains on the books in Syria, Lebanon could be forced to deny extradition of other regime officials in accordance with international law.
Last Tuesday, Lebanon’s public prosecutor, an office with a degree of independence from the government, approved the extradition of former Syrian general Adel Issa under the terms of a 1951 bilateral judicial agreement.
An anonymous official told AFP that legal and judicial requirements for extradition had been met. The transfer, carried out the following day, raises questions about Lebanon’s obligations under the International Convention on Civil and Political Rights, to which it is a party and which imposes a duty on countries to refrain from extraditing individuals to countries where their right to life is at risk.
Controversial amnesty on the heels of abolition
A day after the vote on abolishing the death penalty, Lebanon’s parliament also approved a general amnesty law aimed at reducing rampant prison overcrowding.
The controversial measure could see around one-third of the country’s approximately 8,500 incarcerated people released. The majority of the prison population is comprised of those awaiting trial, and rights groups have previously criticised dangerous conditions for inmates.
The government has publicly disavowed associations between the death penalty abolition law and the general amnesty, though critics attribute the latter’s passage to sectarian demands that could allow former members of extremist groups to walk free.
The exact scope of the amnesty remains unclear, and the law does not provide for broader structural reform to the prison and justice system.
The text of the abolition bill, in addition to removing all death penalty provisions from Lebanese laws, distinguishes between new penalties for prior sentences and future ones.
For previous death sentences, such as those handed down to the estimated 85 individuals still on death row, it substitutes life imprisonment with hard labour; for future prosecutions of crimes previously punishable by death, the highest penalty will be life imprisonment with aggravated hard labour.
Activists and rights groups see the abolition victory as a stepping-stone to greater change, including rehabilitation for those accused of crimes.
“This campaign was for the culture of nonviolence, not just to change the law,” Younan told The New Arab. “We want a civilised state that protects life.”
Paul Hefel-James is an independent journalist based in Beirut, covering migration and refugee issues, the humanitarian sector, and conflict

The European Commission on Monday approved €6.1 billion ($7.1 billion) in new defense aid for Ukraine, including air and missile defense systems, missiles, ammunition and radars.
“On Ukraine's Independence Day, Europe shows our support is unfaltering and concrete,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.
“Today, we have approved €6.1 billion ($7.1 billion) for the air and missile defense systems, missiles, ammunition and radars that Ukraine urgently needs,” she added.

The commission said Russia's increased use of ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones has made it increasingly urgent to strengthen Ukraine's air defenses and accelerate deliveries of critical defense equipment.
The latest approval adds to €16 billion ($18.7 billion) in defense procurement plans already approved under the loan, of which €8.35 billion ($9.7 billion) has been disbursed, according to the commission.
Most of the procurements will be sourced from European defense companies.
The commission said deliveries should be increased through drawing on existing stocks, reprioritizing orders and increasing production.
It added Ukraine can request payments by submitting contracts signed with defense companies.
It will review the contracts before releasing funds to ensure they cover procurements agreed with EU member states and the commission.
The €90 billion ($105.1 billion) Ukraine Support Loan was established by the European Parliament and the EU Council in February 2026.
The EU and its member states have provided €220.2 billion ($256.9 billion) in overall support to Ukraine since 2022, including €3.8 billion ($4.4 billion) from proceeds generated by immobilized Russian assets, according to the commission.
