US threatens toughest sanctions yet against Iran: What we know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:23:11 UTC
19:23:11 KST

US threatens toughest sanctions yet against Iran: What we know
Tehran has threatened to retaliate against any country that joins new US economic measures.
With diplomacy stalled over ending the war on Iran, Washington is seeking to ratchet up pressure on Tehran with “unprecedented” economic pressure.
After United States President Donald Trump threatened to punish any country doing business with Tehran last week, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that a new series of economic measures will “collapse” the Iranian government, calling on countries to join the effort.
On Saturday, Tehran threatened to retaliate against any country that joins the US in economic sanctions against it.
Here’s what we know about what the US is planning and how Iran could respond.
What new measures is the US threatening against Iran?
The Trump administration has already been waging an economic pressure campaign against Iran under the banner of “Operation Economic Fury”, since the launch of the war in February.
In particular, it is currently running a naval blockade on Iranian ports in a bid to prevent oil exports and has targeted companies, brokers and tankers accused of helping Iran sell its oil abroad.
It also has longer standing sweeping sanctions in place on Iran’s oil, shipping and financial sectors, seeking to cut off the revenue Tehran earns from energy exports. It has also imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports.
Now, the US says it will do more.
In a Truth Social post on Wednesday, Trump announced what he called the “most crushing economic operation” against Iran.
Trump said Iran had “failed to take” the opportunity to make a deal, and would face “economic warfare and isolation on an unprecedented scale”.
He also threatened sanctions against any country that does business with Iran.
“ANY country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences,” he wrote.
“Oil smuggling, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries, front companies – it all needs to stop NOW. You know who you are. This will be an ECONOMIC D-DAY, and we need all of our Allies to stand with the United States of America to isolate, and defeat, the Iran threat.”
On Thursday last week, one day after Trump’s social media tirade, Bessent told the news service CNBC that the US would apply the “toughest sanctions in history” on Iran.
“It is a one-two punch. We have the blockade [on Iran], and we are going to have the toughest sanctions in history,” Bessent said. “It is going to work in Iran, and we are going to collapse this regime.”
He then offered a warning to the members of the international community that they, too, could face economic penalties if they continue to trade with Iran.
“We’re going to them and saying: You’re either with us or against us,” Bessent said. “If you insist on doing business with them – either transferring money, buying oil, doing seaborne ship transport – then the US Treasury and the US government, they will put its full might and force towards enforcing against you.”
He billed the US’s strategy as the “greatest coordinated economic isolation in the history of the world”.
“It is time for our allies and the rest of the world to make a decision,” Bessent added.
How has Iran responded?
Iran has decried any new, impending US sanctions – particularly economic action against other countries – as a “complete erosion of sovereignty”.
In a post on X on Saturday, Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said the US announcement was “an assertion of extraterritorial sovereignty” against the United Nations’ member states.
No state can compel foreign banks, enterprises or airports to renounce commerce with Iran, he said.
“The end result would be the complete erosion of sovereignty as the foundational basis of the UN-based inter-State system, and a recipe for an abysmal return to full-scale classic colonialism,” Baghaei said.
Iranian state media pointed out that Tehran has faced US sanctions for decades. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the new measures were “bound to fail”.
“We have seen this movie before,” Araghchi wrote on X, alongside a screenshot of a tweet from former President Barack Obama referencing earlier sanctions in 2012. “Same bull. Different bullies.”
Can Iran target countries that acquiesce to US demands?
On Saturday, Tehran threatened to retaliate against any country that joins the US in economic sanctions against it.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told the IRIB state broadcaster that Iran was appealing to all countries around the world, including its neighbours, not to join the US’s “economic war”.
“Any country that takes part in imposing economic restrictions on us will be regarded as an enemy,” he said, warning of a “seismic” retaliation.
Rezaei described Iran’s strategy as a three-stage sequence starting with talks to de-escalate tensions.
“Of course, we will first negotiate with them. We will hold talks and tell them to step aside and distance themselves from the United States. But if they do not act, we will strike. We will target that country’s interests,” he said.
Rezaei also warned Iran’s neighbours that if they participate in Trump’s economic warfare, “not even a drop of oil” will leave the Gulf region, including by alternative export routes away from the Hormuz chokepoint through which one-fifth of global oil and gas exports pass in peacetime.
Iran has already launched strikes on US military installations, infrastructure and civilian locations in the region since the war began on February 28.
Energy and other facilities in Qatar, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) have also suffered damage, mostly from debris from intercepted strikes by Iran or its proxy groups across the region.
The US operates military facilities in more than a dozen locations across the Middle East and North Africa, including in Gulf nations, such as Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Thousands of US soldiers are also stationed across the region, including in Jordan.
Hamidreza Azizi, a researcher on Iran at the Clingendael Institute, said in a post on X on Saturday: “Tehran appears to be trying to establish deterrence at an earlier stage, by signalling that even preparations for an attack could trigger an Iranian response.”
Azizi said two elements in the new “offensive doctrine” are emerging: preemption, which is aimed at preventing a perceived threat from materialising; and disproportionate retaliation, which is aimed at raising the cost of any attack that does occur.
How have other countries responded to Trump’s demands?
China has pushed back against Trump’s threats.
“Imposing sanctions and pressuring do not help to solve the issue,” China’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Lin Jian told reporters in Beijing on August 20.
“China calls on relevant parties to take responsible measures and solve the issues through diplomatic and political means.”
Gulf countries, which are Iran’s neighbours and also US allies, have increasingly been finding themselves caught in the middle of the war. Therefore, it is unclear if they would all join Washington in economically threatening Iran further.
Last week, the UAE, on which Iran is believed to rely for critical imports and financial services through which it sells oil, announced an indefinite trade embargo on Iran, after accusing Iranian forces of firing two ballistic missiles at the country, an allegation Tehran denies.
However, analysts have told Al Jazeera that many Gulf states fear the chaos that could follow if Iran’s government were to collapse. They said that while regional confidence in diplomacy is low, no country can afford another long war.
“Ultimately, Gulf countries can’t change geography. They have to live and work alongside Iran,” Simon Mabon, a professor of international relations at Lancaster University, told Al Jazeera in an interview last month. “They don’t want the instability that would come from the fall of the Islamic Republic [of Iran]. I think some Gulf states have pushed for harder strikes – not to precipitate its collapse, but to weaken the more hardline elements of the IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps].”
Can China and Russia insulate Iran from US measures?
While the US has made threats against any country that continues to trade with Iran, analysts say that Trump’s leverage over China and Russia, both major trading partners of Iran, is limited.
Paul Musgrave, an associate professor of government at Georgetown University in Qatar, told Al Jazeera last week that “it is going to be very difficult” for Trump to pull off his pressure campaign effectively.
“Trump is trying to unilaterally assert the kind of coordinated sanctions that traditionally has taken multilateral coordination, and that means getting on board China, Russia, the P5 of the UN Security Council,” Musgrave said, referring to the five permanent members of the UNSC.
This is because several sectors in Russia and China have minimal reliance on the American financial system.
Those sectors include most of China’s oil refineries. According to analytics firm Kpler, China bought 80 percent of Iran’s shipped oil in 2025. Evidence of ship-to-ship transfers of Iranian oil off the coast of Malaysia has also shown how Iranian oil continues to be traded.
Analysts say China could also hit back if the US sanctions the major Chinese banks for processing Iranian funds, as the US Treasury has threatened.
“Trump intends to stabilise the ties with China, so [this would happen] as Beijing aims to have a temporary truce with Washington,” Yu Jie, a senior research fellow at the Chatham House think tank’s China, Asia Pacific Programme, told Al Jazeera.
Although Russia is a less significant trading partner for Iran than China, Moscow and Tehran have spent years developing critical commercial and military links designed to sidestep Western channels. Notably, Iran has provided Shahed drones to Moscow for use in its war on Ukraine.

Bangladesh tribunal orders 3 journalists held until trial in 2024 uprising case
DHAKA, Bangladesh (AP) — A special tribunal in Bangladesh’s capital on Monday asked authorities to keep three journalists jailed until their trial in a case involving a mass uprising that ousted former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina from office in 2024, lawyers said.
During the student-led uprising, hundreds of people were killed, and Hasina was later sentenced to death on charges of crimes against humanity. She fled to India two years ago and was tried in absentia.
The tribunal asked that Mozammel Babu, editor-in-chief of private Ekattor Television, its principal correspondent Farzana Rupa and Shyamal Dutta, editor of daily Bhorer Kagoj and former general secretary of the National Press Club in Dhaka, remain jailed.
After they appeared before the tribunal on Monday, the judge fixed Oct. 25 for the next court proceedings and asked the investigators to submit their findings against the journalists.
Global human rights groups have criticized the jailing of the journalists and the denial of bail, asking the government to drop the charges against them and stop criminalizing news reporting.
Prosecutors allege the three journalists incited the suppression of student demonstrators during the uprising. They say that the journalists asked Hasina provocative questions at a press conference on July 14, 2024, that led her to make disparaging remarks about the demonstrators before launching a bloody crackdown on the protesters leading to hundreds of deaths.
The three journalists have been in custody for years following Hasina’s ouster as they face various charges including murder involving the uprising in July-August 2024. They were arrested during an interim government headed by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Muhammad Yunus who handed over power in February to a new government.
The families of the journalists complained that they were held illegally.
“Launching a crimes-against-humanity case against journalists Shyamal Dutta, Mozammel Babu, and Farzana Rupa for simply asking questions at a press conference is outrageous and deeply troubling,” Kunal Majumder, CPJ’s Asia-Pacific Program Coordinator, said in a statement earlier this month.
He added that “editorial decisions may be partisan or ethically questionable, but they cannot be criminalized. Criminalizing editorial judgment sets a dangerous precedent and undermines Bangladesh’s reputation as a democracy. Authorities must immediately release the three journalists and drop the charges.”
Hasina has been in India since Aug. 5, 2024, but recently she said she would return to the country in December. The Yunus-led government and incumbent administration of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman requested India to extradite Hasina, but India refused.

Hungarian air force Gripen jet crashes, pilot ejects safely, prime minister says
BUDAPEST, Hungary (AP) — A Hungarian military pilot ejected safely when his fighter jet crashed on Monday, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said.
The Swedish-made JAS 39 Gripen came down near the city of Szolnok in central Hungary “for reasons that are still unknown,” Magyar wrote in a post on Facebook. An investigation into the incident is underway and Minister of Defense Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi was on his way to the scene, he added.
Ruszin-Szendi said the pilot was “alive and has not sustained any injuries.”
“It appears the pilot did everything he could to ensure the crashed aircraft landed on military property,” Ruszin-Szendi said in a video on Facebook, adding he was traveling to the crash site with the chief of staff of the Hungarian defense forces.
Mihály Győrfi, the mayor of Szolnok, told local media that the pilot “was probably training as usual” at the helicopter base just outside the city, and confirmed that there were no known injuries resulting from the crash.
Hungary has 18 JAS 39 Gripen fighters, 14 of which were acquired through a lease-purchase program launched in 2001 and four others that were ordered in 2024 and joined the fleet this year.

Indonesia intensifies aerial firefighting as forest fires scorch multiple provinces

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24

Indonesia intensifies aerial firefighting as forest fires scorch multiple provinces
JAKARTA, Indonesia (AP) — Indonesia on Monday intensified ground and aerial firefighting operations as huge blazes in central and western parts of the country scorched thousands of hectares of forests and peatland, created a choking haze that blanketed cities and crossed borders.
Indonesian authorities have been battling fires driven by an intensifying El Nino pattern and a prolonged dry season, generating dense smoke that crossed into Malaysia and Brunei, according to Indonesia’s National Disaster Management Agency, or BNPB.
The BNPB said Monday that fires remain active in several regions, while large-scale suppression efforts continue in fire-prone provinces including West, Central and South Kalimantan on Borneo island and in Riau, South Sumatra and Jambi on Sumatra island. The fires are part of a broader surge in wildfire activity across Indonesia this year.
After visiting areas devastated by forest and peatland fires in Central Kalimantan on Saturday, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto flew to fire-affected Riau province on Sumatra island, where more than 11,500 hectares (28,400 acres) have burned, to encourage authorities to get the haze cloud under control.
Prabowo vowed the government would continue supporting firefighting operations, including through the deployment of additional water-bombing helicopters and oxygen supplies for firefighters. He urged authorities to “thoroughly document and report the work being carried out by firefighting teams” directly to him.
The Transportation Ministry said it has authorized the use of 35 foreign-registered aircraft to support wildfire response operations, including water-bombing missions and aerial patrols. The ministry said the aircraft can be rapidly redeployed to disaster-hit areas as conditions change, while complying with Indonesian aviation safety regulations.
The Environment Ministry satellite data on Monday showed South Sumatra recorded the highest number of hot spots nationwide with 1,429, followed by West Kalimantan with 1,226 and Central Kalimantan with 811. East Kalimantan logged 576 hot spots, ahead of Riau with 503, while West Papua and Jambi recorded 468 and 458 hot spots, respectively.
Forestry Ministry data indicated that nearly 94,000 hectares (232,000 acres) burned in July alone.
Drought, strong winds and dry vegetation have complicated efforts to contain the fires, BNPB said in a statement on Monday. Some hot spots remained inaccessible to more than 10,700 ground firefighters who were deployed as of Sunday, prompting local officials to request additional water-bombing support and firefighting vehicles.
Cloud-seeding resumed over Kalimantan on Monday, with 30 helicopters for water-bombing and aerial patrol missions, and another 22 helicopters covering Sumatra.
Fires are a regular problem during dry season in Indonesia, a vast archipelago nation of more than 17,000 islands, and often strain relations with neighbors. Plantation owners and traditional farmers often start fires to clear land for farming. It triggers hazardous haze that reduces visibility, disrupts land and air transportation and threatens public health, sometimes affecting neighboring countries in Southeast Asia.
Meanwhile, Malaysia has suffered severe smoke from the fires, with its eastern state of Sarawak among the hardest hit, prompting the closure of nearly 600 schools and affecting about 200,000 students, the Sarawak government said.
___
Associated Press writer Eileen Ng in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, contributed to this report.

Why Vijay scrapped Chennai’s second airport plan at Parandur
Edited by: Ayush Pandey / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 24, 2026, 15:56 IST
Comments

Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay
NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay on Monday announced that his government would abandon the proposed greenfield airport project at Parandur, saying the project would affect agricultural land and disrupt the livelihoods of farmers and residents.The announcement was made in the assembly as Vijay said Chennai still needed a new airport to meet rising passenger demand, industrial growth and increasing cargo movement. However, he said the new airport should be located at a site where agricultural and residential areas would face minimal disruption."To fulfill the promise I made to the people that day... the steps taken to establish a new airport in Parandur will be abandoned by this government," Vijay said.The government is now considering alternative locations and plans to conduct technical feasibility studies before finalising a new site.
Why Vijay rejected Parandur
Vijay said he had visited Eganapuram and other villages on January 20, 2025, and heard the grievances of residents protesting against the proposed airport in Parandur and 12 surrounding villages."I stand firmly with the people protesting against the airport to be established in Chennai's Parandur and 12 surrounding villages," he said.
The chief minister said farmers were the backbone of the country and backed those protesting to protect their agricultural land.Vijay said he had also opposed the Parandur project at a public meeting in Vikravandi in October 2024, while making clear that he supported industrial development and the role of airports in it."However, this project should not be located in Parandur. The government must reconsider this project," he said.He added that an alternative site should be identified where the impact on agricultural land and people's livelihoods would be minimal.
Chennai airport to be expanded
While dropping Parandur, the government said Chennai's existing airport would be expanded.Vijay said the Meenambakkam airport, operated by the Airports Authority of India, currently has the capacity to handle around 30 million passengers annually. With the under-construction Terminal 3 becoming operational, capacity is expected to rise to 34 million passengers a year.The government plans to expand the airport on its north-western side by constructing a fifth terminal, which is expected to handle another 20 million passengers annually.The government is also considering alternative sites for a new airport, with technical feasibility studies to be conducted by expert teams.
Why Parandur was chosen
The Parandur project had received in-principle approval from the Civil Aviation Ministry in April 2025 for an International Greenfield Airport in Kancheepuram district.The proposed project had faced opposition from residents of villages that were expected to be affected by land acquisition and construction.However, the DMK has criticised the decision to abandon the project, arguing that it could hurt Tamil Nadu's industrial growth and investment prospects.Former chief minister and DMK president MK Stalin said dropping the project would set the state's development back by several years."The announcement made today by the Hon'ble Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu to drop the Parandur International Airport project will set the state's development back by several years. Tamil Nadu's interests cannot be mortgaged for petty political considerations," Stalin said.He also called the decision a setback to employment opportunities for Tamil Nadu's youth.
DMK warns of economic fallout
Former Tamil Nadu minister and DMK MLA Thangam Thennarasu also criticised the decision, saying the Parandur site was selected after studying options for establishing two runways."Possibilities for setting up two runways were all studied and only then Parandur was selected," he said.Thennarasu argued that scrapping the project for political reasons could hurt the state's economy and push industries towards neighbouring Andhra Pradesh."It would be best to have the airport at Parandur. Dropping the Parandur Airport project for political reasons will cause economic damage," he said."Many industries will move towards Andhra Pradesh. We have already lost the Hosur Airport," he added.Thennarasu also said compensation had already been provided to people whose land was acquired for the project and cited the Land Acquisition Act while arguing that the acquired land should be used for its intended purpose.
The announcement triggered an immediate confrontation in the Tamil Nadu Assembly, with DMK MLAs staging a walkout after Speaker JCD Prabhakar denied DMK leader KN Nehru permission to respond to the statement, citing Assembly rules.The opposition accused the government of making a policy U-turn that could affect Tamil Nadu's industrial momentum and prospects of attracting investment.Vijay, however, maintained that the government supports airport-led industrial development but believes the proposed airport should not come at the cost of agricultural land and people's livelihoods.

ALBAWABA - Since Vladimir Putin’s belligerent and illegal invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, there has been a rise in inexplicable attacks on various armament facilities across Europe, Putin is responsible, Western intelligence sources say.

A NATO official said: “In recent years, Russia has accelerated its destabilization campaigns against Allies through cyber attacks, assassination attempts and acts of sabotage,” in what appears to be an attempt to escalate tensions between NATO allies and deter support for Ukraine.

Taiwan environment ministry targets fraudulent grout pen ads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:17:29 UTC
19:17:29 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of Environment said Monday it has never certified or issued permits for grout pens, according to a ministry press release.
The ministry said advertisements on Facebook and YouTube were promoting mold-resistant and waterproof grout pens for bathroom and kitchen tiles while falsely claiming that the products had received ministry certification. It urged consumers not to be deceived by the ads.
A grout pen resembles a felt-tip marker and is used to cover discolored grout between tiles. The ministry said unscrupulous businesses had attempted to deceive consumers by falsely claiming official certification.
The ministry has notified Facebook and Google Taiwan to remove the ads, restrict access to them, or stop displaying them within 24 hours under Article 32 of the Fraud Crime Hazard Prevention Act. It has also asked the Ministry of Digital Affairs to contact Meta and Google’s US headquarters to remove the fraudulent content.
The ministry said consumers should look for the Green Mark when selecting environmentally friendly products. They can verify certified products through the ministry’s Net-Zero Green Living Information Platform.
Suspected fraudulent advertisements can be reported through the ministry’s environmental hotline or the Ministry of Digital Affairs’ online fraud-reporting platform.
The Green Mark is Taiwan’s most authoritative label for environmentally friendly consumption and is based on the principles of recyclability, low pollution, and resource conservation. More than 26,000 certificates have been issued.
The ministry encouraged consumers to look for the label when purchasing cleaning products, building materials, and daily necessities.

Historic Yunlin police bureau to become county history museum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:17:07 UTC
19:17:07 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — A historic former police headquarters in Yunlin County will be restored and transformed into the Yunlin County History Museum, with a ceremony Monday marking the start of the project.
The Yunlin County Government is investing NT$46.5 million (US$1.46 million) in the restoration and adaptive reuse project, which is scheduled for completion in February 2028, per CNA.
The future museum will feature permanent and special exhibitions, historical documents, and digital archives. It will preserve Yunlin’s historical memory while providing resources for research, education, and cultural exchange.
Yunlin County Magistrate Chang Li-shan (張麗善) presided over the ceremony. Chang said Yunlin County was officially established on Oct. 25, 1950, and the existing front building was completed in December of the same year.
The building was subsequently used by the Yunlin County Police Bureau and the Douliu Precinct, witnessing the development of local government and policing in the county.
It was registered as a historic building in 2019. After police operations were gradually relocated to newer facilities, the building became available for a new cultural role.
Chang said the restoration would follow the principles of preserving the original appearance and minimizing intervention while balancing historical preservation, structural safety, and the requirements of future use.
The museum will document Yunlin’s administrative development, local history, and cultural assets while incorporating material from the Yunlin County Gazetteer.
Architect Chen Po-hong (陳柏宏), who is supervising the restoration, said the project would preserve the front building’s postwar government-office characteristics, including its brick and timber construction.
Restoration work will preserve or repair architectural details including the entrance porte-cochere, pebble-finished exterior walls, wooden doors and windows, and window sills.
Structural repairs will include work on the roof tiles, doors, windows, and exterior walls. Water and electrical systems will also be upgraded, along with fire-safety and accessibility facilities.

Children’s Digital Rights Need More Than a False Promise of Safety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:12:01 UTC
19:12:01 KST

By Lisa Dittmer, Amnesty International’s Children’s Digital Rights Researcher, and Paloma Candia and Ahmed Dhman both Amnesty International’s Digital Rights Champions, a global network of child and youth human rights defenders.
This article was first published in TechPolicy.Press
Children’s online safety has become a leading political issue as concerns about Big Tech harms have moved from academic debates to bestseller lists and mainstream news. French President Emmanuel Macron hailed France’s teen social media ban as “leading the way in Europe in protecting our children and our teenagers.” France’s top court later blocked the law, citing privacy and freedom of expression concerns. United Nations (UN) Secretary-General Guterres has called for an artificial intelligence (AI) Child Safety Pledge. Yet amid the flurry of high-level pledges and the rush to protect “our children,” the voices of one demographic are noticeably absent: children themselves.
A brief prerecorded video aside, not a single child got to speak when a new state coalition for the protection of children launched its work at the UN AI Dialogue in July. Kenya, one of the state parties to the coalition, is currently debating a new AI bill that lacks any child-specific protections or consultation mechanism. The absence of children and young people in policymaking spaces and the failure to recognize their demands and needs are clearly linked. Globally, a mixture of Big Tech state capture, political shortsightedness and a rise in digital authoritarian practices is hollowing out children’s rights just as the world proclaims to finally making children safe online.
Mitigating harm rather than fulfilling rights
Children and young people are frequently treated as passive subjects who need to be saved through regulation rather than as participants in shaping the rules that affect them. The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child recognizes children’s right to be heard, but their participation all too often remains tokenistic at best. Inviting comments from a select number of children within predefined confines and without means to materially shape processes and outcomes isn’t meaningful participation.
It is this paternalistic attitude that increasingly reduces children’s digital rights issues to a question of mitigating harm, rather than the fulfillment of their rights and the creation of a positive digital future. While social media harms need urgent addressing, teen social media bans exemplify the resulting performative politics, which seek to appease an adult voter base rather than address the root causes of tech harms.
Child and youth campaigners have long called for solutions that address the manipulative design choices and the privacy violations common to children’s experiences across social media, games and AI chatbots. Youth-led organizations such as ctrl+alt+reclaim, Design it for Us and Flippgen have been vocal advocates for more nuanced solutions that reflect children’s and young people’s lived experiences.
And still, these calls for systemic change all too often go unheard as political leaders embrace supposed quick wins for “our protection.” Risks such as cyberbullying, grooming, online violence, and problematic social media use need to be tackled, but attempting to lock children out who also rely on these platforms for community, information and activism dismisses a whole set of rights for a false promise of safety. Evidence from Australia shows clear flaws in this thinking: children continue to access the harmful platforms they were meant to be locked out of while those who evade the ban or are never excluded remain exposed to the very harms the policy seeks to tackle. Meanwhile, core challenges to children and young people’s digital rights remain unaddressed.
The normalization of online surveillance in children’s lives
Children and young people are growing up in a world where their personal data is constantly collected, tracked and shared, from the moment online platforms and advertisers pick up on a pregnancy to their first exploration of the digital world through videos and games, and on to schools and universities, which increasingly monitor learners through safeguarding tools, biometric attendance registration and AI-enabled performance analysis and behavior management. In this way, children are trained to grow accustomed to surveillance by a largely invisible network of government and private actors, in most cases without free and informed consent.
Many of the same governments currently debating teenage restrictions on social media enthusiastically embrace the AI hype in education, inviting collaborations with major AI firms to bring chatbots into schools despite serious concerns about the lack of child rights safeguards related to online privacy, manipulative design, discriminatory and otherwise harmful outputs, as well as a lack of research evidence of educational benefits and risks.
Children’s data remains poorly protected and is now at risk of being eroded further by the age assurance tools necessary to enforce teen bans. The global drive is one towards stricter age checks, presenting new risks of additional data trails, cybersecurity incidents and online surveillance by both corporate and state actors. France just sidestepped the question of enforcement of its new teen ban law to avoid a clash with European regulation, but so-called Digital Identity Wallets will soon pervade online experiences across the EU, despite concerns from privacy experts.
Governments including Turkey, Vietnam and the United Arab Emirates are seizing the child online safety moment to propose measures that will further add to existing privacy and free expression concerns affecting child and adult internet users alike.
Casting governments as a force for good amidst increasing digital repression
The current debate also ignores the many ways in which governments actively abuse technology to monitor and silence children and young people. The recent wave of influential Gen Z protests across diverse contexts, including, among others, Bangladesh, India, Nepal, Kenya, Madagascar and Peru, has highlighted the power of digitally connected and social media-savvy youths.
On the flip side, governments are increasingly turning young activists’ social media footprints and data trails into tools of censorship and repression. When students took to the streets of Delhi to demand the resignation of the education minister, the Indian government responded by first shutting down mobile data service in central parts of the city, then came for the Bluetooth-based app that young people had turned to amidst the shutdown. In Kenya, Amnesty International documented how authorities weaponized online harassment and surveillance to quell nationwide youth-led protests in 2024 and 2025. Big data analysis tools are already taking state surveillance capacities to new levels, facilitating crackdowns on migrants and protesters alike.
All of these are critical challenges to the digital rights of children and young people, which the current narrow fixation on social media bans overlooks. Politics that attempt to shut out the youth instead of working with them will fail, as Australian teens and Indian students are powerfully proving.
Nothing about us without us
Children and young people finally need to be meaningfully included in all their diversity as critical experts of their own experiences if their rights and safety are to be more than a step toward increased internet control and willful disenfranchisement.
Instead of tokenistic one-off engagements, governments need to create opportunities for children to feed into digital policy processes in safe and meaningful ways, showing accountability for how their input is reflected in policy, just as tech companies need to co-design products with children if they are to be used by children.
Regulators should look to build towards a positive digital future, investing in digital literacy and creating policies that preserve and reward the benefits of the digital world, rather than simply mitigating harms. That means effectively safeguarding children’s and adults’ privacy, regulating online services by mandating meaningful user choice and agency and banning manipulative design, reigning in Big Tech power and setting effective limits on state surveillance powers.
“Nobody should have to choose between their safety and their voice,” Kenyan high school student Mark Igathe recently wrote in his winning entry to Amnesty Kenya’s annual digital rights essay competition. Policymakers would do well to make more space for those voices and to listen.

Ukraine’s offensive against Russia causes petrol panic across Central Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:11:19 UTC
19:11:19 KST

Ukraine’s offensive against Russia causes petrol panic across Central Asia
War-induced shortages set off cross-border fuel runs and deepen energy problems for Russia’s allies.
A Russian woman explained on camera what made her and a smiling, bearded man next to her drive to a petrol station in Kazakhstan.
“Simply to fill the tank,” she said in a viral video that explains new terms in today’s Russia: “fuel tourism” and “gas hunting”.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4‘Long-range sanctions’: Ukraine hopes strikes cause Russia fear and losses
- list 2 of 4‘New level of danger’: Drone incidents scare Europe amid Russia-Ukraine war
- list 3 of 4Russian expert warns of impending social crisis as Ukraine death toll rises
- list 4 of 4How China and Russia could hobble Trump’s plans to isolate Iran
For most of this year, swarms of Ukrainian drones have been burning down Russian oil refineries and fuel depots from annexed Crimea to the Baltic to western Siberia, causing sky-high plumes of putrid smoke.
As Russian President Vladimir Putin refuses to resume peace talks, claiming that his forces “advance in all directions”, tens of millions of Russians face fuel shortages and hours-long queues at petrol stations – with occasional shouting and fist fights.
And those living in regions bordering Kazakhstan – including a string of urban centres along the Volga River, Russia’s most densely populated region – drive to Central Asia’s most oil-rich nation, often hundreds of kilometres, just to fill up.
Even though in late May the Kazakh government banned petrol exports, border guards report thwarting hundreds of attempts to smuggle fuel back to Russia in canisters, makeshift fuel tanks – or in giant fuel trucks.
But some industrious smugglers still make their way across the world’s second-longest land border that stretches 7,644km (4,750 miles) across the barren steppe, according to people interviewed for this article.
“There’s total contraband along the border,” Timur, a businessman in Almaty, Kazakhstan’s capital, told Al Jazeera. He withheld his last name for safety reasons.
Even though Kazakhstan boasts three giant, Soviet-era oil refineries, fuel prices in Kazakhstan increased by 15.6 percent this year, the UlusMedia website reported on July 10 .
Only one of Kazakhstan’s neighbours, Turkmenistan, has large hydrocarbon reserves, but its autocratic leaders isolated the country from the rest of the region in the 1990s.
‘Deficit here for a long time’
Other Central Asian nations feel the ripple effect too – especially Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, resource-poor, mountainous nations that used to get up to 90 percent of their petrol from Russia.
“They’ve been hurt the most,” Galiya Ibragimova, a Moldova-based expert on Central Asia with Carnegie Politika, which is headquartered in Berlin, told Al Jazeera.
Kyrgyzstan is a member of the Eurasian Economic Union, the free trade bloc of five former Soviet nations dominated by Russia and the Kremlin’s political decisions.
Tajikistan is not a member of the group, but it bought discounted Russian fuel as “payment for political loyalty, not because Putin is so kind”, Ibragimova said.
A key source of petrol for Central Asia was Russia’s largest refinery in the city of Omsk in southwestern Siberia.
But it stopped operating after Ukrainian drone attacks in early July that damaged a crude distillation unit.
Around that time, Kyrgyzstan began regulating petrol prices and asked other ex-Soviet nations for help to “ensure sustainable fuel supplies”.
Kyrgyz experts predict long-term problems at Russian refineries will take months or even years to fix.
“Equipment for oil refineries is not a delivery from an online shop or a supermarket,” Kyrgyz energy expert Olzhas Baydildinov said in televised remarks. “The deficit that has come is here for a long time.”
The Kyrgyz government pledged to “provide at least a half” of Kyrgyzstan’s needs – but only after modernising the nation’s largest refinery, deputy energy minister Nasipbek Kerimov said in early July. He did not specify how long it would take.
By the middle of this month, Kyrgyz authorities said they had spent about $11.4m to subsidise petrol prices.
China’s help in drilling
Tajikistan is especially vulnerable because domestic oil processing amounts to 0.5 percent of petrol consumed there. Drivers already face fuel shortages and limits of 20 litres per car at some petrol stations.
“There are problems both in the [processing of oil] and in logistics,” deputy energy minister Daler Juma said in early July, when announcing that the government had amassed fuel reserves that would last “at least 60 days”.
In mid-August, he travelled to Tehran and signed a deal to provide 2.5 million tonnes of oil, petrol and diesel from Iran.
With the help of experts from the giant state-owned China National Petroleum Corporation, Tajikistan has intensified the search for prospective oil fields.
By the end of this year, they are due to submit a report on seismic reconnaissance, a method of quickly assessing potential oil reserves.
“Then, we will decide where we can start drilling,” Tajikistan’s chief geologist, Ilhomjon Oymukhammadzoda, told a news conference in early July.
Uzbekistan’s ‘reserves’ for winter
Both Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan used to resell Russian petrol to neighbouring Uzbekistan, the regional economic powerhouse with a population of almost 39 million and half a dozen car manufacturing companies.
As Uzbekistan processes its own oil into petrol satisfying about two-thirds of its needs, the rest usually comes from Russia. But the new shortages have forced the government to start amassing a strategic reserve.
“We have a separate plan for the fall and winter, we’ve created enough reserves. I can say with confidence that we have enough reserves for two or three months,” deputy energy minister, Umid Mamadaminov, said early last month.
Meanwhile, many Uzbek drivers are happy they switched their engines to run on compressed natural gas – even though huge gas tanks take up most of the boot.
“I switched 15 years ago, saved a lot of money,” Azamat Tolipov, a taxi driver in the Uzbek capital, Tashkent, told Al Jazeera.
Regional governments are trying to find new sources of oil and gas, but the United States and Israeli war on Iran drives global prices up.
“Central Asian nations will convulsively look for new suppliers, but considering what’s going on in the Strait of Hormuz, even if they find an alternative, it will be more expensive,” analyst Ibragimova predicted.
Beijing seems to be the only power to benefit from the fuel crisis as sales of Chinese-made electric cars skyrocketed even before it unfolded.
Electric car sales in Kazakhstan alone grew 36 times between 2022 and 2025, said the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, a Berlin-based think tank in last year’s report titled: “China has flooded Central Asia with electric cars”.

Wildfires erupted across three locations in the northwestern province of Bursa early Aug. 24, triggering a massive response from crews while authorities reported 12 arrests over nationwide blazes.
The fires broke out in Kestel district’s Derekızık and Aktaştepe neighborhoods and Yıldırım district’s Karapınar neighborhood, consuming pine forests along the skirts of Mount Uludağ. Authorities established 20-meter-wide safety zones along highways, stripping soil to mineral levels to stop discarded cigarette butts from igniting vegetation. Reforestation efforts in damaged woodlands yield a 95 percent success rate, preventing alternative land use.

Netherlands won't participate in Eurovision due to Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:07:17 UTC
19:07:17 KST

Breadcrumb
Netherlands won't participate in next year's Eurovision due to Israel
The Netherlands will not participate in next year's Eurovision Song Contest, its broadcaster said Monday, saying the event can "no longer be considered neutral" given divisions over the Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.
"It is undeniable that international conflicts are increasingly affecting the Contest, undermining its neutral character. The Eurovision Song Contest has therefore become a platform for division," said Taco Zimmerman, Director-General of AVROTROS in a statement from the broadcaster.
The contest has recently been hit by a wave of boycotts over Israel's participation.
Earlier this month, organisers announced they were excluding any country involved in an armed conflict from hosting the competition.
"However, the recently announced changes... do not provide sufficient confidence that the independent and neutral character of the Eurovision Song Contest has been restored," said the AVROTROS statement.
Israel came close to winning the competition in both 2025 and 2026, ultimately finishing second on each occasion.
Next year's event, the world's biggest live televised music event, will take place on 15 May in Bulgaria's Black Sea city of Burgas.
It will be the first time that the Balkan nation hosts the contest, coming after Bulgarian singer Darina Yotova, known as Dara, won this year's contest in the Austrian capital Vienna with the catchy floor-filler "Bangaranga".
Since its launch in 1955, Eurovision has become the ultimate pop platform, catapulting Swedish icons ABBA to worldwide fame, as well as boosting the likes of Celine Dion, Cliff Richard and Olivia Newton-John.
The 2026 competition was watched by 131 million viewers, down 35 million on the year before after five countries boycotted it over Israel's participation.
The Netherlands, Iceland, Spain, Ireland and Slovenia all pulled out of the contest, with the latter three refusing to broadcast the show at all due to Israel's inclusion.
The Dutch took part in the very first Eurovision Song Contest back in 1956, and have won on five occasions.
The most recent winner was Duncan Laurence whose song Arcade won the contest in 2019, going on to top charts globally.
It became the first Eurovision entry to reach one billion streams on Spotify, according to the Eurovision website.
The withdrawal is "painful as we would have very much liked to be part of the Contest again next year," said Zimmerman.
"As a public broadcaster, we remain committed to our values. They guide us in everything we do, even when that means stepping away from an event that is very close to our hearts," he added.

Russia’s Arkhangelsk Oblast governor outlines major projects with Belarus
Unknown

Alexander Tsybulsky
                    
                    MINSK, 24 August (BelTA) – Following his meeting with Belarusian President Aleksandr Lukashenko in Minsk on 24 August, Governor of Russia’s Arkhangelsk Oblast Alexander Tsybulsky told the media about major promising projects being discussed to develop cooperation with the Belarusian side, BelTA has learned.
The projects focus on industrial cooperation, transport, and logistics. “We discussed several major, highly feasible initiatives and areas. Together, we came to the conclusion that our current relations and bilateral trade are still far below their true potential. Our primary goal is to significantly boost this trade,” the governor said.
Alexander Tsybulsky first highlighted the potential for cooperation in the joint manufacture of forestry equipment, an area where both Belarus and Arkhangelsk Oblast have strong expertise. “At the end of last year, Arkhangelsk Oblast launched the production of harvester heads, which are complex components of forestry machines. We see great prospects here for collaboration with the Amkodor company,” he stated.
According to the governor, this partnership will help reduce dependence on imported equipment. Alexander Tsybulsky expects the two parties to achieve concrete results in developing this cooperation by the end of 2026. During the meeting with the Belarusian president, the parties discussed utilizing logistics routes through northern ports, particularly Arkhangelsk. “We see great potential in leveraging our current infrastructure. We have the capacity to handle up to 5 million tonnes of cargo and ship it further East via sea routes,” the governor noted. “We are also starting a major project to build a deep-water seaport in Arkhangelsk. This offers another avenue for collaboration, and we could even dedicate specific terminals for Belarusian cargo. As for railway tariffs, we have taken the initiative to address this issue with Russian Railways and the government.”
The discussion also focused on resuming direct flights between Arkhangelsk and Minsk. The governor noted that the Arkhangelsk Air Squadron will be the launch operator for the brand-new Ilyushin Il-114-300 regional passenger aircraft. “The first plane is scheduled for delivery at the end of this year, and we want to use these aircraft to establish a direct route between our capitals,” Alexander Tsybulsky said.
He also highlighted strong partnership in science and education, noting good opportunities for further collaboration. Additionally, the parties have a proven track record and bright prospects in construction and public utilities, with Belarusian elevators seeing strong demand in Arkhangelsk Oblast. Similarly, Belarusian food products and various other consumer goods remain highly popular.
Alexander Tsybulsky noted that he has been to Minsk many times and loves this city very much. “We follow the example of how a city can be kept in such cleanliness and order. One can come here and take masterclasses,” the governor said.

Father of Kahramanmaraş school shooting suspect faces 5.1 mln lira lawsuit

Turkish flags and memorial items adorn the gates of Ayser Çalık Secondary School in Kahramanmaraş following the tragic shooting.
The family of mathematics teacher Ayla Kara, who was killed in a school shooting in southern Türkiye, has filed a 5.1 million Turkish Lira ($106,000) compensation lawsuit against the father of the teenage suspect.
Kara was among 10 people killed when 14-year-old İsa Aras Mersinli opened fire at Ayser Çalık Middle School in Kahramanmaraş on April 15. Nine students and the teacher died in the attack. The teenager allegedly used firearms belonging to his father, police chief inspector Uğur Mersinli, who is currently in custody.
Following the completion of the criminal investigation and the filing of an indictment, Kara’s family launched separate civil proceedings against Mersinli, seeking compensation for their material and non-material losses.
A Kahramanmaraş civil court granted the family’s request to place a precautionary attachment on all of Mersinli’s assets, preventing them from being transferred or disposed of while the case proceeds.
In its ruling, the court cited provisions of Türkiye’s Civil Code concerning parental responsibility for harm caused by children to third parties. It also referred to established rulings by the Court of Cassation, which have treated a child under 15 gaining access to a firearm or other lethal weapon as potentially reflecting shortcomings in parental supervision, education and control.
The court stated that while parents may not face imprisonment for a homicide committed by a child under 15, they may nevertheless be held financially responsible for the material and moral damages suffered by the victims’ families.
Kara’s family subsequently filed a 5.1 million lira compensation lawsuit against Uğur Mersinli at the court.
Özcan Kara, the family’s lawyer and Ayla Kara’s brother-in-law, said they would continue their legal efforts to ensure those responsible for the circumstances surrounding the attack face the strongest possible legal consequences.
He said the compensation claim could later be increased once expert assessments establish the full extent of the family’s financial losses.

Psychology researchers uncover an unexpected benefit of dance training
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:00:39 UTC
19:00:39 KST

Individuals who practice dance may be better at regulating their physical actions when they encounter positive emotional situations. A recent experiment found that dancers were faster at stopping an ongoing movement when shown happy faces, an advantage not seen in people without dance experience. The research was published in the Psychology of Sport & Exercise.
The ability to stop a physical action you have already started is known as response inhibition. This is a core executive function of the brain that people use every day. For example, you use response inhibition when you suddenly stop yourself from stepping into a crosswalk because a car runs a red light.
Psychologists generally divide this ability into two categories. Proactive inhibition involves anticipating that you might need to stop based on your surroundings. Reactive inhibition, which is the focus of this research, involves abruptly canceling a physical movement in reaction to an unexpected external signal.
In daily life, people often have to inhibit their responses while dealing with emotionally charged situations. Emotional information can easily capture human attention. Sometimes this emotional distraction helps the brain process information faster, and other times it disrupts our physical focus.
Dance offers a unique way to study how the brain handles movement and emotion at the same time. Unlike running or weightlifting, dance requires precise musical coordination and active emotional expression. Dancers must constantly adjust their physical movements while conveying feelings and responding to the emotions of their audience or partners.
Researchers wanted to know if this combination of physical and emotional training gives dancers an edge in controlling their actions. Stuti Mehta and Rashmi Gupta of the Indian Institute of Technology Bombay designed a study to test whether emotional distractions affect dancers differently than non-dancers.
The researchers recruited 83 young adults for the experiment. This group included 45 dancers and 38 people with no dance experience. The dancers had at least six months of formal training and currently practiced for at least six hours a week.
To ensure that general fitness was not the cause of any observed differences, the researchers only included participants who reported low to moderate levels of regular physical activity. The two groups were matched in terms of their overall physical exercise habits.
Participants completed two computer-based tests designed to measure reactive response inhibition. In the first test, participants watched a screen and pressed a specific keyboard key when they saw the letter X or O. They were instructed to respond as quickly as possible.
Occasionally, a green circle appeared over the letter immediately after it was shown. This green circle was a signal to stop and withhold the key press. The computer constantly adjusted the timing of this circle in 50-millisecond increments to keep the task challenging, measuring exactly how fast the participant could hit their mental brakes.
The second test followed the exact same rules, but it used emotional distractions instead of a simple green circle. When it was time to stop the key press, a photograph of a face from a standardized psychological database appeared over the letter. These faces displayed happy, angry, or neutral expressions.
The emotional faces were entirely irrelevant to the core task of identifying the letters. The researchers used them specifically to see if background emotional information would unconsciously alter the participants’ ability to stop their physical actions.
After finishing the computer tasks, participants filled out several questionnaires. These surveys measured their current moods, their typical levels of stress and depression, and their general sensitivity to rewards and punishments in life.
On the first test featuring the green circle, the dancers and non-dancers performed identically. The researchers observed no statistically significant differences in their ability to stop their responses. Without emotional information present, dance training provided no measurable advantage for physical response inhibition.
Different patterns emerged during the second test featuring the human faces. Dancers were much better at stopping their actions when the stop signal was a happy face. They made fewer errors when viewing happy expressions compared to when they saw angry or neutral expressions.
The participants without dance experience performed the exact same way across all face types. The happy faces did not give them any advantage or disadvantage in stopping their physical responses. The emotional content of the faces simply did not alter their physical control.
The questionnaire results aligned with the performance data. Dancers reported lower levels of stress and depression than the non-dancers. They also reported experiencing positive emotions more often and showed a more regulated sensitivity to rewards.
Within the dancer group, the researchers found that more years of dance experience correlated with better mental health. The longer a participant had been engaged in formal dance training, the lower their reported levels of depression and stress tended to be.
The study authors suggest that dance training might make people more sensitive to positive emotions. Dance is often associated with expressing joy and experiencing a sense of meaningful contentment. This repeated engagement with positive feelings might train the brain to process happy stimuli more efficiently.
According to psychological models of attention, positive emotions tend to broaden our mental focus. Negative emotions, on the other hand, tend to narrow our focus onto specific threats. Because dancers are highly attuned to positive expression, a happy face might require fewer mental resources for them to process, leaving more brain power available to successfully stop their physical movement.
Prior brain imaging research supports this idea. Studies have shown that dance training increases activity in areas of the brain like the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and the amygdala. These regions are highly involved in managing emotion regulation and executive functions, which might explain the dancers’ rapid processing of the happy faces.
The study compared two different groups of people at a single point in time. This type of research cannot prove that dance training actually caused the improved response control. It is entirely possible that people who are naturally better at processing positive emotions are simply more likely to pursue dance.
The participants were also mostly young adults, which limits how these findings apply to children or older adults. The dancers practiced a variety of different dance styles. This variety makes it difficult to know if specific types of dance, like ballet or hip-hop, provide different cognitive benefits.
Future research could track individuals over time, testing their cognitive control before and after they enroll in a dance program. Researchers could also use brain imaging technology to see exactly which neural pathways activate when dancers process happy expressions during these tasks.
The study, “Happy faces, faster stops: The cognitive benefits of dance in emotional contexts,” was authored by Stuti Mehta and Rashmi Gupta.

The Art of Mess in the AI Era
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

Look closely at a painting, and you might be able to see where an artist changed their mind. Beneath the finished surface, there may be an abandoned line, a figure moved several inches to the left, a color that looked splendid in the morning and became unbearable by night. There may be a smudgy fingerprint at the edge of the canvas. The back may hold a date, a repair, uneven staples, a signature, or the name of a previous owner. These messy marks were once incidental to the artwork. Today they are considered evidence.
AI can produce an image in nano-seconds, then create hundreds of variations before a painter has mixed a color or cleaned a brush. Some of the results are technically bewildering and others inspire disbelief: How is this possible? Yet their abundance is changing our relationship to novelty. When nearly any visual idea can be summoned on demand, newness becomes easier to manufacture but harder to believe in. In an age of effortless images, the mess left behind by making something may become part of what makes it valuable.
So much recent visual culture can appear at once new and strangely familiar. Generative systems learn from immense archives of existing images, then assemble patterns according to statistical relationships. Their output can startle us, though the surprise often arrives cloaked in a recognizable visual fluency: the cinematic light, the dreamlike architecture, the glossy portrait or the eerily composed impossibility. After enough exposure, even the surreal can begin to feel conventional.
A study presented at the 2024 CHI Conference proffers one perspective about how this happens. Participants who used an AI image generator during a visual ideation exercise became more fixed on an initial example and produced fewer ideas, with less variety and originality, than those in the control group. The study involved only 60 people, so its findings should be treated cautiously, though they articulate something many artists and designers have begun to notice: a tool built to accelerate imagination can also narrow it by presenting a polished answer before a more difficult, original idea has had time to form.
Against this flood of frictionless imagery, fine art acquires another kind of presence. A physical artwork occupies time and holds emotion. An artist stood before it, considered it, changed it, ruined it, waited for it, and eventually decided to either finish or abandon it. All artwork contains a sequence of often messy choices that could have gone in any number of directions. The object becomes a record of attention, and attention is becoming one of the scarcest materials we have.
Researchers have already observed a version of this shift. Across six experiments involving 2,965 people, participants consistently valued art labeled “AI-made” less than work labeled “human-made,” even when the images themselves were identical. Awareness of the machine changed the perceived value of the human hand.
This preference extends beyond art. A 2015 study in the Journal of Marketing found that people considered handmade objects more attractive in part because they believed those objects symbolically contained the maker’s love. The participants were projecting on and responding to an imagined human presence embedded in the object, expressed through the perceived time and care required to make it.
Nostalgia is part of the current attraction to the handmade. We remember darkrooms, paste-up boards, paint-stained clothes, and the physical tools that digital technology has made unnecessary or irrelevant, and often forget the expense and tedium the processes demanded. Still, the renewed power of visible erasure or the pleasure of encountering an unrestrained line reaches beyond nostalgia. These marks allow us to envision the intent and the decisions behind them.
AI can attempt to imitate these marks. It can add a false thumbprint, invent pentimenti, reproduce a stray brush bristle, and generate an image that appears to have survived a century in an attic. But mess itself will soon prove very little. Provenance and an intelligible creative process will become more important as appearance ceases to represent authenticity.
In educated hands, AI can still become a profound artistic medium. Photography and digital tools have disrupted ideas about skill and authorship before becoming vehicles for extraordinary art. AI will be shaped by artists whose choices are specific enough to resist its defaults, and those artists may create work we cannot yet imagine. The presence of a tool has never settled the question of artistic value; the depth and consequence of the decisions made with it still matter.
We are entering a period in which polished images and endless variations are available on command. The works we retain or collect may be those that let us encounter another person’s limits: the place where control faltered or the artist had to surrender to something unresolved.
I think our nostalgia for mess is growing from a hunger for evidence that making something still requires time, effort, commitment, and—dare I say it—love.

The Best Multiuse Air Purifier for Home in 2026: BlueAir, Rabbit Air, Dreame

If you're tight on space or just want a more aesthetically pleasing machine, the best air purifier for home depends on your needs.
If you live in a small apartment like me, you may need to have a multifunctional air purifier for a practical reason: space. These compact, dual-purpose machines are useful if you are tight on square footage or don't want to shell out the money for two separate appliances. Or maybe you're aesthetically driven and want something that looks cool in your space rather than a clunky, large air purifier that can be an eyesore.
Regardless of the reason, these multiuse air purifiers look good, save space, and combine appliances into a single, energy-efficient device.

Featured in This Guide
Best Air Purifier That’s Also a Fan
This Dreo offers 99.97 percent HEPA filtration and an air quality sensor. You can control it with a remote, the Dreo app, Google Home, and Amazon Alexa. Best of all, the fan and purifier can operate independently, in case you need just one or the other or want to extend the filter lifespan (replacements run around $40). The 12-month warranty isn’t the greatest, but the device has been trouble-free for nearly two years in our long-term tests. If you're in the market for a fan and purifier in one, this model is definitely worth a look. —Kat Merck
Best Air Purifier That’s Also a Heater
Blueair’s small-room model is a little under 2 feet tall and has built-in heating and cooling. Blueair’s app is easy to use, and I preferred it rather than the actual control panel. The panel did not always illuminate when pressed, making the buttons difficult to use. The app also has more options, like controlling the oscillation speed and angle. Blueair uses both mechanical HEPA filtration and electrostatic technology to capture pollutants in the air. Its CARB certification is listed as electronic, unlike HEPA-only air purifiers that are listed as mechanical.
The ComfortPure 3-in-1 also has an air quality index indicator light that responds to the purifier's built-in sensor to measure particulate matter (PM) 2.5. The easy-to-miss sliver of light glows blue for excellent, green for good, yellow for moderate, orange for polluted, and red for very polluted. It has a control panel lock and filter change indicator light. I also appreciate the cloth handle that makes moving the Blueair easy. —Lisa Wood Shapiro
Best Air Purifier That’s Also a Vacuum
The Eye-Vac Air combines an air purifier with a touchless vacuum. Sweep debris up to the stationary unit, and it'll suck it up. It has two sets of HEPA and activated carbon filters pulling in air from both sides of the purifier. Its filter placement lets you position the Eye-Vac flush against the wall, which is especially useful in kitchen settings. The air filter can clean the air effectively, achieving five air exchanges per hour in a 120-square-foot space. While the large control panel is easy to read, the air purifier and vacuum offer only two options: manual or automatic. Indicator lights show when the bagless vacuum canister is full and when the air purifier filters need replacing. There are three fan speeds, but there are no color-coded indicator lights that correspond to air quality. Instead, three blue bars indicate the fan setting. —Lisa Wood Shapiro
Best Air Purifier That Doubles as Art
After testing a dozen or so air purifiers in my tiny apartment, I realized what an eyesore they can be. This air purifier doubles as art and, at the very least, a conversation piece. With such little space, I generally want my tech to be multifunctional, or at the very least look good. When my mom visited, she thought the MinusA2 was an art TV or a monitor with an art background, until it auto-engaged and ran on high after the Canadian wildfire smoke reached New York this summer. This air purifier comes in several artwork styles, including Monet's Water Lilies and Van Gogh's Starry Night, and can be easily hung flush against the wall by removing the bottom stand and using the included mounting bracket.
You can also customize the six-layer filter system inside, with options for a pet allergy-specific filter (which I opted for), germ defense for viruses and bacteria, a charcoal-enhanced odor remover, and a toxin absorber that reduces formaldehyde, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and harmful chemicals. Along with the custom filter, there is a reusable, washable prefilter; a medium filter for pollen and mold; a HEPA filter; an activated carbon filter for odor control; and a negative ion generator. The filters should last up to two years on average if the unit runs for 12 hours a day and is cleaned regularly. I didn't love that it doesn't have wheels or a handle, but it can be easily mounted if you'd rather display it off the floor. It was also super quiet, even on the highest fan speeds. With the remote or the buttons on the unit, you can change fan speeds or pick settings like auto, sleep, or pollen mode. On the front, there's also an odor sensor and light indicating air quality.
Best Air Purifier That’s Also a Sunrise Alarm Clock
The Mini Restful is part of Blueair’s Sleep Collection, and is nearly the smallest air purifier I’ve tested. Blueair claims the Mini Restful can effectively clean the air at the CDC-recommended five air changes an hour in a 140-square-foot space, but only at its highest setting. My sound level meter registered 60 dB—around the sound of a conversation. No one is sleeping with that noise—the Mini Restful is only quiet on its lowest setting. The sunrise alarm clock feature was easy to program through Blueair’s app, and it has nine sounds to choose from, like Midnight Rain, Happy Rise, and Mantra Breeze. I set the alarm to Nordic Flow, a blend of light harp strings and birds chirping. The alarm is designed to begin the subtle sunrise light anywhere from 15 minutes to 30 minutes before the selected wake-up alarm time. I set the alarm to 5 am and was woken by the light at 4:45 am. Even after moving it to my hallway, I could still wake up successfully to the pleasant sounds of Nordic Flow. —Lisa Wood Shapiro
Best Air Purifier That’s Also a Pet Bed
The PetAir is part of the growing market of pet-focused air purifiers. It has a Pet Mode that quiets the fan speed and reduces the air-cleaning capacity when it senses an animal friend is lying on the unit. It has a prefilter that collects pet hair, a high-efficiency H13 HEPA filter, and an activated carbon filter to capture VOCs and odors. There’s even a storage space for toys. It's only about 10 inches high and sits at ground level, so if you’re looking for a pet-specific air purifier, then this fan/airflow placement might be ideal. It can effectively clean the air with the recommended five air exchanges per hour in a 260-square-foot room. However, for general air purification, I prefer taller models as they seem to react more quickly to pollutants throughout a room, like those created by cooking. As for my two testers, I could not get either cat to lie on the bed successfully, but I did collect cat hair in the prefilter. I also wish the PetAir had a built-in heated pet bed, as I am sure my cats would have used it for warmth. —Lisa Wood Shapiro
Best Air Purifier That’s Also a Side Table
I was excited to try this air purifier/side table hybrid complete with a mood light and phone charger. At first I wanted to place it next to my bed, but as I read the fine print, I saw the SwitchBot Air Purifier Table needs 12 inches of clearance on three sides. Air purifiers, especially cylindrical models, need unobstructed airflow. The SwitchBot Air Purifier Table allows for one side to be 1 inch away from a wall, but not curtains. Those kinds of placement restrictions keep the air purifier from being a side table. If you don’t mind a small table that can stand against the wall, then the air purifier table might work for a small entryway or bathroom. It has both a HEPA filter and an activated carbon filter to remove odor and VOCs. And while the SwitchBot table can exchange the air in a 260-square-foot room at five times an hour, that would be at its highest, loudest setting. The ideal size for the SwitchBot would be more like a 100-square-foot space, such as a mud room, entryway, or bathroom. —Lisa Wood Shapiro

Why Choose a Multiuse Air Purifier?
Small-apartment dwellers need a multipurpose air purifier for a practical reason: space. These compact appliances handle two or more tasks to maximize efficiency, while possibly saving you money too. They also reduce cords, the need for outlets, and storage space when the machine is not in use during off-seasons. Or maybe you're more aesthetically driven and want something that looks cool in the space rather than a clunky, large air purifier.
How I Tested
I tested each model for nearly a month, moving it around my house to test in different locations: when cooking on my unventilated gas stove, under my living room window that draws in a lot of building and exhaust fumes, and outside my cat's litter box. I measured whether and when the air purifier auto-engages, and how long it takes to return to clean air quality. I also used an air quality monitor to check for pollutants and the purifiers' efficacy, and a decibel monitor app on my phone to measure noise level when the appliance is on high. I also tested each setting, paying special attention to the multipurpose features and whether they were actually useful or just gimmicky. When another tester reviews a machine, they use the same metrics.
What I Look For in a Dual-Purpose Air Purifier
One of the main things I considered when testing was whether the extra features were actually useful. Each recommendation on the list has been deemed successful in both air purification and its other marketed “dual-purpose” function. I also considered size and purification ability—that's why the fun terrarium isn't a top pick; while it's super cute, it's not as effective as an air purifier.

California to seek TV channel sales from Paramount: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
09:58:11 UTC
18:58:11 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
California Attorney General Rob Bonta is expected to ask Paramount to divest some TV channels and keep its movie studio separate from Warner Bros. as conditions for approving the $81 billion merger, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal on Sunday.
Bonta and Paramount CEO David Ellison are scheduled to meet Monday to discuss potential settlements to an antitrust lawsuit filed last month by California and 11 other states seeking to block the merger.
Lawyers for both sides met Friday to prepare for the talks, including discussions about Paramount’s cable and film businesses, according to the report.
The states argue the deal would create excessive concentration in theatrical movies and cable television, while also raising concerns about film and television production and employment.
Pressure is growing for the sides to reach an agreement. California Gov. Gavin Newsom and Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass have recently urged them to find common ground.
Paramount faces significant financial pressure to close the transaction. Warner’s agreement includes a “ticking fee” requiring payments of about $650 million per quarter to Warner shareholders beginning Oct. 1. If the trial proceeds as planned, Paramount could owe more than $1 billion.
Paramount has also indicated it could leave California if no agreement is reached before the fee begins, with Tennessee reportedly its preferred alternative.
 
Bonta has insisted on structural remedies, while Paramount has committed to 30 theatrical releases annually but has resisted selling assets or accepting management restrictions that could reduce merger-related savings.

The United States military said it struck a suspected drug-trafficking boat in the Pacific Ocean, killing two people.
