Strait of Hormuz traffic plunges as Iran, US blockades restrict energy shipments

03:56:04 UTC
12:56:04 KST

Fewer than 20 commodity vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz at the weekend, shipping data showed on Monday, as Iranian and US blockades restrict traffic through the chokepoint for energy shipments.
Four vessels crossed the strait on Sunday, initial data from shiptracker Kpler showed by 0228 GMT, with 13 on Saturday. The figures could change as some ships had switched off transponders on their way through.
That compared with Friday's figure of 16 transits, with two empty very large crude carriers (VLCCs) entering the Gulf with the tracking devices switched off, one heading to Iraq and the other to Bahrain, the data showed.
A VLCC carrying 2 million barrels of Emirati crude exited the strait on Thursday.
Eight very large gas carriers transited the strait over the past three days, the data showed, six of them entering empty while the others carried liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) loaded from Iran and exited the Gulf.
Traffic 'well below normal levels'
Overall traffic volumes remained suppressed in the week to August 21, as vessels aborted transit plans or switched routes through the strait's north after attacks, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said in a report.
A total of 89 vessels exited the strait while 103 entered over the seven-day period, the report, based on Automatic Identification System (AIS) data, showed.
"Traffic remains well below normal levels, with AIS-detected transits approximately 90% below pre-conflict baselines and declining since the June 24 to June 26 peak," it added.
Tanker traffic, at 45% of the total, continued to dominate movement through the strait, the agency said. Of these, 56% were tankers that carry crude oil, oil products or chemicals while LPG carriers accounted for a further 24%.
Since July 6, the UKMTO has reported 23 incidents of projectile strikes, leading to bridge, engine-room, and structural damage across vessels in the strait and its vicinity.
A total of 24 commodity vessels sailed through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on Sunday, down from Saturday's figure of 32, which was an increase from 22 on Friday, Kpler data showed.
Two VLCCs entered the Red Sea on Saturday with one carrying Iraqi Basrah crude and the other empty, it showed.

Syria to dismantle Assad regime's chemical weapons legacy 13 years after deadly attack - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
03:55:53 UTC
12:55:53 KST

Thirteen years after the chemical weapons gas attack on Ghouta, Syria's government says it is entering a new phase in dismantling the bitter legacy of the Assad regime’s chemical weapons program.
Statements issued over the past week by Syrian officials, together with the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), reflect a shift toward cooperation with international investigators and renewed efforts to hold those responsible accountable. The international community supports Syria in this endeavor.
The developments come as Syria continues its broader effort to rebuild relations with Western countries following the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024. They also represent one of the clearest examples of the new authorities in Damascus seeking to distinguish themselves from the previous government that ruled Syria for more than five decades.
According to SANA, Syria’s state media, Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Hassan al-Shaibani announced that Syria is beginning "a new phase" in dealing with the country's chemical weapons legacy.
"Tomorrow, the Syrian Arab Republic begins a new phase in addressing the burden of these weapons, as we have initiated the necessary technical and operational measures to eliminate them in cooperation with international partners," Shaibani wrote.
Ghouta attack symbolic of the Syrian Civil War
He added that the work would proceed along with efforts to identify those responsible for the attacks. This will mean efforts to prosecute the perpetrators, and hold them accountable. Why does this matter? The announcement coincided with the anniversary of one of the worst, most horrid, days of the Syrian civil war.
On August 21, 2013, rockets carrying a chemical sarin nerve agent struck areas of Eastern and Western Ghouta outside Damascus. This was an area held by the Syrian rebels. More than 1,400 civilians were killed, according to reports. Thousands more suffered poisoning and other affects.
The Ghouta attack became a key moment in the Syrian conflict. Images of families dying in their homes, children gasping for air, and overwhelmed hospitals circulated around the world. The attack showed the regime would use chemical weapons. It also gave the world a chance to stop the regime. However, the US, UK, and others held back from airstrikes. Hundreds of thousands more people would be killed in the war.
The Assad regime denied responsibility, feeding conspiracy theories.
The Assad family's rule, at the time, stretched back more than half a century. Hafez al-Assad seized power in 1970 and built an authoritarian state dominated by the Baath Party and the security services. After his death in 2000, his son Bashar inherited the presidency, promising reform but instead preserving much of the existing political system.
When peaceful protests erupted in 2011 as part of the Arab Spring, the regime responded by attacking the civilians. It received support from Iran, Hezbollah and Russia.
As the conflict intensified, allegations of chemical weapons use became increasingly frequent.
According to a statement published by SANA, more than 200 chemical weapons attacks occurred between late 2012 and the fall of the Assad regime, resulting in the deaths of more than 1,500 people.
International investigations by the OPCW and the United Nations attributed attacks to the Assad government, including the sarin attack on Khan Shaykhun in 2017 and chlorine attacks in other parts of Syria. The United States and Britain eventually responded with missile strikes targeting facilities linked to Syria's chemical weapons program.
OPCW Director-General Sabrina Dallafior said this week that recent discoveries of previously undeclared chemical munitions demonstrate both the scale of the remaining work and the importance of continued cooperation. According to SANA, Dallafior said discussions with Syria's ambassador to the OPCW had focused on the next steps, adding that recent progress showed "what can be achieved through serious cooperation."
She also emphasized that the OPCW remains committed to ensuring that chemical weapons never again inflict such suffering. The new Syrian government appears eager to demonstrate that cooperation.
Accountability in chemical attacks could change region's outlook
SANA reported that Syria has restored full cooperation with the OPCW following the fall of the Assad government and is now pursuing technical measures to eliminate the remaining elements of the former chemical weapons program.
Damascus says accountability will remain a central priority. Interior Minister Anas Khattab stated that authorities have already arrested several individuals connected to the chemical attacks while continuing efforts to locate additional suspects. "No criminal will escape punishment, regardless of how much time passes," Khattab said, according to SANA.
The emphasis on accountability extends beyond Syria. Syria is a symbol of how a country can do the right thing. France has become one of Damascus's principal partners in documenting crimes committed during the civil war. The joint Syrian-French statement commemorating the Ghouta anniversary reaffirmed both countries' commitment to combatting chemical weapons' use, the reports said.
The statement also described French President Emmanuel Macron's July 2026 visit to Syria as opening "a new phase" in bilateral relations after years of relations being broken due to the Assad regime.
For Syria's new leadership, confronting the chemical weapons legacy serves several purposes. It helps rebuild international credibility, for one.
Justice matters because chemical weapons are not simply another type of weapon. Since World War I, the international community has regarded them as uniquely bad because they deliberately inflict indiscriminate suffering on civilians. acceptable under any circumstances.
Holding those responsible accountable is therefore about more than Syria's past. It reinforces an international norm that has existed for decades. For Syria, accountability offers victims and survivors the possibility of justice after years of impunity.
For the region it is a test of whether one of the world's norms, the prohibition on chemical weapons, can ultimately be enforced. In a changing world order, this matters.

Workers in China worry over being replaced as they adapt to the growing impact of AI on jobs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
03:53:01 UTC
12:53:01 KST

Workers in China worry over being replaced as they adapt to the growing impact of AI on jobs
HONG KONG (AP) — Computer programmer Fei Zhaojun’s boss asked him if artificial intelligence could soon replace humans in coding jobs. Two weeks later, he was laid off from his job in Beijing, together with about 160 of his colleagues.
It’s an increasingly common scenario as artificial intelligence, supported by government policies, reshapes China’s massive job market. Some economists believe that might eventually undermine the overall strength of the world’s second largest economy.
Rapid adoption of AI in many fields, from computer programmers to script writing and physical tasks, is pushing people out of their jobs or leaving them afraid that it might. China is at the vanguard of AI adoption as government policies encourage people and businesses to use AI applications and robotics in all aspects of life, so people like Fei are figuring out how to adapt.
“There appears to be far less anti-AI sentiment in China (than elsewhere). Most people seem either positive, neutral, or mildly interested in AI,” said Shujing He, a Beijing-based senior analyst at advisory and research firm Plenum.
“Individuals who worry about being replaced, as well as those who have already left traditional workplaces, are often eager to experiment with AI-enabled businesses and independent ventures,” she said. “The level of interest is striking.”
Until recently, Fei had doubted AI could do programming work perfectly, even though his bosses thought it was close enough.
“Mid-level coders’ job are essentially replaceable in most of the cases,” said Fei, 40. “Even if it is a disaster that leads to replacing all humans, at this stage, you just have to use it as everyone else is using it.”
Now he’s making vlog-style short videos during a career break while figuring out what he wants to do next. He’s not making a living off of his videos, which are about ordinary people’s lives, but hopes that they might help others.
If you can’t beat them, join them
Du Qinchun, a part-time translator, has been helping to train an AI model to do translations. That’s brought him more work, at least temporarily.
“But it’s true that the pay in the industry has been cut by more than half compared to what it was years ago,” said Du, who is based in southwestern China’s Chengdu city.
The trend is so evident that popular college programs in foreign languages have increasingly fallen out of favor as AI-powered translation tools have become more widespread.
The share of Chinese industrial enterprises saying they use AI models and “agents” jumped to 47.5% last year from 9.6% in 2024, according to the market intelligence firm IDC.
“China’s vibrant open-source model ecosystem fosters greater AI application innovation in industrial settings, gradually closing the gap between foundational model capabilities and real-world enterprise value creation,” said Yanze Du, an IDC senior research manager in Beijing.
Humanoid robots can now, for example, sort parcels in postal centers, although still on a small-scale basis, and are pushing the boundaries in performing more human tasks such as directing traffic and making coffee. Food delivery robots are also gaining ground across the country, potentially threatening the livelihoods of millions of Chinese food delivery workers.
Generative AI increasingly is used for creation, production and distribution in China’s short drama industry. The number of live-action short and vertical video series designed for mobile phones fell about 75% in the first quarter of this year from a year earlier, according to Chinese media reports.
“Tasks that once required specialized training can now be performed by almost anyone with access to AI tools. This is particularly evident in software development and multimedia creation,” said Plenum’s He. “As a result, workers whose roles are narrowly concentrated in these areas may face greater displacement risk.”
A report from International Labor Organization, meanwhile, found that women face higher risks of losing employment due to use of AI than men, as they tend to work in areas more suitable for automation, such as assembling electronics, and remain underrepresented in science and technology.
AI has mixed effects on the slowing economy
Under China’s “AI Plus” initiative and its five-year plan through 2030, the government is pushing to infuse AI across many industries, aiming to gain an edge in China’s technology rivalry with the U.S.
“What is specific to China is that the government is really into diffusing AI across the economy, so AI may get into different domains more quickly comparing to other countries,” said Zilan Qian, a research associate at Oxford China Policy Lab.
China’s economic growth has already been slowing. Consumer spending has lagged partly due to people becoming reluctant to spend because they’re worried about losing their jobs. It’s added to problems stemming from a prolonged downturn in the housing market that has undermined household wealth.
China’s tech industries may be innovative with high productivity, but they may not generate many new jobs, said Eswar Prasad, a professor of economics and trade policy at Cornell University.
“AI is likely to lift productivity across the board but could have a severe disruptive effect on employment, worsening the employment growth problem and resulting in a detrimental effect on social stability,” he said.
Similar to their U.S. rivals, Chinese tech giants have cut or restructured tens of thousands of jobs, partly due to AI. The outlook for the broader jobs market remains uncertain: China’s overall urban unemployment rate hovers around 5%, but unemployment for people aged 16 to 24, excluding students, is roughly triple that.
That said, in the longer run, some experts say unemployment rates could fall, since China’s population of 1.4 billion is rapidly aging and shrinking.
By 2050, China is projected to have fewer than two working-age adults to support each retiree, compared with more than 2.5 in the U.S., said Xuenan Cao, a professor at San Francisco Bay University whose focus includes technology and society.
“Automation could partially offset a shrinking workforce rather than being purely a threat to it,” Cao said.
Some embrace AI to find new ways to make a living
Wang Zhicheng, 32, often used AI for brainstorming and fact-checking in his previous job as a scriptwriter for a company that produces 3D animated educational videos and interactive exercises for children.
After its parent company laid off roughly half of its 13 script writers, he chose to resign and work independently, making illustrated children’s books.
While AI sometimes saved time the scripts it generated, they often felt strange, Wang said. Episodes tended to be repetitive and formulaic and the level of detail devoted to knowledge varied widely.
“You can treat AI as a tool just like (Microsoft) Word,” said Wang, who has started his own studio making picture books and other creative works. “Humans are still the decision makers on which one to pick or pursue among all that AI generates.”
High school chemistry teacher Yang Zheng said he doesn’t consider AI as a threat to his job even though students use AI for help with their homework.
“Teachers cannot be there all the time,” he said. “It is a good thing for students as it generates in real-time so that students can ask follow-up questions,” said Yang, 29. “It often gets things wrong, but it improves over time.”
____
Fu Ting reported from Washington. AP video producer Wu Jia in Beijing contributed to this story.

Why Singapore’s Growing Political Diversity Matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
03:53:00 UTC
12:53:00 KST

Since the watershed election of 2011, one major trend in Singapore politics has been the growth of alternative political forces to the long-dominant People’s Action Party (PAP). General elections now resemble those in democracies, with all seats contested, rallies well attended, and election coverage widely followed across a range of media platforms. While the PAP remains dominant, since the 2020 election it has become expected that the opposition will match or beat its previous seat performance, currently at 10 elected parliamentary seats.
Civil society has also grown in size and significance since 2011, and “activist” is now less of a dirty word. A plethora of advocacy groups, many led by a new generation of activists, now actively champion and gain support for numerous causes such as political literacy, climate justice, death penalty abolition, media freedom, LGBTQ+ rights, workers’ rights, women’s rights, and justice for Palestine. As a prominent recent example, the work of environmental activists has helped increase public opposition to the government’s proposed developments at Maju Forest and Gillman Barracks in the name of environmental protection. These developments have all occurred despite a more challenging legislative environment over the last several years.
There is, however, a related second trend in Singapore politics that demands equal if not more attention than the first. This is the fact that the growth in size and significance of political alternatives to the PAP has come alongside the pluralization of these alternatives. While the opposition parties used to be discussed primarily in terms of their common goal of providing a check on the PAP, they now have more distinguishable ideological positions as well as perceived levels of competence and credibility amongst Singaporeans.
Alongside its growth, civil society has also experienced pluralization in a variety of ways. Besides the diversity of issues tackled, there is now a distinct division between formal registered civil society organizations and informal groups whose main form of institutionalization is their social media presence. This difference also somewhat overlaps with divergent views on the best way to engage in activism in Singapore. While formalized groups are more likely to utilize the more cautious path of “pragmatic resistance,” which involves strategic engagement with the state, informal groups are often more willing to treat the state as its adversary and confront it with sharper language and civil disobedience.
Discourses within civil society have also noticeably diversified. Communitarian ideas about the good of society and liberal rights-based framing remain prevalent, but younger activists are now much more comfortable adopting leftist frameworks and proposals. There are also clear differences of opinion in terms of what democracy really entails and, in turn, how much more democracy Singapore needs.
In some states in the region, like China and Thailand, there is a fear that the people have been “getting old before getting rich,” with aging populations potentially putting the countries at risk of stalling into a middle-income trap. Singapore, of course, faces no such concern about its standard of living. However, for proponents of a more politically open and competitive Singapore, there is a potential concern that the country may be “getting plural before getting democratic.” Paradoxically, greater political pluralization may make it more difficult to coordinate and build the type of broad coalitions required to pressure the ruling party into adopting political reforms.
Real disputes have indeed already emerged between civil society activists over these differences, including on how to protest the Singapore government’s ties with Israel in light of the genocidal massacres in Gaza. This debate is but one example of how diverse perspectives have also become more commonly expressed on matters of foreign policy. Recent anonymized interview research that I conducted with 12 Singaporean activists suggests that there is also significant diversity when it comes to civil society’s views on Singapore’s relations with other countries as well as global affairs more generally.
As countries across the globe look to Southeast Asia for new partnerships amidst the breakdown of the old international order led by the United States, it is important to get a sense of what these emerging voices think of foreign engagement with their countries. This includes their views on foreign support for the pro-democratic and rights-based work of civil society, a matter that remains highly sensitive to Singapore’s PAP government.
The PAP has always been averse to foreign “lecturing” and has long held the position that any foreign engagement with its domestic politics is “an absolute no.” In a July 2025 statement that is becoming increasingly commonplace in regional political parlance, the PAP was firm in its suggestion that “politics should stop at the water’s edge.”
In the interviews I conducted, it was unsurprising that Singapore’s civil society activists, who were selected for their pro-democratic and reformist orientations, have a different view from the PAP when it comes to foreign engagement on matters of human rights, social and environmental justice, and democracy. In fact, 10 out of 12 interviewees suggested that there is some role for foreign states to support their work on these issues. Only two participants took a firm line of completely rejecting foreign engagement on these matters, a position resembling the Singapore government’s own.
What was more revealing was the diversity of views on the ways in which foreign states can legitimately engage with Singapore on these issues. The responses of the 10 interviewees clearly fell along a spectrum between strong cosmopolitan or internationalist views on the one hand and more self-determination or anti-colonial positions on the other.
The three participants at the self-determination end of the spectrum strongly disagreed with foreign states bilaterally pressuring the Singapore government on matters of human rights and democracy. Western states in particular were singled out for their hypocritical stances on these matters considering their own human rights issues and polarization within their political systems. That said, these respondents still saw value in foreign states providing support to Singapore civil society through grants to attend overseas conferences and workshops for knowledge-sharing and capacity-building. They also encouraged foreign embassies to provide a space for civil society actors to gather, discuss, and meet with potential collaborators.
In the middle of the spectrum, four interviewees also argued against foreign states “naming and shaming” Singapore, albeit for different reasons. While the self-determination group argued against bilateral pressure in principle, the middle group of participants argued that such an approach would simply not work with the PAP in power.
Instead, foreign governments would find more success working constructively with the Singapore government, exchanging alternative policy proposals with evidence of effectiveness and making their own commitments to upholding human rights and environmental standards when investing. In terms of engagement with the ground, this group suggested that foreign states ought to go further, providing funding to civil society for specific projects and meeting with activists directly for information-sharing purposes.
The three participants on the internationalist side of the spectrum countered the PAP’s position on bilateral pressure most squarely, stating that foreign governments not voicing their concerns about rights and democracy legitimizes authoritarian structures, emboldens autocratic behavior, and gives a green light to human rights abuses. In addition to backing the aforementioned ways that foreign states can support Singaporean activists and advocates, this group argued that foreign embassies ought to vocally and visibly defend the already limited space for civil society when it is threatened by new repressive legislation or the embassies are pressured to cancel their events.
With such diversity in the political alternatives to the PAP, the next major breakthrough in Singapore’s political evolution may well depend on the extent to which these diverse actors are able to suture a common front capable of providing an effective counterweight to the PAP’s dominance. Part of this process will depend on finding sufficient commonalities, and perhaps even a common program, beyond the low baseline of wanting change.
One interesting point of convergence, at least within civil society, may be shared ideas regarding Singapore’s own foreign policy, including its relations both with its closest neighbors and the wider world. Remarkably, all 12 interviewees, including those who took a firm self-determination line regarding foreign engagement with Singapore, suggested that their own government must aim to be a better neighbor to its regional peers and a more principled actor on the world stage.
For the former, many interviewees called into question destructive sand-mining practices in Indonesia and Cambodia driven by Singaporean demand as well as Singaporean investment into a Myanmar economy dominated by the brutal military regime. For the latter, almost all participants wished to see a much stronger stance on Israel for its military actions in Gaza and beyond. One interviewee went as far as to state that: “I’m starting to get the sense that besides just pure economics and trade deals, there is a growing appetite for Singapore to have a spine and for Singapore to be on the right side of history.”
The Singapore government has already taken note of this shift. In response to Singaporeans’ reactions to events in the Middle East, Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan admitted that “foreign policy now has domestic salience.” Should this salience increase, the desire for a more principled foreign policy may well be one of many threads that stitch together the more vibrant, plural civil society and political alternatives to the PAP.

South Australia reports 2nd suspected mammal bird flu case in seal
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:43:40 CST
12:43:40 KST

CANBERRA, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- South Australian authorities on Monday reported a second suspected case of H5N1 bird flu in a seal, one day after the state reported Australia's first case in a mammal.
South Australia's Department of Primary Industries and Regions said on Monday that the long-nosed fur seal was found at the Pages Conservation Park, a protected area consisting of the North Page and South Page islands located about 18 km off the state's south coast.
The department said that samples have been sent to the Australian Center for Disease Preparedness for confirmatory testing.
It comes after the federal government on Sunday announced that Australia's first confirmed case of the highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza strain in a mammal had been confirmed in a long-nosed fur seal found dead in mainland South Australia on Wednesday.
South Australian Minister for Climate, Environment and Water Emily Bourke said that the two cases were incredibly concerning. The state government on Thursday said that over 1,000 birds had been found dead in suspected H5N1 mass mortality events on three islands, including North Page and South Page.
"We've seen devastation in seals around the world when it comes to bird flu," Bourke told Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) radio on Monday.
According to the National Parks and Wildlife Service, the Page islands are home to one of three large colonies of endangered Australian sea lions in South Australia. The Invasive Species Council has warned that the H5N1 outbreak could be an extinction-level event for the species.
Bourke said that the strain circulating in South Australia potentially arrived in the state from Heard Island, a remote sub-Antarctic Australian territory.
The Australian Antarctic Program said in June that around 13,000 of the estimated 17,000 elephant seal pups on Heard Island had died from H5N1 avian influenza.
Federal Minister for the Environment and Water Murray Watt told ABC television on Monday that the cases in seals were not unexpected and authorities expect to see more mass mortality events. ■

Feature: On the Gobi, western China's oil city Karamay serves up tennis dreams
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:43:36 CST
12:43:36 KST

by sportswriter Sun Zhe
URUMQI, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Karamay's name, derived from the Uygur language, means "black oil," reflecting the resource that shaped the city's development.
Rising from a remote stretch of the vast Gobi Desert, the city grew around its oil fields and developed into a modern industrial hub.
Beneath the vast skies of this once-isolated city, another passion has taken root. Over the decades, tennis has grown from a pastime for a small circle of enthusiasts into an established part of local sporting culture, turning Karamay into an unlikely center for the sport in inland China.
SEED TAKES ROOT
Karamay, in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, is one of modern China's most important energy bases. With a population of fewer than 500,000, the city is home to Xinjiang Oilfield, which has maintained annual crude oil production of more than 10 million tonnes for 24 consecutive years.
Like many of his peers, Alipjan Awut grew up in a family connected to the oil industry.
Inspired by the teamwork and determination of the oil workers around him, he found joy in pursuing a common goal on the football pitch. As a midfielder, he led attacks and captained his primary school team.
"Football is a team sport. It tests cooperation and brings different people together," said the 36-year-old. "But nothing can surpass tennis in my heart."
As oil workers from across China settled in the Gobi city, they brought with them their lifestyles and hobbies. Since the 1980s, tennis has gradually taken root in Karamay, growing from a pastime among a small group of enthusiasts into a sport embraced by the wider community.
At 12, Alipjan got his first taste of tennis when a PE teacher spotted his athletic ability and invited him to pick up a racket for Karamay's first citywide school tennis competition.
"At that time, we didn't even have our own rackets. The school provided them. I just thought it was fun," Alipjan recalled.
After just over a month of training, he finished fifth in the city competition, turning his initial curiosity into a lifelong passion.
With few professional coaches available, Alipjan found his own ways to improve. Whenever a tennis tournament was broadcast on television, he would sit in front of the screen, studying every detail of the players' movements, footwork and technique.
The sport also took him beyond his hometown. During school holidays, coaches brought young players from Karamay to eastern Chinese cities with stronger tennis programs, where the team often drew curious looks.
"They were often surprised to see players from Xinjiang on the tennis court," Alipjan said. "We knew there was a gap, but we wanted to change that perception."
GROWING UNDER SUN
After graduating from university, Alipjan returned to his hometown and became a tennis coach at an amateur sports school.
As part of efforts to make tennis more accessible, Karamay expanded its facilities. A sport once constrained by a lack of courts now has nearly 40 venues across parks, communities and schools, some capable of hosting national competitions.
Alipjan has become busier than ever. More than 100 young players now train at his school, many of whom discovered tennis through short tennis programs offered at local schools.
"Those with potential will be selected into our elite training group, and they do not need to pay any fees," he said.
Among the young players he coaches, one stands out: Alfudin Hasimjan, his younger cousin. Before turning seven, Alfudin had never seriously played any sport, but he quickly fell in love with tennis.
"I don't know why, but I feel like I have some talent for tennis," the youngster said with a smile.
At 14, Alfudin is already over 1.8 meters tall and has won titles in his age group in Xinjiang. He spends almost every summer day on the court, where the intense Gobi sun has left him deeply tanned, but his passion remains undiminished.
"It is a sport under the sun," Alipjan said. "Whether they play for fun or dream of going further, we hope children can stay active. That is what we want to achieve."
As more young players picked up rackets, tennis became increasingly embedded in Karamay's sporting identity. The city has since been recognized by Chinese tennis media as one of the places with the greatest potential for the sport's growth.
BEYOND THE GOBI
At the ongoing 15th Xinjiang Games, nine regions sent under-18 players across two age groups, marking a record turnout. Karamay remains a strong force, but its dominance is facing growing challenges.
Once numbering fewer than 50 players, Xinjiang's youth tennis community has now grown to about 500, with specialized clubs emerging to provide greater support for the next generation.
"Urumqi, the regional capital, is developing quickly, with more courts, coaches and families embracing tennis," Alipjan said. "I'm not worried. The more people play, the stronger Xinjiang tennis will become."
Still, Alipjan knows Karamay has a long way to go to reach the level of the world's leading tennis regions. For him, that gap has always been motivation to improve.
In 2024, Alipjan became a senior coach certified by the Chinese Tennis Association. For him, building a tennis ecosystem in Karamay remains a long-term endeavor.
"Honestly, it is a long process," he said. "But one day, I hope players from my team can also step out of Xinjiang and represent this region on a bigger stage." ■

China, Kuwait hold tea culture exchange event
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:43:20 CST
12:43:20 KST

People participate in the Chinese & Kuwaiti Tea Art and Treats Tasting event at the China Cultural Center in Kuwait in Hawalli Governorate, Kuwait, Aug. 23, 2026. (Photo by Asad/Xinhua)
KUWAIT CITY, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- More than 150 people gathered Sunday evening at the China Cultural Center in Kuwait for the Chinese & Kuwaiti Tea Art and Treats Tasting event, where they savored teas and sweets and learned about tea-making traditions in both countries.
Jointly organized by the China Cultural Center in Kuwait and Kuwait's National Council for Culture, Arts and Letters (NCCAL), the event was part of Kuwait's 18th Summer Cultural Festival. It aimed to introduce Chinese and Kuwaiti tea traditions and promote cultural and people-to-people exchanges between the two countries.
Attendees sampled Chinese green, black, white and oolong teas, accompanied by Chinese sweets. A separate tasting area featured Kuwaiti and Arab beverages, including karak tea, loomi tea and Moroccan mint tea, along with local and Arab sweets.
In his speech, Chinese Ambassador to Kuwait Yang Xin noted that this year marks the 55th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between the two countries, and cultural exchanges constitute "a bridge connecting the hearts of the two peoples."
Speaking to Xinhua at the end of the event, Yang said the occasion represented "a window into China's time-honored culture and a means of promoting cultural exchanges and friendship between China, Kuwait and the Arab world."
NCCAL Secretary-General Mohammad Al-Jassar noted that presenting Kuwaiti and Arab tea traditions alongside Chinese tea reflects the links between cultures and shared daily customs.
The Chinese tea ceremony opens a window into an authentic aspect of Chinese culture and showcases rituals and values passed down through generations, Al-Jassar said.
Liu Jinhong, director of the China Cultural Center in Kuwait, said the center was pleased to see "tea as a bridge to introduce the rich tea cultures of China and Kuwait," noting that the tradition of welcoming guests by serving tea represents a shared value between the two cultures.
Kuwaiti tea cultural expert Sarah Maher AlMajed, a certified tea sommelier and tea master, gave a presentation on Arab tea culture, beginning with an overview of the trade and cultural routes through which tea spread from China to the Arab world.
Nasser Alsaqer, a Kuwaiti enthusiast of Chinese tea culture, shared his experience of studying tea-making in China. He explained the process of Chinese tea production, from picking fresh leaves through processing and manufacturing.
The event also featured a tourism booth showcasing routes and resources related to tea culture in China. It was part of the Tea for Harmony program organized by the China Cultural Center in Kuwait throughout 2026. ■

Shin Bet must protect Eisenkot before political violence brings Israel another tragedy - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
03:20:51 UTC
12:20:51 KST

Israel knows the devastating effects that incitement and political violence can wreak on the fabric of a taut society. It can tear it in two.
One only has to look back to November 4, 1995, when prime minister Yitzhak Rabin, the target of vicious incitement campaigns over his support of the Oslo Accords, was gunned down by far-right ultranationalist Yigal Amir. Israel has not been the same ever since.
Although the country has not experienced another political assassination, the specter remains always just under the surface. Security for elected officials was heightened, and warnings from Israel’s security services about the threat of political violence have accompanied every election campaign since that dark day in November 1995.
That’s why the decision, as reported by N12 on Saturday night, by Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) chief David Zini not to provide Yashar Party head Gadi Eisenkot with a security detail is so perplexing and worrisome.
Eisenkot has emerged as Benjamin Netanyahu’s leading challenger in the October 27 poll. The decision was reportedly made despite regular threats directed at Eisenkot on social media and warnings from the defense sector that Iran and other hostile actors may attempt to target current and former senior officials.
Eisenkot’s campaign field director wrote to Zini and other security officials in June saying the Yashar leader had been forced to hire a private security firm because he was not receiving state protection.
According to the N12 report, Zini’s representatives told Eisenkot’s staff that while the Shin Bet would not provide him with a security detail, the agency would assign a liaison and gather intelligence if concerns emerged about an exceptionally serious incident. However, the request for permanent protection was denied.
Netanyahu, Lapid, leading candidates in 2022 election, both received full security detail
In the last election campaign in 2022, both leading candidates, Yair Lapid and Netanyahu, were provided with full security details - Lapid as sitting prime minister and Netanyahu as a former leader as part of the lifelong package for past heads of government.
Following Zini’s decision, Eisenkot’s campaign submitted its objections in writing to the Shin Bet, Israel Police, and the attorney-general, warning that physical threats against the former IDF chief of staff were escalating, and he called for the decision to be reversed.
“The atmosphere on the Israeli street, as well as on social media, is becoming increasingly heated, and threats are emerging and multiplying,” the letter said.
Just last week, N12 reported that Zini was considering providing Eisenkot with an armed detail amid indications that Iran was increasing efforts to harm Israeli leaders as elections drew close.
The decision not to grant Eisenkot state protection during the campaign is playing with fire. One only has to scroll on social media or watch one of the TV news talk shows to see that the level of vitriol on all sides of the political fence is reaching alarming proportions.
Zini's decision politically motivated?
The suggestion has been raised by the Eisenkot team that Zini’s decision was politically motivated. The letter sent by his team in protest alleged that the government, the Ministerial Committee on Shin Bet Affairs, and the committee’s chairman “are failing to fulfill their personal responsibility for political and ulterior motives and are avoiding carrying out their duties.”
Eisenkot’s campaign further alleged that a consideration in denying the security detail was a desire to avoid images of Eisenkot looking “prime ministerial” by appearing in public surrounded by security personnel – images which could boost his stature in the public eye.
Although that sounds somewhat conspiratorial, it’s worth noting that the chairman of the Ministerial Committee on Shin Bet Affairs is Netanyahu, and its members consist of Defense Minister Israel Katz, Justice Minister Yair Levin, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, and Education Minister Yoav Kisch.
Zini has already faced claims that he’s a Netanyahu appointee who has pledged allegiance to the prime minister. Now is the time to smother those charges and demonstrate that the decisions of the Shin Bet are being made with solely professional considerations in mind, and not according to political alliances.
Granting Gadi Eisenkot a state security detail leading up to the October 27 election is the surest way to clear the air. And more importantly, doing so will help ensure that another devastating national tragedy has less of a chance of taking place.

Taiwan labor insurance rate to rise to 13% in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
03:13:12 UTC
12:13:12 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The labor insurance contribution rate will rise by 0.5 percentage point to 13% in 2027, reaching the statutory ceiling under the Labor Insurance Act.
The increase will raise insurance costs for employers and workers nationwide, with nearly 626,000 businesses expected to incur an additional NT$13.147 billion (US$413 million) in costs next year, while more than 10.51 million workers will see higher rates, per UDN.
Under the current system, the 13% rate includes a 1% employment insurance component, meaning the ordinary labor insurance rate itself will rise to 12% next year. Labor insurance premiums are shared among employers (70%), workers (20%), and the government (10%).
Premiums are calculated according to an insured salary scale rather than directly on an employee's actual salary. The maximum monthly insured salary for labor and employment insurance is NT$45,800.
With the average insured salary of NT$36,511, the 0.5% increase will raise an employer's monthly contribution by an estimated NT$127.79 per worker. Workers will pay an additional NT$36.51 per month, or about NT$438.14 annually.
The increase is expected to generate approximately NT$23.021 billion in additional labor insurance revenue annually.
Employers are also preparing for a possible minimum wage increase next year. Businesses have argued that mandatory labor-related contributions already represent a significant financial burden.
Labor insurance provides social security coverage for insured workers, including eligible foreign and migrant workers. Benefits include payments for ordinary injury or sickness, disability, old age, and death, per a Bureau of Labor Insurance press release.
For ordinary injury or sickness, eligible workers can receive benefits equal to 50% of their average monthly insured salary for up to six months, with an additional six months available under certain conditions.
Occupational injury and disease benefits are now administered separately under the Labor Occupational Accident Insurance and Protection Act. Eligible workers can receive compensation equal to 70% of their average monthly insured salary, subject to statutory limits and conditions.
Labor insurance also provides old-age benefits, including monthly pension payments or lump-sum benefits for eligible workers. Disability and survivor benefits are available to qualifying insured workers and their families.

CHICAGO (AP) — Former NBA center Enes Kanter Freedom was ejected from Sunday night’s Indiana-Chicago WNBA game after he was confronted by Sky guard Natasha Cloud late in the third quarter.
Freedom was sitting along the baseline. He had on a black shirt that read “WOMAN noun. adult human female.”
The Fever called for a timeout after Cloud scored inside with 1:22 left in the third. Cloud then did a chest bump with teammate Aicha Coulibaly before turning around and walking in Kanter’s direction.
Cloud, 34, started yelling and pointing at Kanter, 34, as she approached him. A standing Kanter held his arms out and took one step on the court as security and a handful of Sky players moved in between the two.
“There was just a fan incident and the security handled it, and we’re just going to focus on the game,” Chicago forward Azura Stevens said after the Sky’s 113-90 loss.
Chicago coach Tyler Marsh said Cloud was concerned about being a distraction for the team.
“I told her she wasn’t,” Marsh said. “I told her that we all embrace her as someone that protects our team and protects people that need to be protected and so Tash is always going to stand on that, and we stand for Tash.”
Freedom stopped near the basket to plead his case to security as he was escorted from the court area. He spun around while holding his shirt out and encouraged the crowd to respond as he walked toward the front lobby.
He had a conversation with a group of police officers before departing Wintrust Arena.
“I didn’t see it, we were talking about the next play in our huddle,” Indiana star Caitlin Clark said, “so I think that’s probably a question for Chicago.”
Cloud met with team and league security after the game. She did not speak with the media.
The WNBA has been the subject of recent debates on whether transgender women — people assigned male at birth who transition to align with their gender identity — should be allowed to participate in the league. There has never been such a player in the WNBA.
Although the league’s collective bargaining agreement says the WNBA is restricted to women, it contains no more specific language about gender identity or sex assigned at birth.
Fever guard Sophie Cunningham said in an ESPN profile published last month that she was opposed to transgender girls and women competing in girls’ and women’s sports. Freedom and Royce White, another former NBA player, have declared themselves eligible for the WNBA draft, saying they identify as women.
Kanter joined a small rally in support of Cunningham outside the arena before the game.
Asked if he had a message for Kanter, Marsh praised the league and its players.
“If you come to a game you should probably come to enjoy the basketball,” he said, “and that seems pretty simple to me. I think these players deserve that and have earned that. Being a former basketball player, you should probably understand and feel that too.”

The net income of local banks stood at 13.8 trillion won (10.0 billion U.S. dollars) in the January-June period, down 6.4 percent compared to the same period of last year, according to the Financial Supervisory Service.
Their interest income grew 8.3 percent to hit the first-half high of 32.2 trillion won on the back of higher net interest margins (NIM) and larger interest-bearing assets.
The NIM gained 0.04 percentage points to 1.56 percent in the first half on a yearly basis, while the interest-bearing assets swelled 6.4 percent to 3,628.1 trillion won.
Non-interest income dipped 43.4 percent to 2.9 trillion won as securities-related earnings swung into a deficit amid rising interest rates.
Amid lingering inflationary pressure, the Bank of Korea lifted its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.75 percent in July, marking the first monetary tightening in about three and a half years, since January 2023.
Loan-loss expenses rose 8.6 percent to 3.5 trillion won in the cited period.
Return on assets for domestic banks, a key gauge of profitability, retreated 0.10 percentage points to 0.65 percent, and the return on equity declined 1.15 percentage points to 8.89 percent. (1,000 won equals 0.72 U.S. dollars) ■

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan plans to continue its mental health support initiative in 2027, with NT$429 million (US$13.5 million) proposed for the effort, Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) said Sunday.
Launched in August 2024, the scheme provides people aged 15 to 45 with three free counseling sessions. The allocation is expected to benefit about 100,000 people next year, according to UDN Money and the Ministry of Health and Welfare.
The service was introduced as suicide rates among young and middle-aged people have risen in recent years. Health ministry figures point to growing psychological strain linked to the demands of fast-paced modern life, according to Health News.
The 15-to-45 age group encompasses several major life transitions, from education and entering the workforce to relationships and starting a family. Clinical psychologist Hsu Chun-wei (許峻維) said common concerns discussed in counseling include daily stress, interpersonal and romantic conflicts, academic and workplace demands, and difficulties related to career changes. Symptoms of depression and anxiety are also frequently reported.
Hsu said psychologists and psychiatrists are among the professionals involved in the initiative. The three free sessions are designed to allow participants to discuss their difficulties and, when necessary, connect them with appropriate social resources.
The service is available to Taiwanese citizens aged 15 to 45 as well as foreigners eligible for Taiwan's National Health Insurance. Eligible individuals can make appointments by phone or inquire about the service directly at participating medical institutions, Hsu said.
More than 80,000 people had used the service by the end of October 2025, receiving more than 200,000 counseling sessions. The number of participating institutions had also increased from 523 when the scheme launched to 616.
Funding for the initiative is included in the Cabinet's recently proposed NT$3.9 trillion central government budget for 2027. The package includes more than NT$1 trillion each for national defense, social welfare, and local governments, along with additional allocations for 10 major areas, including cash payouts, population policies, and public infrastructure, according to Capital Futures.

====================================================================================================

Can Kenya’s AI ambitions coexist with Naivasha’s water needs?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
02:09:40 UTC
11:09:40 KST

Can Kenya’s AI ambitions coexist with Naivasha’s water needs?
As Kenya courts data-centre investment, communities fear growing pressure on an already stressed water system.
Naivasha, Kenya – For communities living around Naivasha, water is not an abstract resource. It sustains families, livestock, farms and schools.
That reality has taken on new significance after plans for a major Microsoft-G42 data centre in Olkaria, near Lake Naivasha, stalled in May 2026 over concerns about available power capacity.
Microsoft and United Arab Emirates-based artificial intelligence company G42 announced the project in 2024 as part of a $1bn digital investment package for Kenya. The proposed facility was to run on geothermal energy and eventually scale to as much as 1 gigawatt of capacity.
The uncertainty has also prompted questions about what another major industrial user could mean for water in a region where residents already report shortages.
Microsoft and G42 said the proposed data centre campus would run entirely on renewable geothermal energy and incorporate water conservation technology. The companies did not disclose a project-specific water consumption figure in their 2024 announcement.
Kenya Electricity Generating Company (KenGen) communications director Frank David Ochieng told Al Jazeera that the data centre remains at the design stage and that he could not comment further until the project is ready to proceed.
For residents like Musa Olorkedienye, who spoke to Al Jazeera, water scarcity is already a daily concern. He says communities around Olkaria have seen changes in access to water, including the loss of reliable piped supplies that residents previously received from KenGen.
“Currently, we are relying on water vendors to get water, our animals are walking for kilometres, and we fear things could get worse as demand for water rises,” Olorkedienye says.
Pastoralist Isaac Leshishi, who also spoke to Al Jazeera, says increasingly harsh weather is adding to the pressure.
Why Olkaria?
The choice of Olkaria was closely tied to energy. The area is home to Kenya’s major geothermal operations, making it an attractive location for a power-intensive facility.
KenGen operates the Olkaria geothermal complex, while Microsoft and G42 planned to power the proposed data centre entirely with geothermal energy.
A lake under pressure
Naivasha is a freshwater lake in Kenya’s Rift Valley whose catchment supports agriculture, tourism, livestock and domestic water use. Its basin also hosts geothermal development and other economic activity.
Grace Kimani, a patrol leader with Lake Naivasha and Oloiden, told Al Jazeera that the reservoir is under growing pressure from population growth, agriculture, water abstraction, climate variability, pollution and ecosystem degradation.
“The planned Microsoft-G42 data centre in Olkaria could bring jobs and investment, but its water demand raises concerns about adding pressure to already competing needs, particularly during dry periods,” she said.
Kimani said there is limited public information about the project’s expected water demand, source and cooling technology. She said transparency and an assessment of its cumulative impact on water resources would be important.
She also called for water-efficient or water-free cooling, water recycling and the use of treated wastewater, as well as sustainable abstraction limits and community involvement in monitoring.
Silas Wanjala of the Lake Naivasha Riparian Association, who spoke to Al Jazeera, said the region is heavily dependent on groundwater and that declining water flows are adding to the pressure.
“These industries, especially EcoCloud, which deal with data, will consume a lot of water at a time when rivers are drying, and demand for water is on the rise,” Wanjala said.
Olkaria EcoCloud Data Centre is a local partner in the G42-led development. In 2024, the Kenya News Agency reported that G42, Microsoft and EcoCloud signed a letter of intent for the wider data-centre initiative, with EcoCloud described as a local partner that had previously signed a memorandum of understanding with G42.
Wanjala points to past fluctuations in Lake Naivasha as a warning.
“This lake in 2010 nearly dried up due to over-abstraction, and this could be repeated due to high demand for water by these investors in Olkaria,” he says.
His concern comes against a wider backdrop of water scarcity in Kenya. The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations says Kenya has about 527 cubic metres (527,000 litres) of freshwater available per person, below the 1,000-cubic-metre threshold for water scarcity, and estimates availability could fall to about 475 cubic metres per person by 2030.
The figures do not show what effect the proposed data centre would have on Lake Naivasha. They provide context, however, for why the prospect of another major water user is drawing scrutiny in a region where demand is already high.
How much water would it use?
The amount of water the proposed Microsoft-G42 facility itself would require remains unclear.
The project announcement provides no projected consumption figure.
Existing industrial use offers some context.
A KenGen environmental and social impact assessment records that 195,165 cubic metres of water were abstracted from Lake Naivasha in July 2023 for domestic and commercial uses at Olkaria and for operations and domestic use at Eburru.
Of that total, 153,918 cubic metres were used for commercial operations at Olkaria. The assessment records the abstraction as within Water Resources Authority (WRA) permitted levels.
Those figures relate to existing KenGen operations, not the proposed data centre.
For farmer Eskimos Kobia, who spoke to Al Jazeera, the potential competition extends beyond households and livestock. He says farmers, pastoralists, schools and investors will all face greater pressure as demand increases.
Kimani said climate variability has also led to fluctuations in lake levels, with periods of flooding followed by prolonged dry conditions.
“Water quality is affected by agricultural run-off, untreated wastewater in some areas and invasive species,” she says.
Investment versus local concerns
Not everyone in Naivasha opposes the investment.
Absolom Mukhuusi of the Naivasha Professional Association, who spoke to Al Jazeera, says the technology sector could bring jobs, infrastructure and new businesses to the area. But he says economic benefits should not come at the expense of local communities.
“Even as we welcome the investors, our biggest fear is what happens to our water bodies and communities as water is diverted to Olkaria for the heavy users,” he says.
Could technology help?
Geologist Kenyatta Otieno, who spoke to Al Jazeera, sees another potential benefit.
He recalls the pressure large flower farms once placed on the lake’s ecosystem, saying many have since left or scaled back their operations.
Otieno says the proposed centre would have included a resource centre to monitor lake levels and weather patterns. Such monitoring, he says, could help identify the highest water level over time and guide riparian land zoning.
“The centre being built with water conservation in mind would be futuristic as Naivasha is generally a water-scarce area. It would be a model for future development,” Otieno said.
Kenya already has regulators responsible for managing competing demands. The WRA regulates water abstraction and issues water-use permits, while the National Environment Management Authority (NEMA) oversees environmental impact assessments under the country’s environmental regulatory framework.
Attempts by Al Jazeera to obtain comments from WRA and NEMA officials were unsuccessful. Efforts to reach Microsoft-G42 officials and Kenyan government officials for comment on the project’s status and water requirements were also unsuccessful.
For now, the project’s eventual scale, design and water requirements remain unclear, according to KenGen.
“We are now competing with the multibillion [-dollar] companies for water, and we fear that we shall be the losers in the long run,” Leshishi said.

Ebola cases in DRC hit 5,515 as Pope Leo urges global action to save lives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
02:02:28 UTC
11:02:28 KST

Ebola cases in DRC hit 5,515 as Pope Leo urges global action to save lives
Case fatality rate climbs to nearly 48 percent in the DRC, meaning almost one in two people infected with Ebola are dying.
DR Congo miners risk Ebola to make a living
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has reached 5,515 confirmed cases of infection and killed 2,642 people, with 51 new cases detected in Ituri and North Kivu provinces, according to the latest government figures.
The update on Sunday came as Pope Leo called for international action to help contain the epidemic, which is now the deadliest Ebola outbreak in the DRC’s history.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3How the deadliest Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak can be stopped
- list 2 of 3DR Congo miners risk Ebola to make a living
- list 3 of 3Ebola continues to spread in the DRC as 16,000 vaccine doses arrive
Declared in mid-May, it is the DRC’s 17th Ebola epidemic and was designated a Public Health Emergency of International Concern by the World Health Organization (WHO), its highest alert level, also covering neighbouring Uganda.
The outbreak is now on track to surpass the deadliest Ebola epidemic on record, which was the 2014–2016 outbreak in West Africa that killed more than 11,000 people.
According to government figures, the case fatality rate in the DRC has climbed from about 20 percent in early June to nearly 48 percent now, meaning almost one in two people infected are dying.
Contact tracing, however, has improved sharply, from 30 percent in June to more than 85 percent.
The disease has also proved deadly for those fighting it. About 160 health workers have been infected, and about 45 have died, according to the WHO.
Efforts to contain the outbreak, however, have been hampered by armed conflict in the affected provinces, displacement, attacks on medical personnel and facilities, a mobile working population and a lack of critical infrastructure.
Vaccines arrive in DRC
There is no approved vaccine or treatment for this particular strain of Ebola, known as Bundibugyo, which is rarer than the virus type behind most past outbreaks.
The WHO has pledged 70,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine, which is licensed for Ebola and has been effective in past outbreaks. According to the global body, early data from animal trials suggest it may offer some protection against Bundibugyo.
Some 16,250 doses of the vaccine arrived in the DRC on Friday.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and other officials said the response in the DRC needs to be scaled up two to threefold to contain the outbreak and reach every affected area.
They also called for more support and protection for front-line health workers, including protective equipment, timely payment, and access to rapid diagnosis and high-quality supportive care if they fall ill.
Abdulsalami Nasidi, a public health consultant who helped establish the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, told Al Jazeera that the outbreak was “getting out of hand”.
He blamed weak infection control measures and a lack of trust between authorities and affected communities for the continued transmission.
“This is no longer just a national or regional issue; it is a global issue. If it spreads to neighbouring places with lower immunity, it will be a disaster,” Nasidi added.
The WHO currently rates the risk to the global public as low, but warns that the danger inside the DRC remains very high.
Despite the surging cases, Uganda and several health zones in DRC’s Ituri and South Kivu have interrupted transmission, which the WHO said is evidence that rapid detection, decisive leadership, and community cooperation can break the chain of transmission.
At the Vatican on Sunday, Pope Leo offered prayers for the DRC, “in light of the spread of the Ebola epidemic, which is sadly claiming many lives”.
The pontiff also called for global action to help save lives.
“I urge the international community to respond in a way that also involves local communities in prevention efforts to save as many lives as possible,” he said.

Sean Grayson, former Illinois deputy convicted of killing Sonya Massey, dies in prison, lawyer says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
01:53:01 UTC
10:53:01 KST

Sean Grayson, former Illinois deputy convicted of killing Sonya Massey, dies in prison, lawyer says
CHICAGO (AP) — Sean Grayson, a former Illinois sheriff’s deputy whose fatal shooting of Sonya Massey inside her home became a flashpoint over police use of force, died Sunday while serving a 20-year prison sentence.
Grayson’s attorney, Daniel Fultz, confirmed that his client died earlier Sunday but declined to provide any further details.
Grayson, 32, was convicted of second-degree murder in October in the fatal shooting of Massey, a 36-year-old Black woman who had reported a possible prowler outside her Springfield-area home. Body camera video of the July 2024 encounter showed Massey crouching in her kitchen and apologizing moments before Grayson shot her in the face.
He was sentenced in January to the maximum 20 years in prison.
Grayson had been diagnosed with colon cancer before Massey’s killing, and his attorneys said at his sentencing that the disease had spread to his liver and lungs. In May, only months into his sentence, he sought medical release under an Illinois law for prisoners with terminal illnesses or serious medical conditions. The Illinois Prisoner Review Board denied his request last month.
Massey called 911 early on July 6, 2024, to report someone prowling outside her home. Grayson and another Sangamon County sheriff’s deputy responded.
Video showed Grayson directing Massey to remove a pot of hot water from the stove. As she held the pot, Massey told the deputies, “I rebuke you in the name of Jesus.”
Grayson threatened to shoot her, drew his handgun and ordered her to drop the pot. Massey apologized and ducked behind a kitchen counter before Grayson fired three times.
The other deputy, Dawson Farley, later testified that he did not consider Massey a threat and drew his own weapon only after Grayson did.
Grayson was fired after the shooting and charged with first-degree murder. Jurors convicted him of the lesser charge of second-degree murder after Grayson argued that he feared Massey would throw the hot water at him.
Massey’s killing drew national attention and protests and raised questions about how Grayson had moved through several law enforcement agencies before being hired by the Sangamon County Sheriff’s Office.
Illinois lawmakers later passed the Sonya Massey Act, requiring law enforcement agencies to more closely review an applicant’s previous employment records before hiring an officer.
The Justice Department also opened a civil rights investigation after Massey’s death and later reached an agreement with Sangamon County, its sheriff’s office and other agencies requiring changes to policing and emergency response. Those changes included additional training for interactions with people with behavioral health disabilities and development of a mobile crisis response program.

Libya's Presidential Council refers UN reports on illegal oil exports to prosecutor

TRIPOLI, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Libya's Presidential Council Chairman Mohamed al-Menfi has referred United Nations reports on oil smuggling and illegal exports to the country's Prosecutor General Al-Siddiq Al-Sour for investigation, according to an official statement released Sunday.
The reports, issued by the UN Security Council's Panel of Experts, allege illegal exports of crude oil and petroleum products, fuel smuggling and the diversion of fuel from designated channels. They also contain information on entities and networks allegedly benefiting from proceeds generated by such activities.
Al-Menfi called for a comprehensive and independent judicial investigation, particularly into Arkenu Chemicals Company and related entities and individuals for possible criminal offenses.
The referral also demands probes into the contracts and arrangements cited in the reports, including the quantities of oil involved, revenues generated and beneficiaries, and whether such revenues entered the state's official financial channels.
The Presidential Council further requested tracing related funds and assets inside and outside Libya and activating international judicial cooperation mechanisms.
It also stressed the need to safeguard evidence and protect witnesses, experts and whistleblowers involved in the investigations. ■

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of National Defense tracked two Chinese military aircraft, seven naval vessels, and two official ships around Taiwan between 6 a.m. on Sunday and 6 a.m. on Monday.

How has AI and tech changed your life? Australians share their stories — as it happened
Technology is creeping into every facet of our lives. Whether it is for better or for worse is in the eye of the beholder, but it is certainly here to stay.
Australians are grappling with the prospect of AI replacing jobs, breaching privacy, and creating misinformation and digital exclusion, while also developing technology designed to make everyday tasks easier.
We heard your stories and experiences in our live blog below, plus put your questions to Curtin University cybersecurity expert Mihai Lazarescu and the ABC's AI reporter Cam Wilson.

You're not the only one worried about this! Power is probably the thorniest issue facing policy makers right now. Water, too, is a concern although I would say not to quite the same scale.
It boils down (no pun intended) to the fact that AI needs an enormous amount of power to be trained and to run. It's a huge, unanswered question about whether we can source enough power to feed all the data centres that companies are proposing, let alone sourcing that new capacity with renewables.

AI may be tightening jobs market, but some roles could see stronger demand
While AI is fast becoming ubiquitous in everyday life, there's still limited evidence it has caused widespread job losses.
That's according to a recent Deloitte report, which dubbed 2026 "the year of AI" and offered hope to some occupations it predicts will see a stronger demand when combined with AI.
Those jobs, which are listed below, includes roles like CEOs, teachers and nurses where "AI can boost productivity, but the human element is still critical," Deloitte Access Economics partner David Rumbens said.
However, the list of jobs most exposed to AI has also grown.
What was once concentrated in clerical and administrative roles now extends into professional and managerial occupations, many requiring higher levels of education and expertise.
You can read more of this story by the ABC's national work reporter Bronwyn Herbert.
Key Event
Can workplaces use AI to record us?
My manager has advised that our calls will soon be recorded for preparing training data. I'm concerned about giving my voice, my words, to my workplace and AI vendors to have ownership over. Can workplaces own our words, and can this part of our identity just be harvested and given away?
- Sam
As workplaces integrate AI into everyday technology, people are weighing up the benefits versus concerns. ABC's AI reporter Cam Wilson has answered this question from Sam.
That's an interesting (and a little unsettling) one! The short answer is there might not be a lot you can do.
The longer answer is there's a bit of law that can impact recording for AI training. Some Australian states have laws against one person in a conversation recording the other without permission. There's Australia's privacy law, which essentially rules that, most of the time, data can only be used for the purpose that it is collected for. But if your boss has told you about it and made it clear it's for training AI models, neither of those protections would apply.
My suggestion would be to ask for as much information as possible about what they're collecting and for what purpose. Then you can go see your union or community legal centre for some advice. Also, please send me an email because I am very interested in this, too!
Regional and remote communities still dealing with mobile black spots
We've been talking a lot about how new technology has been impacting Australians.
But what about when they lose access to old technology?
The Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman recently made several recommendations for how telcos, government and regulators could improve services in regional areas, after analysing 27,000 complaints made over two years.
The complaints included a loss of coverage since the 3G network was shut off, unacceptable delays in connections and repairs, and concerns about Triple Zero (000).
ABC's Lauren Pezet spoke to NSW resident Gerry McLaughlin.
Living on the Princes Highway on the NSW South Coast, Mr McLaughlin's reception can be patchy, but when it does drop out he can still call 000.
So, it came as a shock earlier this year when he spotted a new satellite symbol on his phone.
"It said this function only has the ability to send text messages, move to an area of mobile coverage if you need to ring Triple Zero," he said.
He was concerned calling may no longer be an option, especially given he is in a bushfire-prone area that was razed during the Black Summer bushfires.
"I rang [Telstra] up and they told me that if you need emergency service, just text a friend and get them to call it."
Let us know if you have any questions about mobile coverage or the digital divide.

I use it for a lot of research in every aspect of life ... I also use it for writing short poems and restoring old photos.

Has AI become integral to our lives in the same way email and mobiles have?
In my circles AI is derided and mocked. I hope the bubble bursts soon. Do any of you feel it'll become integral to our lives in the same way email and mobile phones have?
- Jay
Thank you, Jay. The ABC's AI reporter Cam Wilson has tackled this one for you.
There are definitely a lot of strong feelings about AI at the moment! I suspect the raft of highly visible, AI-powered features being shoved into a lot of popular apps and products is probably contributing to this.
My guess is that AI, specifically the generative AI tech that's been popularised in the past three years, will be a big part of computing for a long time to come. And, as it becomes more ubiquitous, it'll also fade into the background like other forms of computing.
Like, we don't talk about the neural networks in mobile phone cameras processing, we just say "oh my camera is better in low light". Similarly, I think we'll just be like "here's a new app" or "here's a new feature".

Take AI results 'with a mountain of salt', our guest expert says
How can we ensure that AI does not return content (or worse make decisions) based primarily on companies that pay the AI provider the most to search their data. Eg: similar pricing model to search engines. In short, how can we avoid bias based on profit.
- Ian Bertram
Good question, Ian! Associate Professor Lazarescu has an answer below.
There is no way to avoid bias in the results, and yes, money will be a big factor.
It is, in my opinion, a critical issue with all the models that are being trained in the sense that one can manipulate the training to get a specific outcome.
To make matters worse, the vetting of the training data is non-existent. The models just read in what they are "fed" and no-one has the means or time to check if the data is correct or valid.
My advice is to take everything that the AI generates with a mountain of salt.

It's a good question! We know Australians are increasingly using AI as companions or for emotional support, particularly younger generations.

That's not necessarily a problem or something unique to AI. I'll dob myself in and say there's been (plenty of) times when I've stayed in rather than go out to watch a movie. But, clearly at some point, over-reliance on AI as a companion can become a problem.

Could AI help us detect diseases earlier?
It's clear not everyone is in the anti-AI camp. Stephen Pech from Adelaide is one person we've heard from who believes AI has a lot of potential to make our lives better, particularly in healthcare.
He's working to develop AI-powered technology designed to detect osteoporosis and coronary disease in regular chest x-rays, which is currently being studied in conjunction with Flinders University.
"It's really about proactive, preventative medicine," he said.
"We're taking a chest x-ray that you would have had for a completely different reason, for example a respiratory issue or an injury. While that's being looked at for that reason, we're also looking at it for other reasons.

Rush to vaccinate little penguins against H5N1 as another seal is diagnosed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
01:22:08 UTC
10:22:08 KST

In brief
- Five suspected H5 bird flu cases were recorded in South Australia on Monday, including a long-nosed fur seal.
- 5,000 little penguins in Victoria are receiving a vaccine to protect them against the deadly virus.
Bird flu has likely spread to a second seal, one day after the first mammal in Australia was confirmed to have contracted the virus.
Five suspected H5 bird flu cases were recorded in South Australia on Monday, including a long-nosed fur seal at The Pages Conservation Park, the state's Department of Primary Industries and Regions said in a statement on Monday morning.
The Pages — which covers two small islands between Kangaroo Island and the mainland — is a haven for the endangered Australian sea lion.
The fur seal has been tested for bird flu, with results expected in the coming days.
The first positive case of the virus in a mammal was confirmed on Sunday in a long-nosed fur seal at Beachport, 300km south of Adelaide, which authorities believed was contracted from wild birds.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Before the new case was announced, Environment Minister Murray Watt said the spread from birds to mammals was inevitable and the government was examining whether further vaccination programs were needed.
"We are likely to see mass mortalities of birds and mammals, and I know that is a very distressing thing for Australians to hear. But we also need to be realistic," he told ABC TV on Monday.
"This is what we've seen happen overseas. Australia is very fortunate that we've been the last continent on Earth to have this strain of bird flu happen. But we are likely to see those kind of events as we have overseas."
Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said the federal government was investigating whether bird flu vaccines were available for use in mammals.
"There are trials underway in North America, in California and Hawaii, and this is using a vaccine that's been developed for cattle," she told ABC radio.
"There certainly is nothing commercially available, but we do continue to look at that research."
Bird flu vaccinations have been rolled out to at-risk species, including the little penguins on Victoria's Phillip Island.
Many were corralled into pens to receive the first of two vaccinations on Sunday night.
With case numbers on the rise, authorities have stepped in to do what they can to defend the 5,000-strong colony.
The penguins' nightly ritual of returning to the same burrow, along the same path, made them ideal candidates for vaccination, Phillip Island Nature Parks reserve manager Ben Thomas said.
As a world-first in scale, the process has taken some experimentation and fine-tuning.
"We've had our teams out late into the night for a week now and learning a lot along the process," Thomas said.
"We started on some of the quieter penguin pathways to fine-tune the whole process and get it working as quickly as we can, so we can process as many penguins as we can each night.
"We've now moved to the western end of the penguin parade, where the larger numbers are, and it's working really well."
A further 600 penguins were vaccinated over the weekend, taking the total number that have received a first dose at Phillip Island and St Kilda to about 1,000.
